front: How can a "pluralizer" function use a dictionary of irregular plurals (`person` → `people`) and fall back to adding `s`?
back:
Create the function once with the dictionary (a closure), and when pluralizing, look the word up first and fall back to the default rule:

```js
const isPlural = num => Math.abs(num) !== 1;

const pluralizer = (dictionary = {}) => (num, word) =>
  !isPlural(num) ? word
  : Object.hasOwn(dictionary, word) ? dictionary[word]
  : `${word}s`;

const pluralize = pluralizer({ person: 'people', child: 'children' });
pluralize(0, 'apple');  // 'apples'
pluralize(1, 'person'); // 'person'
pluralize(3, 'child');  // 'children'
```

`Object.hasOwn` matters: a plain `dictionary[word] || ...` finds inherited properties, so `pluralize(2, 'constructor')` would return a *function* instead of `'constructors'`. A `Map` avoids the problem too. For real i18n, a library with `Intl.PluralRules` is the robust choice.

One solution:

```js
!isPlural(num) ? word : Object.hasOwn(dictionary, word) ? dictionary[word] : `${word}s`
```

The outer function captures `dictionary` in a closure, so callers only pass `(num, word)`. `Object.hasOwn` avoids picking up inherited keys like `constructor`; `` dictionary[word] ?? `${word}s` `` works for most words but has that edge case.

front: What does `String.raw` do, and why does the template literal `` `C:\web\index.html` `` not produce the path you typed?

back:
One solution:

```js
const path = String.raw`C:\web\index.html`;
```

`String.raw` is a template-literal tag that skips escape processing, so each `\` stays in the string. The alternative is doubling every backslash in a normal string: `'C:\\web\\index.html'`.

front: How do you generate a random alphanumeric string of a given length in JavaScript, and when is `Math.random()` not good enough?

back:
One solution:

```js
  return Array.from(bytes, b => chars[b % chars.length]).join('');
```

`crypto.getRandomValues` fills the array with cryptographically strong random bytes (0–255); `b % chars.length` maps each to an index into the alphabet. `Math.random().toString(36)` is shorter but predictable, so never use it for tokens or passwords.

front: What do the regex anchors `^`, `$`, `\b` and `\B` match, and why are they called "zero-width"?
back:
Anchors match *positions*, not characters, so they consume nothing ("zero-width"). `^` is the start of the string, `$` the end (with the `m` flag: start/end of each line), `\b` a word boundary (between a word character and a non-word character or the string edge), and `\B` any position that is *not* a word boundary.

```js
'cat catalog'.replace(/\bcat\b/g, 'dog'); // 'dog catalog' (whole word only)
'a\nb'.match(/^\w/g);   // ['a']
'a\nb'.match(/^\w/gm);  // ['a', 'b'] (m: ^ at every line start)
'catalog'.replace(/\Bat/g, 'AT'); // 'cATalog' ("at" not at a word start)
```

`\b` is the easy way to do whole-word search and replace. Like `\w`, it is ASCII-based, so it treats `é` as a non-word character.

front: What do the regex quantifiers `?`, `*`, `+`, `{n}`, `{n,}` and `{n,m}` mean, and what changes when you add `?` after one (e.g. `+?`)?
back: They say how many times the previous item may repeat: `?` 0 or 1, `*` 0 or more, `+` 1 or more, `{3}` exactly 3, `{3,}` 3 or more, `{3,5}` 3 to 5. By default they are *greedy* (take as much as possible); adding `?` makes them *lazy* (take as little as possible). ```js 'x'.match(/<.+>/)[0]; // 'x' greedy: runs to the last > 'x'.match(/<.+?>/)[0]; // '' lazy: stops at the first > /^\d{3,5}$/.test('1234'); // true ``` A quantifier applies only to the single item before it: `ab+` means "a, then one or more b". To repeat a sequence, group it: `(?:ab)+`.

front: In a regex, what is the difference between `(ab)`, `(?:ab)`, `(?<name>ab)` and `(a|b)`?
back:
All parentheses group, so a quantifier or `|` applies to the whole group. `(ab)` also *captures* the text (available as `match[1]`), `(?:ab)` groups without capturing, `(?<name>ab)` captures under a name (`match.groups.name`), and `|` inside a group chooses between whole alternatives, not single characters.

```js
'2024-03'.match(/(\d{4})-(\d{2})/).slice(1); // ['2024', '03']
'grey gray'.match(/gr(?:e|a)y/g);            // ['grey', 'gray']
/^(?:ab)+$/.test('ababab');                  // true
```

`(cat|dog)` matches the word "cat" or the word "dog". For single-character choices, a class like `[ea]` is simpler and faster.

front: What do the JavaScript regex flags `g`, `i`, `m`, `s`, `u`, `v`, `y` and `d` do, and which one makes `test()` behave statefully?
back:
- `g` global: find all matches (and makes the regex remember `lastIndex`)
- `i` ignore case
- `m` multiline: `^`/`$` match at each line start/end
- `s` dotAll: `.` also matches newlines
- `u` Unicode: enables `\p{...}` and treats emoji as one character
- `v` (ES2024) an upgraded `u` with set operations in classes
- `y` sticky: match only at exactly `lastIndex`
- `d` hasIndices: adds start/end positions of groups

The stateful one is `g` (and `y`): `test()`/`exec()` continue from `lastIndex`, so reusing one regex gives alternating results.

```js
const re = /o/g;
re.test('foo'); // true  (lastIndex is now 2)
re.test('foo'); // true  (lastIndex 3)
re.test('foo'); // false (resets to 0)

/a.b/.test('a\nb');  // false
/a.b/s.test('a\nb'); // true
```

Drop `g` when you only need a yes/no `test()`.

front: What do the regex character classes `.`, `\w`, `\s`, `\d`, `[abc]`, `[^abc]` and `[a-z]` match?
back:
Each matches exactly one character:
- `.` any character except line breaks (unless the `s` flag is set)
- `\w` a word character: `[A-Za-z0-9_]`; `\W` the opposite
- `\s` whitespace (space, tab, newline, Unicode spaces); `\S` the opposite
- `\d` a digit `[0-9]`; `\D` the opposite
- `[abc]` one of a, b, c; `[^abc]` any character except those
- `[a-z]` one character in the range; ranges combine: `[a-zA-Z0-9]`

```js
/\w/.test('é'); // false: \w and \d are ASCII-only
/[.]/.test('x'); // false: inside [...], '.' is a literal dot
```

Escape special characters with `\` to match them literally outside a class (`\.`, `\(`, `\[`, `\/` in a literal). For letters in any language, use `\p{L}` with the `u` flag.

front: How do you remove accents from a string (`'Exupéry'` → `'Exupery'`), and how does `normalize('NFD')` make it possible?
back:
Call `str.normalize('NFD')`, which splits an accented letter into its base letter plus a separate "combining" accent mark, then delete the marks with a regex for the combining range `\u0300`–`\u036f`.

```js
const removeAccents = str =>
  str.normalize('NFD').replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, '');

removeAccents('Antoine de Saint-Exupéry'); // 'Antoine de Saint-Exupery'
'é'.length;                  // 1
'é'.normalize('NFD').length; // 2 ('e' + combining acute)

removeAccents('Łódź Øresund straße'); // 'Łodz Øresund straße'
```

Letters like `Ł`, `Ø` and `ß` are separate letters, not letter+accent, so they survive. Use this for search keys and URL slugs, but never to change names you store or display. `/\p{Diacritic}/gu` is a broader alternative to the fixed range.

front: What does `str.replace(/[^\x20-\x7E]/g, '')` remove, and what does it destroy that you might not expect?
back:
It keeps only *printable* ASCII (space `\x20` to tilde `\x7E`) and removes everything else. That includes all non-ASCII characters, but also newlines and tabs, which are ASCII control characters outside that range.

```js
const removeNonASCII = str => str.replace(/[^\x20-\x7E]/g, '');

removeNonASCII('äÄçÇhello-worldöÖ');  // 'hello-world'
removeNonASCII('line1\nline2\ttab');  // 'line1line2tab' (line breaks gone!)
removeNonASCII('café');               // 'caf'

// Keep line breaks: remove only characters above 0x7F
'line1\nline2 café'.replace(/[^\x00-\x7F]/g, ''); // 'line1\nline2 caf'
```

To keep readable text, first strip accents with `normalize('NFD')` (`café` → `cafe`), then remove what's left. Stripping non-ASCII from user content usually loses real data; prefer handling UTF-8 properly.

front: How do you replace every occurrence of a plain substring using `replace()` and a regex, and why must the substring be escaped first?
back:
Build a global regex from the substring: `str.replace(new RegExp(escapeRegExp(sub), 'g'), rep)`. The `g` flag replaces all matches (a string pattern replaces only the first); escaping stops characters like `.` from acting as regex syntax.

```js
const escapeRegExp = s => s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
const replaceAll = (str, sub, rep) =>
  str.replace(new RegExp(escapeRegExp(sub), 'g'), rep);

replaceAll('1.5.2', '.', '-');               // '1-5-2'
'1.5.2'.replace(new RegExp('.', 'g'), '-');  // '-----' (unescaped . = any char)
'1.5.2'.replace('.', '-');                   // '1-5.2' (first only)
```

Today, `'1.5.2'.replaceAll('.', '-')` does this directly (ES2021, all current browsers and Node). You'll still see the regex version in older code.

front: How does `String.prototype.replaceAll()` behave with a string pattern vs a regex, and what two gotchas does it have?
back:
With a string pattern, `replaceAll` replaces every literal occurrence, with no escaping needed. With a regex, the regex *must* have the `g` flag.

```js
'Hello World'.replaceAll('o', 'x'); // 'Hellx Wxrld'
'1.5.2'.replaceAll('.', '-');       // '1-5-2' ('.' is literal here)

'aaa'.replaceAll(/a/, 'b');   // TypeError: needs the g flag
'aaa'.replaceAll(/a/g, 'b');  // 'bbb'

// Gotcha 2: '$' patterns in the replacement string are still special
'price: X'.replaceAll('X', '$&');       // 'price: X' ($& = the match)
'price: X'.replaceAll('X', () => '$&'); // 'price: $&' (function: literal)
```

When the replacement comes from user input or data (e.g. a price like `'$5'`), pass a function so `$` sequences aren't interpreted.

front: How do you replace only the **last** occurrence of a string or regex match in a JavaScript string (e.g. the last `', '` in `'Alice, Bob, Carol'`)?

back:
One solution:

```js
  return str.slice(0, i) + replacement + str.slice(i + sub.length);
```

`lastIndexOf` gives the start of the final occurrence; everything before it is kept, the replacement goes in, and the text after the matched part (`i + sub.length`) is appended. For a regex, use `[...str.matchAll(re)].at(-1)` and its `index` the same way.

front: How do you turn a CSS color string like `'rgb(255, 12, 0)'` into numbers such as `[255, 12, 0]` or `{ red, green, blue }`?


`match` with the `g` flag returns every number substring, and `map(Number)` converts them. The optional `(?:\.\d+)?` keeps `0.5` together; `/\d+/g` alone would split it into `0` and `5`.

front: How do you convert identifiers like `'firstName'` or `'IAmEditingSomeXMLAndHTML'` to snake_case (e.g. for database column names)?

Complete `toSnakeCase` so the words found by `words()` are lower-cased and joined with underscores.

```js
const words = str =>
  str.match(/[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)|[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*|[A-Z]|[0-9]+/g) ?? [];

const toSnakeCase = str => ____;

toSnakeCase('camelCase');  // 'camel_case'
toSnakeCase('some text');  // 'some_text'
toSnakeCase('userID');     // 'user_id'
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const toSnakeCase = str => words(str).map(w => w.toLowerCase()).join('_');
```

The word regex already splits `camelCase` into `['camel', 'Case']` and `userID` into `['user', 'ID']`; lower-casing and joining with `_` produces snake case. Kebab case is identical with `'-'`.

front: How does the regex `/[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)|[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*|[A-Z]|[0-9]+/g` split `'XMLHttpRequest'` into words for case conversion?
back:
It tries four alternatives, left to right, at each position:

1. `[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)`: an acronym of 2+ capitals, but only if followed by a capitalized word or a word boundary. The lookahead stops `XMLH` being taken: it matches `XML`, leaving `Http`.
2. `[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*`: a normal word, optionally capitalized, with trailing digits (`Http`, `version10`).
3. `[A-Z]`: a lone capital (the `I` in `IAm`).
4. `[0-9]+`: a run of digits.

Separators like spaces, `-` and `_` match none of these, so they are skipped.

```js
const re = /[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)|[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*|[A-Z]|[0-9]+/g;
'XMLHttpRequest'.match(re);    // ['XML', 'Http', 'Request']
'some-mixed_string'.match(re); // ['some', 'mixed', 'string']
'crème'.match(re);             // ['cr', 'me'] (ASCII-only!)
```

It is a heuristic: `'user2FA'` gives `['user2', 'FA']`. For non-English text, swap the classes for `\p{Lu}`/`\p{Ll}` with the `u` flag.

back:

```js
  return s.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + s.slice(1);
```

`charAt(0)` is the first character (`''` for an empty string, so it never throws), upper-cased and joined to the rest of the string unchanged.

front: How do you convert `'backgroundColor'` or `'Some Title'` to kebab-case (`'background-color'`, `'some-title'`), and where is kebab case used?
back:
Split into words, lower-case them, and join with `-`. Kebab case is used for CSS properties and class names, HTML attributes, file names and URL paths.

```js
const words = str =>
  str.match(/[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)|[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*|[A-Z]|[0-9]+/g) ?? [];

const toKebabCase = str => words(str).map(w => w.toLowerCase()).join('-');

toKebabCase('backgroundColor');          // 'background-color'
toKebabCase('IAmEditingSomeXMLAndHTML'); // 'i-am-editing-some-xml-and-html'
toKebabCase('Café au lait');             // 'caf-au-lait' (é dropped!)
```

For URL slugs from user-written titles, strip accents first (`normalize('NFD')`) so non-ASCII letters aren't silently lost.

front: How do you convert `'some_database_field_name'` to PascalCase (`'SomeDatabaseFieldName'`), and where is PascalCase the convention?
back:
Split into words, capitalize each one (first letter upper, rest lower), and join with no separator. PascalCase is the convention for class names and React components in JS/TS, and for types, methods and properties in C#.

```js
const words = str =>
  str.match(/[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)|[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*|[A-Z]|[0-9]+/g) ?? [];

const toPascalCase = str =>
  words(str).map(w => w.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + w.slice(1).toLowerCase()).join('');

toPascalCase('some_database_field_name'); // 'SomeDatabaseFieldName'
toPascalCase('some-javascript-property'); // 'SomeJavascriptProperty'
toPascalCase('XMLHttpRequest');           // 'XmlHttpRequest'
```

Lower-casing the rest of each word flattens acronyms (`XML` → `Xml`). Many style guides prefer that; if you want to keep `XML`, don't lower-case words that are all capitals.

front: How do you turn `'some_database_field_name'` into a Title Case label (`'Some Database Field Name'`), and what does this simple approach not handle?
back:
Split into words, upper-case the first letter of each (leaving the rest as-is), and join with spaces.

```js
const words = str =>
  str.match(/[A-Z]{2,}(?=[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]*|\b)|[A-Z]?[a-z]+[0-9]*|[A-Z]|[0-9]+/g) ?? [];

const toTitleCase = str =>
  words(str).map(w => w.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + w.slice(1)).join(' ');

toTitleCase('some_database_field_name'); // 'Some Database Field Name'
toTitleCase('some-package-name');        // 'Some Package Name'
toTitleCase('user_id');                  // 'User Id'
```

front: What does `str.includes(sub)` return, and what two details (case, second argument) should you remember?
back:

```js
const str = 'Hello world';

str.includes('World');    // false (case-sensitive)

```

front: When checking for a substring, why is `if (str.indexOf(sub))` a bug, and when is `indexOf` still the right choice over `includes`?


front: Why is `Boolean('false')` `true`, and how do you safely convert strings like `'TRUE '` or `'false'` (from env variables or query params) into booleans?

```js
const toBoolean = (value, truthyValues = ['true']) =>
  truthyValues.includes(String(value).trim().toLowerCase());

toBoolean(' TRUE ');          // true
toBoolean('false');           // false
toBoolean('YES', ['yes', '1']); // true
toBoolean(undefined);         // false (unset env var)
```

Typical uses: `process.env.FEATURE_X`, `?debug=true`, or a CSV column. `String(value)` makes it safe for numbers and `undefined`; keep `truthyValues` lower-case since the input is lower-cased.

front: How do you turn a post title like `'Crème Brûlée: 10 Tips!'` into a URL slug (`'creme-brulee-10-tips'`)?
back:
Strip accents, lower-case and trim, remove characters other than letters/digits/spaces/hyphens, collapse runs of spaces, `_` and `-` into one `-`, and trim hyphens from the ends.

```js
const slugify = str =>
  str
    .normalize('NFD').replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, '') // é -> e
    .toLowerCase()
    .trim()
    .replace(/[^\w\s-]/g, '')   // drop punctuation
    .replace(/[\s_-]+/g, '-')   // spaces/underscores -> one hyphen
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');   // no leading/trailing hyphens

slugify('Crème Brûlée: 10 Tips!'); // 'creme-brulee-10-tips'
slugify('Hello World!');           // 'hello-world'
```

Without the accent step, `\w` (ASCII-only) deletes `è` and `û`, giving `'crme-brle-10-tips'`. Slugs aren't unique: store them in a column with a unique index and append `-2` on collisions, or include the id (`/posts/42-creme-brulee`).

front: How do you split text into words with `Intl.Segmenter`, and why is it better than `str.split(' ')`?

```js
const splitIntoWords = (str, locale) =>
  [...new Intl.Segmenter(locale, { granularity: 'word' }).segment(str)]
    .filter(s => s.isWordLike)
    .map(s => s.segment);

splitIntoWords('I love javaScript!!', 'en');  // ['I', 'love', 'javaScript']
'I love javaScript!!'.split(' ');             // ['I', 'love', 'javaScript!!']
splitIntoWords("don't stop", 'en');           // ["don't", 'stop']
splitIntoWords('我喜欢编程', 'zh');             // ['我', '喜欢', '编', '程']
```

`Intl.Segmenter` is supported in all current browsers and Node 16+. Good uses: word counts, search indexing, or truncating at a word boundary.

front: How do you swap the case of every letter in a string (`'Hello'` → `'hELLO'`), and why isn't `swapCase(swapCase(s))` always equal to `s`?

```js
const swapCase = str =>
  [...str]
    .map(c => (c === c.toLowerCase() ? c.toUpperCase() : c.toLowerCase()))
    .join('');

swapCase('Hello world!');           // 'hELLO WORLD!'
swapCase('ß');                      // 'SS'
swapCase(swapCase('Straße'));       // 'Strasse' (not 'Straße')
```

Case mapping isn't always one-to-one: German `ß` upper-cases to two letters `SS`, which lower-case back to `ss`. Such rules are also why case-insensitive comparisons are safer with `localeCompare`/`Intl.Collator` than with manual case tricks. This is mostly a practice exercise.

front: How do you truncate a string to at most `lim` characters *including* an ellipsis (`'boomerang'`, 7 → `'boom...'`)?

```js
const truncateString = (str, lim) =>

truncateString('boom', 7);      // 'boom'
truncateString('boomerang', 2); // 'bo...' (5 chars: over the limit when lim <= 3)

// Single-character ellipsis saves space
const truncate = (str, lim) => (str.length > lim ? str.slice(0, lim - 1) + '…' : str);
truncate('boomerang', 7); // 'boomer…'
```

If you only need it to *look* truncated in the UI, CSS `text-overflow: ellipsis` (with `overflow: hidden; white-space: nowrap`) does it without touching the data. Truncate in JS for fixed-length things like notification text or database fields.

front: What is the simplest way to cap a string at `n` characters in JavaScript, and what can go wrong with emoji?
back:
`str.slice(0, n)` returns at most the first `n` characters; if the string is already shorter it's returned unchanged, so a `length` check is optional.

```js
'boomerang'.slice(0, 6); // 'boomer'
'boo'.slice(0, 6);       // 'boo'

// slice counts UTF-16 code units, so it can split an emoji in half
'hi😀'.slice(0, 3);                // 'hi\ud83d' (broken character)
[...'hi😀'].slice(0, 3).join('');  // 'hi😀' (split by code point)
```

For user-generated text (names, comments), slice by code points with `[...str]`, or by graphemes with `Intl.Segmenter`, to avoid a broken character (shown as `�`) at the end. Also note a DB `VARCHAR(n)` limit may count bytes, not characters, depending on the database.



`a || b` returns `a` if `a` is truthy, otherwise it returns `b`. So it returns one of the operands, not always a boolean: `or('', 'Anonymous')` gives `'Anonymous'`, and `or(0, null)` gives `null` because both are falsy and the last operand wins.

This is why `name || 'Anonymous'` works as a fallback for an empty form field. Pitfall: `||` also replaces valid falsy values such as `0` or `''`. Use `??` when only `null`/`undefined` should trigger the fallback (`0 ?? 5` is `0`).

front: What does JavaScript's `!` operator return for non-boolean values such as `''`, `0` or `'0'`, and what does `!!value` do?
back:
`!` first converts its operand to a boolean (truthy or falsy), then negates it, so it always returns `true` or `false`. `!!value` negates twice, which simply converts any value to its boolean.

```js
!true;     // false
!'';       // true   ('' is falsy)
!0;        // true   (0 is falsy)
!'0';      // false  ('0' is a non-empty string, so truthy)
!!'hello'; // true
!![];      // true   (every object, even empty, is truthy)
```

The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy. Pitfall: form inputs give you strings, so `!'0'` is `false`. Convert with `Number()` first if you mean the number.

front: How do you debug a Node.js script with Chrome DevTools, and what is the difference between `node --inspect` and `node --inspect-brk`?
back:
Start Node with an inspector flag, open `chrome://inspect` in Chrome, and click **Open dedicated DevTools for Node**. You then get breakpoints, stepping, the call stack and variable inspection for your server code.

```shell
node --inspect server.js       # runs normally; attach whenever you like
node --inspect-brk server.js   # pauses on the first line until a debugger attaches
```

Use `--inspect` for a long-running process such as an API server, then hit the endpoint you want to debug. Use `--inspect-brk` for a short script that would finish before you could attach and set breakpoints. You can also write `debugger;` in your code to pause there when DevTools is attached. VS Code's JavaScript Debug Terminal does the same thing without leaving the editor.

front: Why should a Node.js static file server serve from a dedicated folder such as `public/` and build file paths with `path.join()` instead of string concatenation?

Without the root rule, `/` would fall through to `join('/', 'index.html')`, which also works here, but the explicit check makes the intent obvious and avoids a disk lookup for `/.html`.

front: How do you stop a Node.js static file server from serving files outside its public folder, for example a request for `/../../.env`?

back:

```js
const isInsideRoot = filePath.startsWith(root + sep);
```

`resolve()` collapses `..` segments, so `/../../.env` becomes an absolute path outside `root`, and the check fails. Adding `sep` (the OS path separator) matters: `'/srv/public-old/x'.startsWith('/srv/public')` is `true`, but `startsWith('/srv/public/')` is `false`. An alternative is to check that `path.relative(root, filePath)` neither starts with `..` nor is absolute (on Windows a different drive gives an absolute result).

front: When a promise rejects, why does `p.catch(fallback).then(show)` behave differently from `p.then(show).catch(fallback)`?

`.catch(fallback)` turns the rejection into the value `{ name: 'Guest' }`, and the next `.then(show)` receives it. The reverse order, `.then(show).catch(fallback)`, logs nothing: the rejection skips `show`, and the fallback value is never used.

The wrapper appends its own callback after the caller's arguments. A truthy `err` rejects the promise; otherwise it resolves with `result`. In `delay`, `setTimeout` calls `cb()` with no arguments, so `err` is `undefined` and the promise resolves. In real Node code, use `util.promisify` from `node:util`.

front: What two conditions make a function pure, and which of these is pure: `arr => [...arr].sort()` or `arr => arr.sort()`?

```js
  Math.max(Math.min(num, max), min);

getNumber();          // random value between 0 and 1
getNumber(0, 1, 0.5); // 0.5
```

One solution:

```js
const getNumber = (min = 0, max = 1, num = Math.random()) =>
```

The default expression `Math.random()` runs each time the function is called without `num`, so normal callers still get randomness, and tests can inject a known value. This is dependency injection in its smallest form.

front: How do you read a text file synchronously in Node.js into an array of lines, and when is the synchronous version acceptable?

back:
One solution:

```js
readFileSync(path, 'utf8').trimEnd().split(/\r?\n/);
```

The `'utf8'` encoding makes `readFileSync` return a string instead of a `Buffer`. Most text files end with a newline, so a plain `split('\n')` returns an extra `''` at the end; `trimEnd()` removes it. The regex `/\r?\n/` splits on both `\n` and `\r\n`.

front: How do you read a text file into an array of lines in Node.js without blocking the event loop?

back:
One solution:

```js
const lines = await readFileLines('todo.txt');
```

An `async` function always returns a Promise. `await` pauses until it settles and gives you the resolved value. Without `await`, `lines` would be a Promise and `lines.length` would be `undefined`. Top-level `await` works in ES modules; elsewhere use `readFileLines('todo.txt').then(lines => ...)`.

front:
Why does `'line1
line2
'.split('
')` return an extra empty string, and how do you split file contents into lines reliably?

back:
One solution:

```js
fileContents.trimEnd().split(/\r?\n/);
```

`trimEnd()` removes the final newline, so `split` doesn't produce a trailing `''`. The regex splits on both Unix (`\n`) and Windows (`\r\n`) line endings. A plain `split('\n')` would return `['line1\r', 'line2', 'line3', '']`.

front: What does Node's `fs.readFile()` give you when you don't pass an encoding, and how do you get a string instead?
back:
It gives you a `Buffer`, which holds the raw bytes. Pass an encoding such as `'utf8'` to get a string, or call `buffer.toString('utf8')` afterwards.

```js
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

readFileSync('notes.txt');          // <Buffer 6c 69 6e 65 31 0a ...>
readFileSync('notes.txt', 'utf8');  // 'line1\nline2\n'

await readFile('notes.txt');         // <Buffer ...>
await readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8'); // 'line1\nline2\n'
```

Node has three styles: `readFileSync` (blocks and returns the data), `readFile` from `node:fs` (takes a callback), and `readFile` from `node:fs/promises` (returns a Promise). Prefer the promise version with `await` in server code. Keep the Buffer (no encoding) for binary files such as images.

front:
Reading files in Node.js. Reading without an encoding returned a `Buffer`. Fill in the blank so `text` is the file's contents as a string.

```js
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const buf = await readFile('notes.txt');
console.log(buf);   // <Buffer 6c 69 6e 65 31 0a ...>

____
console.log(text);  // 'line1\nline2\n'
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const text = await readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8');
```

Passing an encoding makes `readFile` decode the bytes for you. Converting the Buffer you already have also works: `const text = buf.toString('utf8');`. Without an encoding you get raw bytes, which is what you want for images or other binary files.

front: How do you force Node.js to reload a CommonJS module that `require()` has already cached, and when doesn't that trick work?

back:
One solution:

```js
delete require.cache[require.resolve(modulePath)];
```

`require.cache` is keyed by absolute file path, and `require.resolve()` turns `'./config.js'` into that path. Deleting the entry makes the next `require()` load the file again. This only works for CommonJS files, not for built-ins like `'fs'` or ES modules.

front: How do you write a `rearg(fn, indexes)` helper that calls `fn` with its arguments reordered, and what is usually a better fix for a confusing argument order?
back:
Return a function that builds a new argument list by picking `args[i]` for each index in `indexes`, then spreads it into `fn`.

```js
const rearg = (fn, indexes) => (...args) =>
  fn(...indexes.map(i => args[i]));

const rearged = rearg((a, b, c) => [a, b, c], [2, 0, 1]);
rearged('b', 'c', 'a'); // ['a', 'b', 'c']
```

`indexes[0]` says which incoming argument becomes the first parameter, and so on. In application code, a function with many positional arguments is usually better redesigned to take one options object, such as `createUser({ name, email, role })`, so the order stops mattering.

front:
Rearranging arguments. Fill in the blank so `rearg` calls `fn` with the arguments reordered: the i-th parameter receives `args[indexes[i]]`.

```js
const rearg =

  (...args) =>

const rearged = rearg((a, b, c) => [a, b, c], [2, 0, 1]);
rearged('b', 'c', 'a'); // ['a', 'b', 'c']
```
back:
One solution:

```js

```

`indexes.map(i => args[i])` builds the new argument list: `[args[2], args[0], args[1]]`, which is `['a', 'b', 'c']`. Spreading it passes the values to `fn` as separate arguments.

front: How do you write a `flip(fn)` helper that moves a function's first argument to the end, and why is that useful with `Number.parseInt`?

Flipping arguments. Fill in the blank with a `flip(fn)` helper that returns a function passing its first argument to `fn` last.

```js
____

const parseInteger = flip(Number.parseInt);
parseInteger(8, '10'); // 8  (10 in base 8)

const parseIntegerBase16 = parseInteger.bind(null, 16);
parseIntegerBase16('10'); // 16  (10 in base 16)
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const flip = fn => (first, ...rest) => fn(...rest, first);
```

The parameter list `(first, ...rest)` separates the first argument from the others, and `fn(...rest, first)` puts it at the end. So `parseInteger(8, '10')` calls `Number.parseInt('10', 8)`.

front: How do you create a promise that resolves with a given value after a delay of N milliseconds?

back:
One solution:

```js
setTimeout(() => resolve(value), delay);
```

The Promise executor runs immediately and schedules a timer. When the timer fires, `resolve(value)` settles the promise, and any `.then` or `await` waiting on it continues. Writing `setTimeout(resolve(value), delay)` would be a bug: it calls `resolve` right away.

front: How do you run a list of async tasks one after another instead of all at once, and why must the list contain functions rather than promises?

back:
One solution:

```js
ps.reduce((p, next) => p.then(next), Promise.resolve());
```

`reduce` starts with an already-resolved promise and chains each task with `.then(next)`. `then` calls `next` only after the previous promise resolves, and waits for the promise `next` returns. The same thing, more readably: `for (const task of ps) await task();`.

front: In semantic versioning (SemVer), what do `0.x.y` versions and pre-release tags such as `1.0.0-beta.2` mean?
back:
A `0.x.y` version means the package is in initial development: its public API is not yet considered stable, and anything may change between releases. A tag after a hyphen, such as `-alpha.1` or `-beta.2`, marks a pre-release: a test build of an upcoming version that is not yet final.

```text
0.4.2          initial development, API may still change
1.0.0          first stable public API
1.0.0-beta.2   pre-release of 1.0.0; sorts before 1.0.0
2.0.0-rc.1     release candidate for 2.0.0
```

Pre-releases sort before the final version (`1.0.0-beta.2 < 1.0.0`). npm ranges ignore them unless you ask explicitly: `^1.0.0` will not install `1.1.0-beta.1`. Many packages start at `0.1.0` rather than `1.0.0`. Release `1.0.0` when others depend on your API.

front: In `package.json`, which versions do the ranges `^1.2.3` and `~1.2.3` allow, and what does `npm install pkg@1.2.3` do?
back:
`^1.2.3` allows any compatible version with the same major number (`>=1.2.3 <2.0.0`), so minor and patch updates are allowed. `~1.2.3` allows only patch updates (`>=1.2.3 <1.3.0`). `npm install pkg@1.2.3` installs exactly that version.

```shell
npm install express         # installs the latest version, saves "^x.y.z"
npm install express@4.21.2  # installs 4.21.2 (saved as "^4.21.2" by default)
npm install --save-exact express@4.21.2   # saves "4.21.2" exactly
```

| Range | Allows |
| ----- | ------ |
| `1.2.3` | exactly 1.2.3 |
| `~1.2.3` | `>=1.2.3 <1.3.0` (patches only) |
| `1.2.x` | `>=1.2.0 <1.3.0` |
| `^1.2.3` | `>=1.2.3 <2.0.0` |
| `1.x` | `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0` |
| `^0.2.3` | only `<0.3.0` (for 0.x, caret is stricter) |

The range only decides what a fresh resolve may pick. `package-lock.json` pins the exact versions actually installed, and `npm ci` installs exactly those.

front: Before refactoring working code that has a test suite, what goals should you set, and what job do the tests do during the refactor?
back:
Aim to reduce complexity, make the code less error-prone and easier to maintain, while keeping behavior identical and readability at least as good. The tests are the safety net: they pin down current behavior, so you run them after every small change and any failure means that step changed what the code does.

```shell
npx vitest --watch   # keep tests re-running on every save while you refactor
```

Refactoring means changing structure, not behavior. Don't change a test to make it pass mid-refactor unless you meant to change behavior. Shorter code is not a goal in itself: squeezing code into as few characters as possible ("code golf") is fun, but it often hurts readability.

front: During a refactor, when should you inline a small helper function into its callers, and what does that look like?

back:
One solution:

```js
export const namedGroup = name => wrapSegments(`(?<${name}>`, ')');
```

Unlike the other two groups, the prefix depends on a value (the group name), so `namedGroup` is a function that builds the prefix and then calls `wrapSegments`. That's why it is called twice: `namedGroup('year')` returns a builder, and the builder takes the expressions. `(?<year>...)` is a named capture group, which you read back as `match.groups.year`.

front: How does currying a helper into the form `toGroup(prefix)(...expressions)` let you define `captureGroup` and `nonCaptureGroup` as one-liners?

back:
One solution:

```js
const toGroup = prefix => (...expressions) =>
```

The two arrows split the arguments into two calls: `toGroup('(')` returns a function, and calling that with the expressions builds the RegExp. The rest parameter `...expressions` collects any number of arguments into an array.

front: Why remove a wrapper class like `Segment` when all it does is wrap a `RegExp`, and what does the replacement `toSegment` function do?

back:
One solution:

```js
return new RegExp(sanitize(expression));
```

In a regex, characters like `$`, `.` and `(` have special meanings, so `new RegExp('$9.99')` does not match the text `'$9.99'`. Escaping them first makes the string match literally. Always escape user input (such as a search box value) before building a RegExp from it. Newer runtimes add a built-in `RegExp.escape()` for this, but Node 22 doesn't have it yet.

front: How can you check whether a refactor actually made a front-end library's bundle smaller, and which size number matters most to users?
back:
Run the production build before and after the change and compare the sizes it prints. The gzip size matters most, because it is close to what browsers actually download.

```text
$ npm run build        (runs "vite build")
dist/readex.js  6.04 kB │ gzip: 1.63 kB   before
dist/readex.js  4.08 kB │ gzip: 1.36 kB   after
```

Here the raw file shrank by 32.5%, but the gzipped size only by about 17%: compression already removes much of the repetition that a refactor cuts out. Measure the same way each time (same build command, same mode) so the numbers are comparable.

front:
Measuring bundle size. `package.json` defines `"build": "vite build"` under `"scripts"`. Fill in the blank with the terminal command that runs that script so you can read the bundle size.

```shell
____
# > readex@1.0.0 build
# > vite build
# dist/readex.js  4.08 kB │ gzip: 1.36 kB
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
npm run build
```

`npm run <name>` runs the script with that name from `package.json`, using the project's local `node_modules/.bin` tools such as `vite`. Only a few scripts (`test`, `start`, `stop`, `restart`) have shortcuts like `npm test`; `build` always needs `npm run`.

front: After a refactor, how do you judge whether it was worth it?
back:
It was worth it if the tests still pass unchanged (behavior is the same), the code is smaller or has fewer concepts to understand, and a teammate can read it at least as easily as before. Measurable wins, such as a smaller bundle or faster build, are a bonus.

```text
Tests:        all green, none edited      -> behavior kept
Code:         fewer helpers, one pattern  -> less to learn
Readability:  about the same              -> acceptable
Bundle:       6.04 kB -> 4.08 kB          -> bonus
```

If the new code is shorter but harder to follow, it usually wasn't worth it. Code is read far more often than it is written.

front: Several helpers each join some expressions and wrap the result in a prefix and suffix. How can a higher-order function remove that duplication?

back:
One solution:

```js
(prefix = '', suffix = '', separator = '') =>
```

The outer call fixes what varies between helpers, and the inner `(...expressions) =>` function does the shared work. Defaults of `''` let callers omit a suffix or separator: `wrapSegments('(', ')')` joins with no separator.

front: How can a single Vite config produce both a readable build and a minified build of a library?

back:
One solution:

```js
const __dirname = dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
```

`import.meta.url` is the module's own `file:///...` URL. `fileURLToPath` converts it to a normal file path, and `dirname` removes the file name, leaving the folder. In plain Node 20.11+ you can write `import.meta.dirname` instead. The CommonJS globals `__dirname` and `__filename` don't exist in ES modules.

front: How can adding an optional `mapFn` parameter to a generic helper like `toSegments` let you delete a special-case function?
back:
If the special case differs from the generic helper only by transforming each input first, add that transformation as a parameter with an identity default (`x => x`). Normal callers don't notice, and the special case becomes one more preset call.

```js
export const toSegments =
  (prefix = '', suffix = '', separator = '', mapFn = x => x) =>
  (...expressions) =>
    new RegExp(`${prefix}${expressions
      .map(e => toSegment(mapFn(e)).source)
      .join(separator)}${suffix}`);

const toCharacterSet = expression =>
  Array.isArray(expression) && expression.length === 2
    ? toSegments('', '', '-')(...expression)   // ['a', 'z'] -> a-z
    : toSegments()(expression);

export const anythingFrom = toSegments('[', ']', '', toCharacterSet);
anythingFrom(['a', 'z'], '_'); // /[a-z_]/
```

Pitfall: inside `[...]`, `|` is not "or", it is a literal pipe character. The original used `'|'` as the separator here, which made `[a-z|_]` also match `|`.


`x => x` is the identity function: it returns its argument unchanged, so callers that don't pass `mapFn` get the old behavior. Callers that need to transform each expression first, like a character-set builder, pass their own `mapFn`.

front: How do you find what to refactor in code that already works and has tests?
back:
Read it looking for two things: complexity that isn't needed, and repeated patterns that could become one abstraction. Then change one thing at a time and run the tests after each step.

```text
Unneeded complexity         -> helpers that only forward arguments (inline them)
                            -> classes that only wrap a built-in (use the built-in)
Repeated patterns           -> functions with the same body but different values
                               (extract a higher-order function)
Wasted work                 -> two .map() calls in a row (merge into one)
```

Small steps keep each change easy to review and easy to undo. If a test fails, you know exactly which step caused it. Commit after each green step.

```js
export const joinSegments = (expressions, separator = '') =>
```

Calling `toSegment(e)` and reading `.source` inside the same callback does both steps in one loop, so there is no intermediate array. The output is identical to the two-`map` version.

front: What does throttling a function do, and how would you write a `throttle(fn, wait)` for a scroll or resize handler?

back:
One solution:

```js
const remaining = wait - (Date.now() - lastTime);
```

`Date.now() - lastTime` is the time since `fn` last ran. If a full `wait` has passed, `remaining` is zero or negative and `fn` runs now. Otherwise one trailing call is scheduled for exactly when the window ends, and `clearTimeout` makes sure only the latest call's arguments are used.

front: How can you check whether a value is a Node.js stream, and what are the limits of that check?
back:
Check that it is a non-null object with a `pipe` method. This is duck typing: judging a value by the methods it has rather than by its class.

```js
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

const isStream = val =>
  val !== null && typeof val === 'object' && typeof val.pipe === 'function';

isStream(createReadStream('todo.txt')); // true
isStream({ pipe() {} });                // true, a false positive
isStream(new ReadableStream());         // false (web streams use pipeTo)
```

Limits: any object with a `pipe` method passes. Web streams, such as a `fetch()` response body, are a different API and fail the check. For a stricter check of Node streams, use `val instanceof Stream`, with `Stream` imported from `node:stream`.

front:
Duck typing a stream. Fill in the blank so `isStream` returns `true` only for a non-null object that has a `pipe` method.

```js
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

const isStream = val =>
```
