isStream(createReadStream('todo.txt')); // true
isStream(null);                         // false
```
back:
One solution:

```js
val !== null && typeof val === 'object' && typeof val.pipe === 'function';
```

The `null` check comes first because `typeof null` is `'object'`, and reading `null.pipe` would throw. Checking `typeof val.pipe === 'function'` is duck typing: anything with a `pipe` method counts as a stream.

front: How do you cancel an in-flight `fetch()` request, for example when the user types a new search before the old one returns?

back:
One solution:

```js
fetch('/api/users', { signal: controller.signal })
```

`fetch()` only listens for cancellation if you hand it the controller's `signal`. Calling `abort()` afterwards makes the returned promise reject with an `AbortError`. Without the `signal` option, `abort()` does nothing to the request.

front: Can you use an arrow function as an `addEventListener` callback? What changes compared to a regular `function` callback?
How do you turn `function square(a) { return a * a; }` into the shortest arrow function, and what does each step remove?
back:
`const square = a => a * a;`. You drop the `function` keyword and add `=>`. Because there is exactly one simple parameter you can drop its parentheses. Because the body is a single expression you can drop the braces and `return`.

```js
function square(a) { return a * a; }    // declaration
const square1 = (a) => { return a * a; }; // arrow, block body
const square2 = a => { return a * a; };   // one param: () optional
const square3 = a => a * a;               // expression body: implicit return
```

Parentheses are still required for zero parameters `() => ...`, two or more `(a, b) => ...`, and default or destructured parameters `({ id }) => ...`.

front: When does an arrow function return a value implicitly, and why does `() => { id: 1 }` return `undefined`?
back:
An arrow function returns implicitly only when its body is a single expression with no braces. With braces `{ }` the body is a block and you need an explicit `return`. `() => { id: 1 }` is read as a block containing a label `id:`, not as an object, so it returns `undefined`.

```js
const square = a => a * a;        // returns a * a
const squareBlock = a => { a * a; }; // returns undefined (no return)

const bad = () => { id: 1 };      // undefined
const good = () => ({ id: 1 });   // { id: 1 }: wrap objects in ()
```

This bites most often in `.map()`, for example `users.map(u => ({ id: u.id, name: u.name }))`.

One solution:

```js
a => a * a
```

One parameter means no parentheses are needed. A single-expression body means no braces and no `return`: the expression's value is returned automatically.

front: What happens if you call `new` on an arrow function, and why?

back:
One solution:

```js
this.name = name;
```

With `new`, a regular function gets a fresh object as `this`, and that object is returned automatically. Arrow functions cannot be called with `new` at all, so the second call throws before its body runs.

front: Inside a click listener, what is `this` for a regular `function` versus an arrow function? Can `.call()` or `.bind()` change it?

back:
One solution:

```js
button.addEventListener('click', () => {
```

It does not log the button. The arrow uses the `this` of the surrounding code: `undefined` at the top of an ES module, `window` in a classic script. To get the element in an arrow listener, take an `event` parameter and use `event.currentTarget`.

front: Why can't an arrow function use its own `arguments` object, and what should you use instead?

back:
One solution:

```js
const sum = (...nums) => {
```

`...nums` is a rest parameter: it collects all passed arguments into a real array, so `reduce` works directly. Don't name it `arguments`. That name cannot be used for a parameter or variable in strict mode, and ES modules are always strict.

front: Why does an arrow function used as an object-literal method fail to read `this.x`, and when is an arrow "method" actually useful?

back:
One solution:

```js
describe() {
```

Method shorthand (or `describe: function () {`) gets `this` from the call `cart.describe()`, so `this` is `cart`. An arrow function (`describe: () => {`) would use the outer `this` and never see `cart.total`.

front: Besides `this`, `arguments`, and `new`, what else can arrow functions not do?
back:
Arrow functions have no `prototype` property, and they cannot be generators: there is no arrow form of `function*`, and `yield` is not allowed in their body. They also have no `super` or `new.target` of their own; they use the enclosing function's.

```js
(() => {}).prototype;      // undefined
function* ids() { yield 1; } // generators need `function*`

const load = async () => { /* ... */ }; // async arrows ARE fine
```

In day-to-day code this rarely matters. Use `function*` when you need a generator and a `class` when you need a constructor.

front: What three states can a Promise be in, and can a promise change state after it settles?
What is the difference between `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled`, `Promise.race`, and `Promise.any`?

back:
One solution:

```js
const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([userPromise, ordersPromise]);
```

`Promise.all` fulfills with an array whose order matches the input array, not the order the requests finished in. So destructuring `[user, orders]` is safe. Both requests were started before the `await`, so they run at the same time. If either rejects, the `await` throws.

front: When does the function passed to `new Promise(...)` run, and how do you use it to wrap a callback-style API?

back:
One solution:

```js
const delay = ms => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
```

`setTimeout` calls `resolve` after `ms`, which fulfills the promise and resumes the `await`. No `reject` is needed because a timer can't fail. In Node you can also use `import { setTimeout as delay } from 'node:timers/promises'`.

front: What does calling an `async` function return, and how do you handle a failed `await` inside it?

back:
One solution:

```js
const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
```

`await` unwraps the promise. If it rejects, the error is thrown right at that line and caught by `catch`. Note that `fetch` rejects only on network errors. A 404 or 500 still fulfills, so real code also checks `res.ok`.

front: How do you compose async functions left-to-right, so `pipeAsync(f, g, h)(x)` waits for each step before starting the next?

Fill in the blank so `pipeAsync` runs the functions left to right, awaiting each result before passing it on.

```js
const pipeAsync = (...fns) => arg =>
  ____;

const slowAdd2 = x => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(x + 2), 100));
await pipeAsync(x => x + 1, slowAdd2, async x => x * 10)(5); // 80
```
back:
One solution:

```js
fns.reduce((p, f) => p.then(f), Promise.resolve(arg))
```

`Promise.resolve(arg)` gives the chain a starting promise. Each `.then(f)` waits for the previous step and passes its resolved value to `f`. Functions that return plain values and functions that return promises both work.

front: How does `composeAsync(f, g, h)` differ from `pipeAsync(f, g, h)`, and what single change implements it?
back:
`composeAsync` runs the functions right to left: `h` first, then `g`, then `f`, like math composition `f(g(h(x)))`. The implementation is the same as `pipeAsync` except it uses `reduceRight` instead of `reduce`.

```js
const composeAsync = (...fns) => arg =>
  fns.reduceRight((p, f) => p.then(f), Promise.resolve(arg));

const slowAdd2 = x => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(x + 2), 100));
await composeAsync(async x => x * 10, slowAdd2, x => x + 1)(5); // 80
```

Pick one direction for a codebase. Left-to-right "pipe" usually reads more naturally as a list of steps.

front:
Fill in the blank so `composeAsync` runs the functions right to left, awaiting each step.

```js
const composeAsync = (...fns) => arg =>
  ____;

const slowAdd2 = x => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(x + 2), 100));
await composeAsync(async x => x * 10, slowAdd2, x => x + 1)(5); // 80
```
back:
One solution:

```js
fns.reduceRight((p, f) => p.then(f), Promise.resolve(arg))
```

`reduceRight` walks the array from the last function to the first, so `x => x + 1` runs first and `x * 10` runs last. Otherwise it is identical to `pipeAsync`.

front: How can a helper `attempt(fn, ...args)` turn a thrown error into a return value, and what is the trade-off?

back:
One solution:

```js
return e instanceof Error ? e : new Error(e);
```

JavaScript lets you `throw` any value, not only `Error` objects. Checking `instanceof Error` and wrapping everything else gives callers one consistent type to test for, with `.message` and a stack trace.

front: What is a "boolean trap" in a call like `results.reload(false)` or `new User(true)`, and how do you avoid it?

back:
One solution:

```js
createUser('ada@example.com', { isAdmin: true });
```

The key name documents the flag at every call site. Destructuring with defaults (`{ isAdmin = false } = {}`) keeps the option optional, so `createUser(email)` still works.

front: Why is `input.setInvalid(false)` harder to read than it looks, and what would be a clearer API?
back:
It is a double negative: the reader must work out that "set invalid to false" means "valid", and they have to do that every time they read the line. Name the method and flag positively, or use two explicit methods.

```js
input.setInvalid(false);   // wait... so it's valid?

input.setValid(true);      // clearer
input.markValid();         // clearest: no boolean at all
input.markInvalid('Email is required');
```

Positive names like `isEnabled`, `isVisible`, and `isValid` for booleans avoid a whole class of `!isNotX` bugs.

front: How do you write `once(fn)` so the wrapped function runs only on its first call, keeping `this` and all arguments?

back:
One solution:

```js
return function (...args) {
```

It must be a regular `function`, not an arrow. Only a regular function gets `this` from how it is called (for example, the element in an event listener). The rest parameter `...args` collects every argument, and `apply` forwards them to `fn`.

front: What makes a callback "asynchronous", for example the function passed to `.then()` after a `fetch`?

Fill in the blank so the numbers from the API are each passed to `printDoublePlusOne`.

```js
const printDoublePlusOne = n => console.log(2 * n + 1);

fetch('/api/nums') // responds with [1, 2, 3]
  .then(res => res.json())
  ____ // logs 3, 5, 7
```
back:
One solution:

```js
.then(nums => nums.forEach(printDoublePlusOne));
```

The callbacks in `.then()` run asynchronously, once the data is ready. The first `.then` turns the `Response` into parsed JSON. The second receives the array and passes each number to the synchronous `forEach` callback.

front: What is a synchronous callback? Show an array-method example and when it runs relative to the next line.
back:
A synchronous callback is called immediately, during the function that receives it, and finishes before that function returns. Array methods like `forEach`, `map`, and `filter` work this way.

```js
const nums = [1, 2, 3];

nums.forEach(n => console.log(2 * n + 1)); // logs 3, 5, 7
console.log('done');                       // logs after them
```

Use `forEach` for side effects like logging. Use `map` when you need the new array. Calling `map` just to log creates an array you then throw away.

front:
Fill in the blank to call `printDoublePlusOne` synchronously for each number.

```js
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
const printDoublePlusOne = n => console.log(2 * n + 1);

____ // logs 3, 5, 7
console.log('done'); // runs after all three
```
back:
One solution:

```js
nums.forEach(printDoublePlusOne);
```

You pass the function itself, with no `()`. `forEach` calls it once per element before returning, which is why `'done'` prints last. `map` would also call it, but it would build an unused array of `undefined` values.

front: In Node.js, what does `process.argv` contain when you run `node my-script.js --name=John --age=30`?

back:
One solution:

```js
'/path/to/my-script.js',
```

`process.argv[0]` is the Node binary and `process.argv[1]` is the absolute path of the script being run. That's why user arguments start at `process.argv.slice(2)`.

front: How can a Node script check whether flags like `-s` or `--test` were passed on the command line?

Fill in the blank so `hasFlags` checks `process.argv` and treats `'test'` as `'--test'`.

```js
const hasFlags = (...flags) =>
  flags.every(flag =>
    ____
  );

// $ node my-script.js -s --test
hasFlags('-s');         // true
hasFlags('test', '-s'); // true
hasFlags('special');    // false
```
back:
One solution:

```js
process.argv.includes(/^-{1,2}/.test(flag) ? flag : '--' + flag)
```

The regex `/^-{1,2}/` tests whether the flag already starts with `-` or `--`. If it doesn't, the helper adds `--`. `every` returns `true` only if all requested flags are present.

front: How do you get only the arguments a user passed to a Node script, without the node and script paths?
back:
Use `process.argv.slice(2)`. It skips the first two entries (the Node executable and the script path) and returns a new array of the user's arguments.

```js
const getCmdArgs = () => process.argv.slice(2);

// $ node my-script.js --name=John --age=30
getCmdArgs(); // ['--name=John', '--age=30']
```

`slice` does not modify `process.argv`. It returns a copy.

front:
Fill in the blank so `getCmdArgs()` returns only the user-supplied command-line arguments.

```js
____

// $ node my-script.js --name=John --age=30
getCmdArgs(); // ['--name=John', '--age=30']
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const getCmdArgs = () => process.argv.slice(2);
```

Indexes 0 and 1 of `process.argv` are the Node binary and the script path, so the user's arguments start at index 2.

front: In Node, how do you synchronously create a directory, including any missing parent folders, without an error if it already exists?
back:
Call `mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })`. With `recursive: true`, it creates any missing parent folders and does not throw if the directory already exists.

```js
import { mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';

mkdirSync('uploads/avatars', { recursive: true }); // creates both
mkdirSync('uploads/avatars', { recursive: true }); // no error
```

The older pattern `if (!existsSync(dir)) mkdirSync(dir)` has a race: another process can create the folder between the check and the create. Without `recursive`, `mkdirSync` throws `EEXIST` for an existing folder. Sync fs calls block the event loop, so keep them to startup scripts and CLIs.

front:
Fill in the blank so `ensureDirSync` creates the folder, and any missing parents, and does not throw if it exists.

```js
import { mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';

const ensureDirSync = dir => ____;

ensureDirSync('uploads/avatars'); // creates both folders
ensureDirSync('uploads/avatars'); // no error the second time
```
back:
One solution:

```js
mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })
```

`recursive: true` makes `mkdirSync` behave like `mkdir -p`: it creates missing parents and treats an existing directory as success. There is no separate existence check, so there is no race condition.

front: With `fs/promises`, how do you create a directory only if it doesn't exist, without a check-then-create race?
back:
`await mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })`. With `recursive: true` the promise fulfills even if the directory already exists, and missing parents are created too. Without that option, `mkdir` rejects with `EEXIST` when the folder exists.

```js
import { mkdir } from 'node:fs/promises';

await mkdir('uploads/2024/avatars', { recursive: true });
await mkdir('uploads/2024/avatars', { recursive: true }); // fine
```

Avoid `access(dir).catch(() => mkdir(dir))`. Another request or process can create the folder between the two calls, and then `mkdir` fails anyway.

One solution:

```js
await mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });
```

`recursive: true` treats "already exists" as success and creates any missing parent folders. Letting `mkdir` decide in one call avoids the race in "check with `access()`, then create".

front: How does a generic `curry(fn)` decide when to finally call `fn`, and what does it return until then?

back:
One solution:

```js
: (...rest) => curried(...args, ...rest)
```

The new function remembers `args` through a closure. It merges them with the next batch and calls `curried` again. The recursion ends once `args.length` reaches `fn.length`.

front: How do you "uncurry" `x => y => z => x + y + z` so it can be called as `f(1, 2, 3)`?

back:
One solution:

```js
const uncurry = (fn, arity = 1) => (...args) => {
```

`uncurry` takes the curried function and its arity, and returns a variadic function (`...args`). The body then feeds the arguments into the curried chain one by one with `reduce`.

front: What does debouncing a function do, and how does a `debounce(fn, ms)` helper implement it?

back:
One solution:

```js
timeoutId = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), ms);
```

Saving the new timer id lets the next call cancel it with `clearTimeout`. So `fn` only runs when `ms` passes with no new call, which means one search after the user pauses typing. The arrow function keeps the wrapper's `this` and `args`.

front: What does deferring a function with `setTimeout(fn, 1)` change about when it runs, and why would a web app do it?

back:
One solution:

```js
const defer = (fn, ...args) => setTimeout(fn, 1, ...args);
```

`setTimeout` accepts extra arguments after the delay and passes them to `fn`. The callback waits on the task queue until the current synchronous code has finished, so `'b'` logs first.

front: A function reads a global like `Math.random`. What makes that kind of closure acceptable, and how can a default parameter make it testable?
back:
Reading stable, shared things like constants or built-in APIs from outer scope is fine. Expose the dependency as a parameter with a default: normal callers get the real API, and tests can pass their own.

```js
const randomNumber = (limit = 100, random = Math.random) =>
  random() * limit;

randomNumber(10);            // e.g. 4.37 (random each time)
randomNumber(10, () => 0.2); // 2, always
```

The same trick works for `Date.now`, `fetch`, or a logger, and it avoids module-mocking in tests. Closures only turn risky when they hide mutable state that other code changes.

front:
Fill in the blank: `randomNumber` should use `Math.random` by default but let tests inject a fake random function.

```js
____

randomNumber(10);            // a random number from 0 up to (not including) 10
randomNumber(10, () => 0.2); // 2
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const randomNumber = (limit = 100, random = Math.random) => random() * limit;
```

The default parameter makes `Math.random` the normal dependency. Passing `() => 0.2` swaps it for a predictable function, so the test result is exactly `2`.

front: What is "hidden state" in a closure like `initCounter()`, and when does it become a problem?

back:
One solution:

```js
let value = start;
```

`value` lives in `initCounter`'s scope. The returned functions close over it, so they share it and can change it, but no outside code can read or set it except through those functions. It must be `let` because `increment` reassigns it.

front: How do you wrap a function so it receives only its first `n` arguments, and why is that useful?

Fill in `nAry` so it calls `fn` with only the first `n` arguments it receives.

```js
____

const firstTwoMax = nAry(Math.max, 2);
[[2, 6, 'a'], [6, 4, 8], [10]].map(x => firstTwoMax(...x)); // [6, 6, 10]
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const nAry = (fn, n) => (...args) => fn(...args.slice(0, n));
```

Rest parameters gather every argument into an array. `slice(0, n)` keeps the first `n`, and spreading them back calls `fn` normally. For `[2, 6, 'a']`, `Math.max` only sees `2, 6`, so it returns `6` instead of `NaN`.

front: How do you convert a function that takes an array into one that takes separate arguments, and the reverse?

Fill in `toVariadic` so the wrapped function can be called with separate arguments instead of one array.

```js
____
const fromVariadic = fn => args => fn(...args);

const allPromises = toVariadic(Promise.all.bind(Promise));
allPromises(Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)).then(console.log); // [1, 2]

fromVariadic(Math.max)([1, 2, 3]); // 3
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const toVariadic = fn => (...args) => fn(args);
```

The rest parameter `...args` gathers the separate arguments into an array, which is exactly what `Promise.all` expects. `bind(Promise)` is needed because `Promise.all` must be called with `this` set to `Promise`.

front: Why does `['2', '1', '0'].map(Math.max)` return `[NaN, NaN, NaN]`, and how does a `binary` wrapper fix it?
back:
`map` calls its callback with three arguments: `(value, index, array)`. `Math.max` uses all of them, and the array argument converts to `NaN`. A `binary` wrapper passes only the first two arguments, so each call compares the value with its index.

```js
const binary = fn => (a, b) => fn(a, b);

['2', '1', '0'].map(Math.max);         // [NaN, NaN, NaN]
['2', '1', '0'].map(binary(Math.max)); // [2, 1, 2]
// Math.max('2', 0), Math.max('1', 1), Math.max('0', 2)
```

The general lesson: passing a function straight to `map`/`forEach` also passes the index and array. Write `x => fn(x)` unless you know `fn` ignores extra arguments.

front:
Fill in `binary` so the wrapped function receives exactly two arguments.

```js
____

['2', '1', '0'].map(binary(Math.max)); // [2, 1, 2]
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const binary = fn => (a, b) => fn(a, b);
```

`map` calls the wrapper with `(value, index, array)`. The wrapper forwards only `value` and `index`, so `Math.max('2', 0)` is `2` and the array never turns the result into `NaN`.

front: Why does `['6', '8', '10'].map(parseInt)` return `[6, NaN, 2]`, and how does a `unary` wrapper fix it?
back:
`map` passes `(value, index)`, and `parseInt` treats its second argument as the radix (number base). So the calls are `parseInt('8', 1)` → `NaN` and `parseInt('10', 2)` → `2`. A unary wrapper forwards only the first argument.

```js
const unary = fn => val => fn(val);

['6', '8', '10'].map(parseInt);        // [6, NaN, 2]
['6', '8', '10'].map(unary(parseInt)); // [6, 8, 10]
['6', '8', '10'].map(Number);          // [6, 8, 10] (simplest)
```

When you parse form or query-string values, write `s => parseInt(s, 10)` or use `Number(s)`. Never pass `parseInt` to `map` directly.

front:
Fill in `unary` so `parseInt` receives only the string, not `map`'s index.

```js
____

['6', '8', '10'].map(unary(Number.parseInt)); // [6, 8, 10]
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const unary = fn => val => fn(val);
```

Without the wrapper, `map` passes the index as `parseInt`'s radix and you get `[6, NaN, 2]`. The wrapper accepts one parameter and ignores the rest.

front: Why would you limit how many arguments a function receives ("fixed arity")?
What is a nullary wrapper (`fn => () => fn()`), and what bug does it prevent in `button.addEventListener('click', refresh)`?
back:
A nullary wrapper calls `fn` with no arguments, whatever the wrapper itself receives. With `addEventListener('click', refresh)`, `refresh` gets the click `event` as its first argument. If `refresh(options)` has an optional parameter, the event is silently used as `options`.

```js
const nullary = fn => () => fn();

function refresh(options = { force: false }) { /* ... */ }

button.addEventListener('click', refresh);          // options = MouseEvent!
button.addEventListener('click', nullary(refresh)); // options = default
button.addEventListener('click', () => refresh());  // same, inline
```

The inline arrow is the everyday form. The point is to be deliberate about which arguments a callback receives.

front: How would you implement your own `bind(fn, context, ...boundArgs)` using `apply`?

back:
One solution:

```js
fn.apply(context, [...boundArgs, ...args])
```

`apply` takes the `this` value and an array of arguments. Spreading `boundArgs` before `args` gives partial application: the pre-filled values come first. `fn.call(context, ...boundArgs, ...args)` is equivalent.

front: Where do `call`, `apply`, and `bind` actually show up in modern code?
How does a `bindKey(obj, 'method')` helper differ from `obj.method.bind(obj)`?

back:
One solution:

```js
context[key].apply(context, [...boundArgs, ...args])
```

Reading `context[key]` inside the returned function means the method is resolved on every call, not once up front. `apply(context, ...)` sets `this` so `this.user` works.

front: What's the difference between `fn.apply(obj, args)` and `fn.apply(obj, ...args)` when `args` is an array?

back:
One solution:

```js
printThisAndData.apply(obj, data);
```

`apply` takes `this` (`obj`) and the arguments as a single array. Writing `apply(obj, ...data)` would throw a `TypeError`, because `1` isn't an array-like object.

front: When `data` is an array, how do `fn.call(obj, data)` and `fn.call(obj, ...data)` differ?

back:
One solution:

```js
printThisAndData.call(obj, ...data);
```

`call` expects arguments one by one after `this`. The spread operator turns `[1, 2, 3]` into `1, 2, 3`. Passing `data` unspread gives the function one array argument.

front: How do you permanently bind several of an object's methods to that object, so they still work when passed as callbacks?

back:
One solution:

```js
obj[name] = obj[name].bind(obj);
```

`bind` returns a new function whose `this` is fixed to `obj` and which forwards all arguments. After the reassignment, destructuring `click` or passing `view.click` as a listener still works.

front: What does it mean that JavaScript functions are "first-class objects", and which built-in function methods control `this`?
What practical benefits do pure functions and immutable data give you when testing and debugging?
back:
A pure function's output depends only on its inputs, and immutable data can't be changed behind your back. Tests need no setup or mocks (input in, expect output), and when a value is wrong you only have to look at the function that produced it, not at every place that might have mutated it.

```js
// Pure: trivial to test
const totalPrice = items => items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
totalPrice([{ price: 5, qty: 2 }]); // 10, every time
```

Small pure functions are also easy to reuse and combine (compose) into bigger features. The rest of the app, which does I/O and state updates, then calls them at the edges.

front: Is `const push = (arr, val) => arr.push(val)` a pure function? What would a pure version look like?
back:
No. It mutates the caller's array (a side effect), and it returns the new length, not an array. A pure version returns a new array and leaves the input untouched.

```js
const push = (arr, val) => arr.push(val);     // impure
const append = (arr, val) => [...arr, val];   // pure

const a = [1];
push(a, 2);   // 2  (the length!), and a is now [1, 2]
append(a, 3); // [1, 2, 3], and a is still [1, 2]
```

A pure function returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself: no mutation, no I/O, no global writes.

One solution:

```js
const concat = (arr, val) => [...arr, val];
```

Spreading copies the existing elements into a new array literal, then adds `val`. The input array is untouched. `arr.concat(val)` also works, but it flattens `val` one level if `val` is itself an array.

front: What makes a function "higher-order"? Show it with a helper that turns `isEven` into `isOdd`.

Fill in the higher-order `inverse` so `isOdd` returns the opposite of `isEven`.

```js
const isEven = num => num % 2 === 0;

____
const isOdd = inverse(isEven);

isOdd(3); // true
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const inverse = fn => (...args) => !fn(...args);
```

`inverse` takes a function and returns a new function. The returned function forwards all its arguments to `fn` and negates the result.

front: How do you add an item to an array without mutating it, and why does that matter for React state?
back:
Create a new array: `[...items, newItem]`. The original stays unchanged. React compares state by reference, so mutating the existing array (`push`) and setting the same reference may not trigger a re-render.

```js
const items = [1, 2, 3];
const next = [...items, 4]; // next: [1, 2, 3, 4], items still [1, 2, 3]

setTodos([...todos, newTodo]);  // correct
todos.push(newTodo);             // mutation: avoid
setTodos(todos);                 // same reference, no re-render
```

`const` does not make an array immutable. It only stops reassignment. Non-mutating helpers such as `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, and `with` (ES2023) return copies.

One solution:

```js
const newArr = [...otherArr, 4];
```

Spread copies the elements into a new array, so `otherArr` keeps its original contents. Compare `otherArr.push(4)`, which changes the original array in place.

front: What are the core ideas of functional programming, as used in everyday JavaScript?
back:
Four ideas: **pure functions** (same input gives same output, no side effects), **immutability** (make new values instead of changing old ones), **higher-order functions** (functions that take or return functions), and **composition** (building bigger behavior by chaining small functions).

```js
const activeNames = users
  .filter(u => u.active)   // higher-order, pure callback
  .map(u => u.name)        // returns a new array
  .toSorted();             // non-mutating sort
```

You don't need a full FP style to benefit. Keeping calculations pure and state updates immutable already makes React and API code easier to test.

front: How do you write a generator that cycles through an array's values forever, for example rotating through `['red', 'green', 'blue']`?

back:
One solution:

```js
const cycle = function* (arr) {
```

The `*` makes it a generator function. Calling it returns an iterator instead of running the body, and each `next()` runs the body up to the next `yield`. Arrow functions can't be generators.

front: How can a generator receive a value through `next(value)`? Show it with a "repeat" generator whose value can be changed.

back:
One solution:

```js
if (newV !== undefined) v = newV;
```

`yield v` returns whatever the caller passed to `next()`. A plain `next()` passes `undefined`, so the check keeps the current value unless a new one was sent.

front: How do you write a generator `generateWhile(seed, predicate, next)` that keeps yielding values while a condition holds?

back:
One solution:

```js
while (predicate(val)) {
```

The predicate is checked before every `yield`. Once `val` becomes `6`, `6 <= 5` is false, the loop exits, and the generator is done.

front: Why is `data.filter(isEven).reduce(add, 0)` an example of higher-order functions, and what do you gain from writing it this way?

Fill in the predicate so `filter` keeps only even numbers.

```js
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
____

const data = [2, 3, 1, 5, 4, 6];
data.filter(isEven);                // [2, 4, 6]
data.filter(isEven).reduce(add, 0); // 12
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const isEven = num => num % 2 === 0;
```

A predicate returns true or false for one item. `filter` calls it for every element and keeps the ones that return true. Naming it makes the pipeline read like a sentence.

front: In Node, how do you save a JavaScript object to a `.json` file?

back:
One solution:

```js
writeFileSync(`${filename}.json`, JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2))
```

`fs` writes strings or bytes, not objects, so you serialize first. The third argument of `JSON.stringify` indents the output, making the file readable in diffs.

front: In the browser, how do you let the user download a JavaScript object as a `.json` file?

back:
One solution:

```js
const blob = new Blob([JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2)], {
```

A `Blob` is raw file data held in memory. It takes an array of parts (here, a single JSON string) plus a MIME type. `URL.createObjectURL(blob)` then gives it a temporary `blob:` URL that the `<a download>` link can save.

front: What does `a && b` actually return in JavaScript, and why can `{count && <List />}` render a stray `0` in React?
back:
`&&` returns one of its operands, not necessarily a boolean. If `a` is falsy it returns `a`, otherwise it returns `b`. With booleans that works out to the usual AND table, but with other values you get the value itself.

```js
const and = (a, b) => a && b;

and(true, false); // false
and('a', 'b');    // 'b'
and(0, 'x');      // 0   (first falsy operand)
and(null, 1);     // null
```

In React, `{count && <List />}` renders `0` when `count` is `0`, because `0` is falsy and gets returned. Write `{count > 0 && <List />}` instead.

front:
Fill in `and` using the logical AND operator.

```js
____

and(true, true);  // true
and(true, false); // false
and(0, 'x');      // 0 (not false!)
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const and = (a, b) => a && b;
```

`&&` returns the first falsy operand, or the last operand if all are truthy. That's why `and(0, 'x')` is `0`. Use `Boolean(a && b)` if you need a real boolean.

front: How do you express NAND ("not both true") in JavaScript, and for which inputs is it `true`?
back:
`!(a && b)`. It is `true` unless both operands are truthy. By De Morgan's law it is the same as `!a || !b`, meaning "at least one is false".

```js
const nand = (a, b) => !(a && b);

nand(true, true);   // false
nand(true, false);  // true
nand(false, false); // true
```

A real use is a disabled check: `disabled={!(isValid && isOnline)}`, which disables the button unless the form is valid and the user is online.

front:
Fill in `nand` so it returns `false` only when both inputs are `true`.

```js
____

nand(true, true);   // false
nand(true, false);  // true
nand(false, false); // true
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const nand = (a, b) => !(a && b);
```

AND the values, then negate the result. The equivalent `!a || !b` reads as "at least one is false". Both return a real boolean because of the `!`.

front: How do you express NOR ("neither is true") in JavaScript, and what's an equivalent form?
back:
`!(a || b)`. It is `true` only when both operands are falsy. By De Morgan's law it equals `!a && !b`, meaning "not a and not b".

```js
const nor = (a, b) => !(a || b);

nor(true, true);   // false
nor(true, false);  // false
nor(false, false); // true
```

Example: `const showEmptyState = !(hasItems || isLoading);`. Show the empty state only when there are no items and nothing is loading.

front:
Fill in `nor` so it returns `true` only when both inputs are `false`.

```js
____

nor(true, true);   // false
nor(true, false);  // false
nor(false, false); // true
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const nor = (a, b) => !(a || b);
```

OR the values, then negate the result. It is equivalent to `!a && !b`.

front: How do you combine two predicate functions with AND or OR, for example `both(isEven, isPositive)`?

back:
One solution:

```js
const both = (f, g) => (...args) => f(...args) && g(...args);
```

`both` returns a new function. That function forwards all its arguments to each predicate and ANDs the results. `-2` is even but not positive, so the result is `false`.

front: What does `a || b` return in JavaScript, and why is `??` often better for default values?
back:
`||` returns the first truthy operand, or the last operand if none is truthy. It does not have to return a boolean. That makes `value || fallback` a default pattern, but it also replaces valid falsy values like `0` and `''`. `??` falls back only for `null` or `undefined`.

```js
const or = (a, b) => a || b;
or(false, true); // true
or('', 'x');     // 'x'

const pageSize = input || 10;  // input 0  → 10 (bug)
const pageSize2 = input ?? 10; // input 0  → 0
```

For form fields and API values where `0`, `''`, or `false` are meaningful, use `??` for defaults.

front: How do you get a one-letter weekday label (like `M` for Monday) from a JavaScript `Date`, and why can't you use it as a unique key?
back:
Call `date.toLocaleDateString(locale, { weekday: 'narrow' })`. It returns the locale's shortest weekday form, usually one letter, but letters repeat: in English Tuesday and Thursday are both `'T'`, and Saturday and Sunday are both `'S'`.

```js
const narrowDayName = (date, locale) =>
  date.toLocaleDateString(locale, { weekday: 'narrow' });

const mon = new Date(2024, 4, 27); // May 27 2024, local time (month is 0-based)
narrowDayName(mon, 'en-US'); // 'M'
narrowDayName(mon, 'de-DE'); // 'M' (Montag)
narrowDayName(new Date(2024, 4, 28), 'en-US'); // 'T' (Tuesday)
narrowDayName(new Date(2024, 4, 30), 'en-US'); // 'T' (Thursday)
```

Use it only for display, such as calendar column headers. For logic, use `date.getDay()` (0 = Sunday … 6 = Saturday). Leaving `locale` as `undefined` uses the user's default locale. Watch out for `new Date('2024-05-27')`: a date-only ISO string is parsed as UTC midnight, so in the Americas it shows as Sunday in local time.

front:
Dates: return the single-letter weekday label (`'M'`, `'T'`, …) for `date` in the given locale. Fill in the function body.

```js
const narrowDayName = (date, locale) =>
  ____

const mon = new Date(2024, 4, 27); // May 27 2024, local (month is 0-based)
narrowDayName(mon, 'en-US'); // 'M'
narrowDayName(mon, 'de-DE'); // 'M' (Montag)
```
back:
One solution:

```js
  date.toLocaleDateString(locale, { weekday: 'narrow' });
```

The `weekday` option accepts `'long'` (`'Monday'`), `'short'` (`'Mon'`) and `'narrow'` (`'M'`). Narrow labels are not unique (Tuesday and Thursday are both `'T'` in English), so use them for display only and use `getDay()` for logic.

front: When a library function takes a main input plus required "special" arguments (e.g. a regex builder's `repeat(pattern, times, lazy)`), where should the special arguments go in the signature, and why?

back:
One solution:

```js
const result = repeat(3, true, 'a');
```

Required settings that change how the function behaves (count, lazy flag) go first so they are easy to spot and hard to forget; the main input comes last. Bare `3, true` is still unclear, which is why many APIs take an options object instead: `repeat({ times: 3, lazy: true }, 'a')`.

front: In a regex-builder library, how can a single `anythingFrom()` function accept both individual characters and ranges, and what regex should `anythingFrom(['a', 'c'], ['x', 'z'])` produce?
back:
Treat each string argument as a single character and each two-element array as a range `[start, end]`; join them all into one character class. So `anythingFrom(['a', 'c'], ['x', 'z'])` produces `[a-cx-z]`, instead of the clumsy `(?:[a-c]|[x-z])` you get by combining `or()` and `range()`.

```js
anythingFrom(['a', 'z']);                   // [a-z]
anythingFrom(['a', 'c'], ['x', 'z']);       // [a-cx-z]
anythingFrom('a', 'b', 'c', 'x', 'y', 'z'); // [abcxyz]
anythingBut(['0', '9']);                    // [^0-9]
```

The design idea: when a use case is very common, give it one direct function whose argument shapes (string vs. pair) are easy to tell apart. A matching `anythingBut()` builds the negated class `[^...]`. A real implementation must also escape `]`, `\`, `^` and `-` inside the class.

front:
Regex-builder API: `anythingFrom()` takes single characters as strings and ranges as `[start, end]` arrays, and returns one character class. Write the call that matches any of a–c or x–z.

```js
anythingFrom(['a', 'z']);                   // [a-z]
____
anythingFrom('a', 'b', 'c', 'x', 'y', 'z'); // [abcxyz]
```
back:
One solution:

```js
anythingFrom(['a', 'c'], ['x', 'z']); // [a-cx-z]
```

Each two-element array becomes a range and everything is merged into one character class. The alternative `or(range('a', 'c'), range('x', 'z'))` gives the longer `(?:[a-c]|[x-z])`, which is why the library offers `anythingFrom()` for this common case.

front: When naming parts of a library whose users already know the domain (e.g. a regex builder), why call `\b` `wordBoundary` rather than a friendlier invented name like `wordSeparator`?

back:
One solution:

```js
const wordBoundary = '\\b';
```

`\b` is a word boundary: a zero-width position between a word character and a non-word character. Using the standard term lets users who know regex recognize it immediately. In a JS string you write `'\\b'` because `'\b'` alone is the backspace character.

front: Your library has consistent API conventions, but a new feature doesn't fit them. What is a good way to handle such edge cases?
back:
Handle them one at a time, but decide each one against the general strategy you already wrote down (e.g. "special arguments first", "use standard terms"), so the exception still feels consistent to users. Change the design only when several edge cases show the rule is wrong.

In practice:

- Pick the option that breaks the fewest existing conventions.
- Document the exception next to the rule it bends.
- If the same kind of exception keeps coming back, change the rule instead of adding more exceptions.

front: Which JavaScript value is not equal to itself, and how should you check for it (e.g. after `Number(input.value)` on a form field)?
back:
`NaN` ("Not a Number") is the only value where `x === x` is `false`, so `value === NaN` never works. Check with `Number.isNaN(value)`. Avoid the older global `isNaN()`: it converts its argument to a number first, so `isNaN('hello')` is `true` even though `'hello'` is a string, not `NaN`.

```js
const x = Math.sqrt(-1); // NaN
const y = 0 / 0;         // NaN

x === y;                 // false
x === NaN;               // false
Object.is(x, NaN);       // true

Number.isNaN(x);         // true
Number.isNaN('hello');   // false
isNaN('hello');          // true (coerces 'hello' to NaN first)

const qty = Number('abc'); // NaN from bad form input
Number.isNaN(qty);         // true -> show a validation error
```

Pitfall: `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is `-1`, but `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is `true`, because `includes` uses SameValueZero, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself. Also `Number('')` is `0`, not `NaN`, so check for empty input separately.

One solution:

```js
  if (Number.isNaN(qty)) return 'Enter a number';
```

`NaN` is the only value not equal to itself, so `===` can't detect it. `Number.isNaN()` returns `true` only for an actual `NaN`. The global `isNaN()` coerces first (`isNaN('hello')` is `true`), which is why `Number.isNaN()` is preferred.

front: Can you declare the same variable twice in one scope with `var`? With `let` or `const`?
back:
With `var`, yes: the second declaration is allowed (in strict mode too) and just reassigns. With `let` or `const`, no: it is a `SyntaxError`, and because the error is found while parsing, none of the script runs.

```js
var a = 'first';
var a = 'second'; // allowed, a is now 'second'

let b = 'first';
let b = 'second'; // SyntaxError: Identifier 'b' has already been declared
```

The same error appears if you mix them (`var q; let q;`). This is a feature: in a long file, accidentally reusing a name like `user` is caught immediately instead of silently overwriting the first value.

front:
Redeclaration: fill in the line that makes this script fail with the `SyntaxError` shown.

```js
var a = 'first';
var a = 'second'; // fine: var allows redeclaration

let b = 'first';
____ // SyntaxError: Identifier 'b' has already been declared
```
back:
One solution:

```js
let b = 'second';
```

`let` and `const` cannot be redeclared in the same scope, while `var` can (strict mode or not). The error is reported at parse time, so the whole script fails before any line runs. Reassigning is fine: `b = 'second';` works for `let`.

front: At the top level of a classic browser `<script>`, what is the difference between `var a` and `let b` regarding the global object (`window` / `globalThis`)?
A variable is declared inside an `if` or `{ }` block. When is it still accessible after the block closes: with `var`, or with `let`/`const`?

back:
One solution:

```js
  console.log(c); // 'var'
```

`var` is function-scoped, so `c` survives the end of the block and keeps its value. `let` and `const` are block-scoped, so `d` doesn't exist outside the `{ }` and reading it throws `ReferenceError`.

front: What happens if you read a variable before its declaration line: with `var` versus with `let`/`const`?

back:
One solution:

```js
  console.log(a); // undefined
```

The `var a` declaration is hoisted to the top of the function and initialized to `undefined`; the assignment `= 'var'` runs only when that line is reached. `let b` is hoisted too but stays in the temporal dead zone, so reading it early throws.

front: What habits keep hoisting (JavaScript moving declarations to the top of their scope) from causing bugs?
back:
Declare things before you use them, use `const`/`let` instead of `var`, and let a linter enforce it. Strict mode does not turn hoisting off, so don't rely on it for this.

- Declare variables, functions and classes above the code that uses them. ESLint's `no-use-before-define` rule flags violations.
- Default to `const`; use `let` only when you reassign; avoid `var`. Early use then throws a clear `ReferenceError` instead of giving `undefined`.
- Pick one function style per codebase (arrow functions in `const`, or `function` declarations). Only `function` declarations can be called before their line, so mixing styles makes the rules harder to predict.
- Use ES modules or `'use strict'`. Modules are strict automatically. Strict mode catches other mistakes, such as assigning to an undeclared variable, but hoisting still happens.

front: What error do you get if you call a function stored in a `const` (or read a `let`, or use a `class`) before its declaration line, and why?
back:
A `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'g' before initialization`. `let`, `const` and `class` declarations are hoisted, but they are not initialized to `undefined`; until the declaration line runs they are in the temporal dead zone (TDZ), and any access throws.

```js
console.log(y); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'y' before initialization
g();            // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'g' before initialization

let y = 2;
const g = () => 'Hey!';

console.log(y); // 2
g();            // 'Hey!'
```

Compare with `var`, which quietly gives `undefined`, and with `function g() {}` declarations, which are fully hoisted and callable before their line. The loud error points you straight at the ordering bug. (Each commented error stops the script; the lines are shown together for comparison.)

front:
Hoisting: `g` is an arrow function stored in a `const` and called before its declaration. What error is thrown? Fill in the comment.

```js
g(); // ____

const g = () => 'Hey!';
g(); // 'Hey!'
```
back:
One solution:

```js
g(); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'g' before initialization
```

`const` (like `let` and `class`) is hoisted but left uninitialized in the temporal dead zone until its line runs. If `g` were a `function g() {}` declaration, the early call would work, because function declarations are hoisted with their body.

front: If you call `f()` before `var f = () => 'Hi!'`, why do you get `TypeError: f is not a function` rather than a `ReferenceError`?
back:
Because only the `var f` declaration is hoisted and set to `undefined`; the arrow function is assigned when its line runs. So `f` exists but is `undefined`, and calling `undefined` is a `TypeError`.

```js
console.log(x); // undefined
f();            // TypeError: f is not a function

var x = 1;
var f = () => 'Hi!';

console.log(x); // 1
f();            // 'Hi!'
```

With `const f = ...` the same early call would throw `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'f' before initialization`, and with `function f() {}` it would work. The `TypeError` is your clue that a `var` was hoisted without its value. (The error stops the script; lines are shown together for comparison.)

front:
Hoisting: `f` is a `var` holding an arrow function, called before its line. What does the early call throw? Fill in the comment.

```js
console.log(x); // undefined
f(); // ____

var x = 1;
var f = () => 'Hi!';
```
back:
One solution:

```js
f(); // TypeError: f is not a function
```

`var f` is hoisted and initialized to `undefined`; the function is assigned only when its line runs. Calling `undefined` gives a `TypeError`, not a `ReferenceError`, because the variable itself exists.

front: What is "scope" in JavaScript, and how do global, function and block scope differ for `var`, `let` and `const`?
Of `var`, `let` and `const`, which should you use by default in modern JavaScript, and why?
What makes a thrown error useful to both the developer reading it and the code that catches it?

back:
One solution:

```js
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
```

A subclass inherits `name = 'Error'` from `Error.prototype` unless you set it, and `name` is what appears in logs and stack traces. Catch code can still tell the errors apart with `err instanceof ValidationError`.

front: When you catch an error from a lower-level call, how can you rethrow it with more context without losing the original error, and when should you handle it instead?

back:
One solution:

```js
    throw new Error(`Failed to load user ${id}`, { cause: err });
```

The `cause` option (ES2022, supported in all modern browsers and Node) stores the original error on `newError.cause`, so logs show both what you were doing and the underlying failure. Concatenating `err.message` into a string instead would lose the original stack trace.

front: What is a "silent fail" such as `.catch(() => {})` or an empty `catch` block, and why is it harmful?

Replace the silent `.catch(() => {})` so a failed orders request is logged to the console and the user sees an error message (`showError(message)` is available). Fill in the line.

```js
fetch('/api/orders')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(renderOrders)
  ____
```
back:
One solution:

```js
  .catch(err => { console.error('Loading orders failed:', err); showError('Could not load orders'); });
```

An empty `.catch(() => {})` swallows the error: the page just stays empty and nobody knows why. Logging keeps the cause for debugging, and `showError` tells the user something went wrong. Also note that `fetch` does not reject on HTTP 404/500; check `res.ok` and throw if it is false so those errors reach the `catch` too.

front: Why is a function that mutates its argument (e.g. `user.age++`) riskier than one that returns a new object, and how do you write the non-mutating version?

back:
One solution:

```js
const birthday = user => ({ ...user, age: user.age + 1 });
```

The spread copies all properties into a new object and `age` overrides the copied value. The parentheses are required: without them `{ ...user, ... }` is parsed as a function body and is a `SyntaxError`. This is the same pattern as React's `setUser(u => ({ ...u, age: u.age + 1 }))`.

front: Your `calculateInvoice` function keeps growing as discounts and shipping are added. How should you restructure it, and why?

back:
One solution:

```js
  items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity, 0);
```

`reduce` walks the array carrying a running total; the `0` start value matters, because without it an empty cart would throw a `TypeError`. Pulling this step into its own named function is what keeps `calculateInvoice` short and each step testable.

front: How do you flatten deeply nested `if`s and loops, such as order processing that checks paid, has items, item active and item value?

back:
One solution:

```js
  if (!order.paid || order.items.length === 0) return;
```

A guard clause handles the "nothing to do" case first and returns, so the rest of the function isn't wrapped in `if (order.paid) { if (order.items.length > 0) { ... } }`. Moving the condition into a named predicate (`if (!isProcessable(order)) return;`) is an equally good answer.

front: How do you add N minutes to a JavaScript `Date` without changing the original, and why multiply by `60_000`?

back:
One solution:

```js
d.setTime(d.getTime() + n * 60_000);
```

`getTime()` returns the timestamp in milliseconds and a minute is `60 * 1000` ms. `setTime()` mutates the date it is called on, which is why the function works on the copy `d` instead of the argument.

front: How do you add N hours to a `Date`, and on a daylight-saving (DST) day, how does "+24 hours" differ from "same time tomorrow"?

back:
One solution:

```js
d.setTime(d.getTime() + n * 3_600_000);
```

One hour is `1000 * 60 * 60 = 3_600_000` ms. Adding milliseconds to the timestamp moves the instant by exactly N hours; across a DST switch the local clock time will shift by an hour, which is correct for a duration.

front: How do you add N calendar days to a `Date`, and why is `setDate(getDate() + n)` safer than adding `n * 86_400_000` ms?

back:
One solution:

```js
d.setDate(d.getDate() + n);
```

`setDate()` accepts out-of-range values and rolls over (Oct 38 → Nov 7), so month and year boundaries are handled for you. It keeps the local wall-clock time, so it stays correct on DST days where adding `86_400_000` ms would drift by an hour.

front: Which two `Date` methods let you add N seconds to a date, and why must you copy the date before calling them?

back:
One solution:

```js
d.setTime(d.getTime() + n * 1000);
```

`Date` works in milliseconds, so seconds are multiplied by `1000`. `setTime()` mutates, which is why it is called on the copy `d`, not on `date`.

front: Why is `new Date(2020, 9, 20) === new Date(2020, 9, 20)` false, and how do you check that two `Date` objects represent the same moment?

Dates: return `true` when two `Date` objects represent the same instant. Fill in the comparison (`===` on the objects themselves won't work).

```js
const isSameDate = (dateA, dateB) =>
  ____;

isSameDate(new Date(2020, 9, 20), new Date(2020, 9, 20)); // true
new Date(2020, 9, 20) === new Date(2020, 9, 20);          // false
```
back:
One solution:

```js
dateA.getTime() === dateB.getTime()
```

`===` compares object references, so compare the numeric timestamps instead. `dateA.toISOString() === dateB.toISOString()` also works, but throws a `RangeError` if either date is invalid.

front: Why does `dateA > dateB` correctly compare two `Date` objects, when `dateA === dateB` does not?
back:
Relational operators (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) convert both objects to primitives first, and a `Date` converts to its millisecond timestamp via `valueOf()`. So `>` compares numbers. `===` does no conversion and compares object identity.

```js
const isAfterDate = (dateA, dateB) => dateA > dateB;

isAfterDate(new Date(2020, 9, 21), new Date(2020, 9, 20)); // true
new Date(2020, 9, 21).valueOf(); // a number like 1603263600000 (depends on time zone)
```

Real-world use: "is this coupon expired?" → `new Date() > coupon.expiresAt`. Make sure both sides are `Date` objects, not strings: comparing two ISO strings with `>` compares text, which only works when both use the same format and offset.

front:
Dates: write `isAfterDate`, returning `true` when `dateA` is later than `dateB`, in the same style as `isBeforeDate`.

```js
const isBeforeDate = (dateA, dateB) => dateA < dateB;
____

isAfterDate(new Date(2020, 9, 21), new Date(2020, 9, 20)); // true
isAfterDate(new Date(2020, 9, 20), new Date(2020, 9, 21)); // false
```
back:
One solution:

```js
const isAfterDate = (dateA, dateB) => dateA > dateB;
```

`>` converts both `Date` objects to their millisecond timestamps via `valueOf()`, so it compares instants. `dateA.getTime() > dateB.getTime()` is the explicit equivalent.

front: How do you count the calendar months between two dates with `getFullYear()`/`getMonth()`, and what does that formula ignore?
back:
Months have different lengths, so don't divide milliseconds. Instead: `(yearB - yearA) * 12 + (monthB - monthA)`. This counts month boundaries crossed and **ignores the day of the month**: Jan 31 → Feb 1 counts as 1 month, Jan 1 → Jan 31 as 0.

```js
const dateDifferenceInMonths = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  Math.max(
    (dateFinal.getFullYear() - dateInitial.getFullYear()) * 12 +
      dateFinal.getMonth() - dateInitial.getMonth(),
    0
  );

dateDifferenceInMonths(new Date(2017, 11, 13), new Date(2018, 3, 29)); // 4 (Dec → Apr)
```

`Math.max(…, 0)` clamps a reversed range to 0. If you need "full months elapsed", subtract 1 when `dateFinal.getDate() < dateInitial.getDate()`. Avoid `new Date('2018-04-01')` here: date-only strings parse as UTC and can land in March in US time zones.

One solution:

```js
(dateFinal.getFullYear() - dateInitial.getFullYear()) * 12 + dateFinal.getMonth() - dateInitial.getMonth()
```

Years × 12 plus the month difference. Month lengths vary, so this uses calendar fields instead of dividing milliseconds. It ignores the day of the month (Jan 31 → Feb 1 counts as 1).

front: How do you compute the difference between two dates in weeks, and why might the result come out fractional?
back:
Subtract the dates (which gives milliseconds) and divide by the milliseconds in a week: `(b - a) / 604_800_000` (`1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 7`).

```js
const dateDifferenceInWeeks = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 604_800_000;

dateDifferenceInWeeks(new Date(2023, 0, 1), new Date(2023, 0, 8)); // 1
dateDifferenceInWeeks(new Date(2023, 0, 1), new Date(2023, 0, 11)); // 1.4285714285714286
```

The result is fractional whenever the span isn't whole weeks, and a span that crosses a DST change in local time is an hour short or long (e.g. 0.994…). Wrap it in `Math.floor()` for "full weeks" or `Math.round()` for "about N weeks".

front:
Dates: return the difference between two dates in weeks. Fill in the body.

```js
const dateDifferenceInWeeks = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  ____;

dateDifferenceInWeeks(new Date(2023, 0, 1), new Date(2023, 0, 8)); // 1
```
back:
One solution:

```js
(dateFinal - dateInitial) / 604_800_000
```

Subtracting two `Date` objects converts them to millisecond timestamps. A week is `1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 7 = 604_800_000` ms.

front: What does subtracting one `Date` from another return in JavaScript, and how do you turn it into seconds?
back:
`dateB - dateA` returns a **number of milliseconds**: the `-` operator converts each `Date` to its timestamp. Divide by `1000` for seconds.

```js
const dateDifferenceInSeconds = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 1_000;

dateDifferenceInSeconds(
  new Date(2020, 11, 24, 0, 0, 15),
  new Date(2020, 11, 24, 0, 0, 17)
); // 2
```

Typical use: measure how long a request took (`const ms = Date.now() - startedAt`). The result is negative if the "final" date is earlier. In TypeScript, write `b.getTime() - a.getTime()`; the compiler rejects arithmetic on `Date` objects.

front:
Dates: return the number of seconds between two dates. Fill in the body.

```js
const dateDifferenceInSeconds = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  ____;

dateDifferenceInSeconds(
  new Date(2020, 11, 24, 0, 0, 15),
  new Date(2020, 11, 24, 0, 0, 17)
); // 2
```
back:
One solution:

```js
(dateFinal - dateInitial) / 1_000
```

`-` converts both dates to millisecond timestamps, so the difference is in ms; divide by 1000 for seconds.

front: How do you compute the hours between two `Date`s, and when is "the same clock time on the next day" not 24 hours apart?
back:
Subtract the dates and divide by the milliseconds in an hour: `(b - a) / 3_600_000`. The result is real elapsed time, so across a daylight-saving change, 10:25 today to 10:25 tomorrow is **23 or 25 hours**, not 24.

```js
const dateDifferenceInHours = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 3_600_000;

dateDifferenceInHours(new Date(2021, 3, 24, 10, 25), new Date(2021, 3, 25, 10, 25)); // 24

// US time zones (DST began Mar 14 2021):
dateDifferenceInHours(new Date(2021, 2, 13, 10, 25), new Date(2021, 2, 14, 10, 25)); // 23
```

That is usually correct for billing or shift length ("how long was this open?"), but surprising if you expected calendar math.

front:
Dates: return the number of hours between two dates. Fill in the body.

```js
const dateDifferenceInHours = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  ____;

dateDifferenceInHours(new Date(2021, 3, 24, 10, 25), new Date(2021, 3, 25, 10, 25)); // 24
```
back:
One solution:

```js

const isWeekend = date => date.getDay() % 6 === 0;

In US time zones that is still Friday evening locally, and `getDay()` reads local time, so it returns 5. front: An API sends `created_at: 1704326400` (a Unix timestamp). How do you convert between Unix timestamps and JavaScript `Date` objects?

const toTimestamp = date => Math.floor(date.getTime() / 1000);
const fromTimestamp = timestamp => new Date(timestamp * 1000);

toTimestamp(new Date('2024-01-04T00:00:00Z')); // 1704326400
fromTimestamp(1704326400).toISOString();       // '2024-01-04T00:00:00.000Z'
Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);                 // "now" as a Unix timestamp
```

Classic bug: `new Date(1704326400)` without `* 1000` gives a date in January 1970. Timestamps are time-zone independent; the zone only matters when you display the date.

const dayOfYear = date =>

    Date.UTC(date.getFullYear(), 0, 0)) / 86_400_000;

dayOfYear(new Date(2024, 8, 28)); // 272
dayOfYear(new Date(2024, 0, 1));  // 1
dayOfYear(new Date(2024, 11, 31)); // 366 (leap year)
```

`Date.UTC(y, 0, 0)` uses day 0 of January, which rolls back to Dec 31. The naive local version returns 271 for Sep 28 2024 in US time zones.

```js
const isDateValid = (...val) => !Number.isNaN(new Date(...val).valueOf());

isDateValid('1995-12-17T03:24:00'); // true
isDateValid('Duck');                // false
isDateValid(1995, 11, 17);          // true
isDateValid(1995, 11, 17, 'Duck');  // false

// Still "valid", but probably not what the user meant:
isDateValid(2023, 1, 31);  // true — rolls over to Mar 3 2023
isDateValid(null);         // true — null becomes 0 (Jan 1 1970)
```

For form input, validate the format yourself (e.g. `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/`) and check the parts round-trip (`d.getMonth() === month`). Non-ISO strings like `'December 17, 1995'` parse in browsers but the format is implementation-defined.

Create **February 29** of that year: `new Date(year, 1, 29)` (month 1 = February). In a leap year it stays in February; otherwise it rolls over to March 1. So check `getMonth() === 1`.

```js
const isLeapYear = year => new Date(year, 1, 29).getMonth() === 1;

isLeapYear(2019); // false
isLeapYear(2020); // true
isLeapYear(1900); // false (century, not divisible by 400)
isLeapYear(2000); // true
```

The explicit rule is `(y % 4 === 0 && y % 100 !== 0) || y % 400 === 0`. It relies on the same day-overflow behaviour that makes `setDate(getDate() + n)` work. Watch out: years 0–99 in the constructor are treated as 1900–1999.

front: What does `date.toISOString()` return, and what happens to a `Date` when you `JSON.stringify` it for an API request?
back:
`toISOString()` returns the instant in **UTC** in the fixed format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ` (the `Z` means UTC). `JSON.stringify` calls `Date.prototype.toJSON()`, which uses `toISOString()`, so dates in a request body are sent as that string automatically.

```js
const d = new Date('2024-01-06T19:20:34+02:00');
d.toISOString();               // '2024-01-06T17:20:34.000Z'
JSON.stringify({ dueAt: d });  // '{"dueAt":"2024-01-06T17:20:34.000Z"}'
```

This is the right format for storing and transmitting instants. Two gotchas: `JSON.parse` does **not** turn the string back into a `Date` (call `new Date(str)` yourself), and `toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value` on an Invalid Date.

const minDate = (...dates) => new Date(Math.min(...dates));
const maxDate = (...dates) => new Date(Math.max(...dates));

  new Date(2018, 2, 12),
  new Date(2016, 0, 9),

minDate(...dates).toDateString(); // 'Sat Jan 09 2016'
maxDate(...dates).toDateString(); // 'Mon Mar 12 2018'
minDate();                        // Invalid Date (Math.min() is Infinity)
```

Guard the empty case in real code (e.g. "latest order date" for a user with no orders). For very large arrays, spreading can exceed the argument limit; `dates.reduce((a, b) => (b < a ? b : a))` avoids that.

front: Why does `Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100` give `1` instead of `1.01`, and how does the `` `${n}e${decimals}` `` trick fix it?

`1.005` can't be stored exactly in binary; `1.005 * 100` is `100.49999…`, which rounds down. Building the string `'1.005e2'` and letting `Math.round` convert it parses the decimal text directly as `100.5`, which rounds to `101`; then `'101e-2'` shifts back.

```js
const round = (n, decimals = 0) =>
  Number(`${Math.round(`${n}e${decimals}`)}e-${decimals}`);

round(1.005, 2);                // 1.01
Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100;  // 1
round(1234.5678, 1);            // 1234.6
```

Limits: it returns `NaN` for numbers that already print in exponent form (`round(1e-7, 2)`), and `Math.round` rounds halves toward +∞, so `round(-1.005, 2)` is `-1`. It returns a number for further math; for display, use `Intl.NumberFormat`, and for money, store integer cents.

front: How do you display order number `1234` as the fixed-width string `'001234'`, and what goes wrong with negative numbers?
back:

```js
const padNumber = (n, l) => `${n}`.padStart(l, '0');

padNumber(1_234, 6);   // '001234'
padNumber(123_456, 3); // '123456' (never truncates)
padNumber(-5, 3);      // '0-5'  ← the sign gets padded too
```

front: What does `num.toLocaleString()` with **no arguments** output, and why should you usually pass a locale explicitly?
back:
It formats with the **runtime's default locale**: `'123,456'` in an `en-US` browser, `'123.456'` in a German one. That makes the output depend on the machine running the code, not on your app's settings.

```js
const formatNumber = (num, locale) => num.toLocaleString(locale);

formatNumber(123_456);                  // depends on the environment
formatNumber(123_456, 'en-US');         // '123,456'
formatNumber(15_675_436_903, 'de-DE');  // '15.675.436.903'
```

Real-world bug: a server-rendered React page formats with the server's locale, the browser re-renders with the user's, and you get a hydration mismatch. Pass the user's chosen locale (or `navigator.language` on the client only) explicitly. Reuse one `Intl.NumberFormat` instance when formatting long lists.

front: How do you write an awaitable `sleep(ms)` in JavaScript, and does `await sleep(300)` freeze the page?

back:
One solution:

```js
new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
```

`setTimeout` calls `resolve` after the delay, which settles the Promise and lets the `await` continue. The delay is a minimum, not a guarantee: a busy main thread can make it later.

front: What does `setTimeout(fn, ms, ...args)` do with the arguments after `ms`, and what does it return?

```
back:

const delay = (fn, ms, ...args) => setTimeout(fn, ms, ...args);
```

Arguments after the delay are forwarded to the callback. Returning the timer ID lets the caller cancel it with `clearTimeout`.

front: How do you get the full weekday name of a `Date` (`'Monday'`, `'Montag'`) in a given language?
back:

```js
const dayName = (date, locale) =>
  date.toLocaleDateString(locale, { weekday: 'long' });

const d = new Date(2024, 4, 27); // May 27 2024 (month is 0-based)
dayName(d, 'en-US'); // 'Monday'
dayName(d, 'de-DE'); // 'Montag'
dayName(d, 'fr-FR'); // 'lundi'
```

No hand-written `['Sunday', 'Monday', …]` array needed, and it's translated for free. Avoid building dates from strings like `'05/27/2024'`: non-ISO string formats are implementation-defined.

```

Every element has `scrollLeft`/`scrollTop`: the number of pixels its content is scrolled. `document.documentElement` (`<html>`) scrolls the page, so the default gives the same values as `window.scrollX`/`window.scrollY`.

Both properties are writable: `el.scrollTop = 0` jumps a chat panel back to the top.

front: How do you measure the width of the page's vertical scrollbar in JavaScript, and why might it return `0`?
back:
Subtract the `<html>` element's inner width from the window's width: `window.innerWidth` includes the scrollbar, `document.documentElement.clientWidth` does not.

```js
const getScrollbarWidth = () =>
  window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth;

getScrollbarWidth(); // 15 on Windows desktop, 0 on most phones
```

It returns `0` when the page doesn't overflow, or when the OS uses overlay scrollbars (mobile, macOS by default) that take no space.

Typical use: when you open a modal and set `overflow: hidden` on `<body>`, the scrollbar disappears and the page jumps sideways; adding `padding-right` equal to this width prevents the jump. In modern CSS, `scrollbar-gutter: stable` on `<html>` solves the same problem without JavaScript.

front: How can you apply several inline styles to an element in one call, and which kind of CSS property does that trick silently fail to set?

back:
One solution:

```js
const addStyles = (el, styles) => Object.assign(el.style, styles);
```

`el.style` is a `CSSStyleDeclaration` object whose properties are CSS properties in camelCase, so `Object.assign()` sets them all at once and leaves other inline styles alone.

Caveat: custom properties like `'--accent'` can't be set this way; use `el.style.setProperty()`.

front: What's the most reliable way to set one inline CSS property on an element when the property name is a string like `'font-size'` or `'--accent'`?
back:
Use `el.style.setProperty(name, value)`. It takes the real CSS name (kebab-case), and it is the only way that also works for CSS custom properties (`--*`).

```js
const setStyle = (el, prop, value) => el.style.setProperty(prop, value);

setStyle(document.querySelector('p'), 'font-size', '20px');
setStyle(document.documentElement, '--accent', '#0a7'); // theme variable
```

Plain assignment, `el.style.fontSize = '20px'`, is fine when you write the name in code. `el.style['font-size'] = '20px'` also works in modern browsers, but `el.style['--accent'] = '#0a7'` silently does nothing.

To remove an inline style, use `el.style.removeProperty('font-size')` (or set it to `''`).

One solution:

```js
const setStyle = (el, prop, value) => el.style.setProperty(prop, value);
```

`setProperty()` takes the CSS name exactly as written in a stylesheet, so kebab-case and `--custom` names both work. Assigning `el.style[prop] = value` works for normal properties but silently ignores custom properties.

Setting a variable on `document.documentElement` (`:root`) updates every rule that uses `var(--accent)`.

front: Why can `el.style.fontSize` be `''` even though the text is clearly 16px, and how do you read the style the browser actually applied?
back:
`el.style` only contains **inline** styles (the `style="..."` attribute). To read the final value after all stylesheets, inheritance and defaults are applied, use `getComputedStyle(el)`.

```js
const getStyle = (el, prop) => getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue(prop);

const p = document.querySelector('p');
p.style.fontSize;         // '' (no inline style)
getStyle(p, 'font-size'); // '16px'
```

Computed values are *resolved*: lengths come back in `px` and colors as `rgb(...)`, even if the CSS said `1rem` or `#fff`. The object is read-only; to change a style, write to `el.style` or toggle a class.

`getPropertyValue()` takes kebab-case names and works for custom properties too (`getStyle(document.documentElement, '--accent')`).

front: How do you get an element's distance in pixels from the top of the whole document (not just the viewport)?
back:
Take its position relative to the viewport, `el.getBoundingClientRect().top`, and add how far the page is scrolled, `window.scrollY`.

```js
const getVerticalOffset = el =>
  el.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY;

getVerticalOffset(document.querySelector('.comments')); // 1240
```

The older approach loops up the `offsetParent` chain, summing `offsetTop` (distance to the nearest positioned ancestor):

```js
let offset = 0;
for (let node = el; node; node = node.offsetParent) offset += node.offsetTop;
```

That loop ignores CSS transforms and ancestor borders, and `offsetParent` is `null` for `display: none` or `position: fixed` elements, so prefer `getBoundingClientRect()`.

To actually scroll there, `el.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' })` is simpler than computing the offset.

front: In Node.js, how do you compute the SHA-256 hex digest of a string, and does wrapping the call in `setTimeout` make it non-blocking?

back:
One solution:

```js
createHash('sha256').update(val).digest('hex')
```

`createHash()` makes a `Hash` object for the algorithm, `update()` feeds it data (call it repeatedly for chunks), and `digest('hex')` finishes and returns the hash as hex. A `Hash` can't be reused after `digest()`.

This is synchronous. Wrapping it in `setTimeout` or a `Promise` doesn't make it non-blocking; it still runs on the main thread.

front: Can the browser's `crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', ...)` code run in Node.js, and will it give the same hash as Node's `createHash('sha256')` for the same input?
How do you compute a SHA-256 hex string of a string in the browser with the Web Crypto API?

back:
One solution:

```js
[...new Uint8Array(buf)].map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('')
```

`digest()` resolves to an `ArrayBuffer`, which you can't read directly; wrap it in a `Uint8Array` to get the 32 bytes. Each byte becomes two hex characters: `toString(16)` converts to hex and `padStart(2, '0')` keeps leading zeros (`10` → `'0a'`). Without the padding the result is shorter than 64 characters and wrong.

front: How do you remove a CSS class from an element without affecting its other classes, and what happens if the class isn't there?
back:
Call `el.classList.remove('name')`. It removes only that class and leaves the rest of `class="..."` intact. If the class isn't present, it does nothing (no error), so you don't need to check first.

```js
const field = document.querySelector('#email');

field.classList.remove('is-invalid');         // after the user fixes the input
field.classList.remove('is-invalid', 'shake'); // several at once
```

Avoid editing `el.className` with string replacement: it's easy to break other classes (removing `'active'` from `'inactive'`, leftover spaces). `classList` handles the token list for you.

One solution:

```js
const removeClass = (el, className) => el.classList.remove(className);
```

`classList` is a `DOMTokenList`, a set-like view of the `class` attribute. `remove()` deletes just that token and is a no-op if it's missing. It also accepts several names: `remove('a', 'b')`.

```

`classList.toggle()` flips the class and returns `true` if it's present afterwards. Pass a boolean second argument to set it explicitly: `el.classList.toggle('open', isOpen)`, which is safer than flipping when you already know the desired state.

front: How do you check whether an element has a given CSS class, and what should you use instead to test a whole CSS selector?
back:
Use `el.classList.contains('name')`, which returns `true` or `false` and checks the exact class token (so `'active'` does not match `'inactive'`).

```js
const btn = document.querySelector('#save');

btn.classList.contains('is-loading'); // true
btn.matches('.btn.is-loading');       // true, tests a full selector
btn.closest('.modal');                // nearest ancestor matching, or null
```

`el.matches(selector)` is the tool when you need more than one class or an attribute check, and `closest()` walks up to ancestors (handy in event delegation: `e.target.closest('.delete-btn')`).

Real-world tip: don't use classes as your app's source of truth ("is it loading?"). Keep that in a variable or state and render the class from it.

front: How do you add a CSS class to an element without wiping out the classes it already has, and what happens if the class name contains a space?
back:
Call `el.classList.add('name')`. It appends the class, keeps existing ones, and does nothing if the class is already there. Pass several names as separate arguments.

```js
const field = document.querySelector('#email');

field.classList.add('is-invalid');
field.classList.add('is-invalid', 'shake'); // multiple classes
field.classList.add('is-invalid shake');    // throws InvalidCharacterError
```

A class name can't contain whitespace, so `'a b'` throws. Split first if you have a string: `add(...str.trim().split(/s+/))` (a plain `split(' ')` on `'a  b'` yields an empty string, and `add('')` throws too).

Compare with `el.className = 'is-invalid'`, which *replaces* every class on the element and is a common source of "my other styles vanished" bugs.

One solution:

```js
const addClass = (el, className) => el.classList.add(className);
```

`classList.add()` appends the token and ignores duplicates. Assigning `el.className = className` instead would overwrite `intro`. Names can't contain spaces (`add('a b')` throws); pass separate arguments for several classes.
