```shell
# 9a8b7c6 Update API docs
# 1f3e4d5 Fix network bug
```

Every commit from the split point onward gets a new hash (even "Update README"), so this rewrites history. Do it on your own branch; if it was already pushed, push with `--force-with-lease` and only when nobody else builds on it. To split changes inside a single file, stage parts of it with `git add -p`.

front: How do you stage a single file, all files matching a pattern, or everything with `git add`, and what exactly does `git add .` cover?
back:
`git add <pathspec>` stages the current content of whatever matches: a file, a glob, or a directory. `git add .` stages every change (new, modified and deleted files) under the current directory; `git add -A` does the same for the whole repository, wherever you are in it.

```shell
git add src/components/LoginForm.jsx   # one file
git add 'src/*.json'                    # quoted: Git expands the glob
git add .                               # everything under this folder
git add -p                              # pick changes hunk by hunk
```

Quote globs so Git, not your shell, expands them; Git's pathspec `*` also matches files in subfolders and deleted files. Check `git status` before committing so you don't stage `.env` or build output, and list those in `.gitignore`.

front:
Stage every `.json` file under `src/` (including subfolders) by letting Git, not the shell, expand the pattern.

```shell
git add README.md
# Stages one file

____
# Stages src/a.json, src/config/b.json, ...

git add .
# Stages all changes under the current directory
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git add 'src/*.json'
```

Quoting the pattern passes it to Git as a pathspec. In a Git pathspec, `*` also matches `/`, so it picks up `.json` files in subfolders and even deleted ones. Unquoted, your shell expands `src/*.json` first, and only to files that exist directly in `src/`. Double quotes (`"src/*.json"`) work too.

front: You ran `git add .` and accidentally staged `.env`. Which command unstages it without losing your edits to the file?
back:
`git restore --staged .env`. It resets the file's entry in the staging area to match the last commit and leaves your working-tree file untouched. It takes any pathspec, so `git restore --staged .` unstages everything.

```shell
git restore --staged .env     # unstage one file
git restore --staged .        # unstage everything
echo ".env" >> .gitignore     # stop it happening again
```

Don't confuse it with `git restore .env` (no `--staged`), which discards your working-tree changes. Older tutorials use `git reset HEAD <file>` for the same unstage. If `.env` was already committed, `git rm --cached .env` stops tracking it, but the secret stays in history, so rotate it.

front:
Unstage the accidentally staged `.env` file while keeping the file itself.

```shell
git add .
git status -s
# A  .env
____
git status -s
# ?? .env
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git restore --staged .env
```

`--staged` makes `git restore` act on the staging area only: the file goes back to how it is in the last commit (here, not tracked at all, so it shows as `??` untracked again) and your working copy is untouched. Without `--staged`, `git restore` would instead throw away working-tree changes. Add `.env` to `.gitignore` so `git add .` skips it next time.

front: You're mid-change and need to switch branches for an urgent fix. How do you stash your work with a label, including brand-new files?
back:
`git stash push -u -m "label"`. `push` saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) as a new stash and resets the working tree to the last commit. `-u` also stashes untracked (new) files, and `-m` sets the message.

```shell
git stash push -u -m "WIP: signup validation"
git switch main          # clean tree: do the hotfix
git switch -             # back to your branch
git stash pop
```

The message needs `-m`: `git stash push "WIP"` treats the text as a file path and fails with "pathspec did not match". Plain `git stash` is short for `git stash push`, and `git stash save` is deprecated. Ignored files such as `node_modules` are never stashed unless you use `-a`.

front: How do you see exactly what's inside a stash before applying it, and why does plain `git stash show` look so short?
back:
`git stash show -p stash@{1}` prints the stash's full diff. Without `-p`, `git stash show` prints only a diffstat (changed files with +/- counts). Leave out the name to use the latest stash, `stash@{0}`.

```shell
git stash list
git stash show               # diffstat of the latest stash
git stash show -p            # full diff of the latest stash
git stash show -p stash@{1}  # full diff of an older one
```

Untracked files stashed with `-u` are not shown by default; add `--include-untracked` (Git 2.32+). In PowerShell, quote the ref (`'stash@{1}'`), because braces are special there.

front: How do you delete one stash versus all of them, and can a dropped stash be recovered?
back:
`git stash drop [<stash>]` deletes one stash (the latest if you name none); `git stash clear` deletes them all. A dropped stash can be recovered while you still have the hash Git printed.

```shell
git stash drop stash@{1}
# Dropped stash@{1} (4f2a9c1e...)
git stash apply 4f2a9c1e     # undo the drop: re-apply by hash

git stash clear              # remove every stash
```

Stashes removed with `clear` have no printed hashes and are hard to find (you'd need `git fsck`), so treat `clear` as permanent. After a drop the remaining stashes renumber, so check `git stash list` before dropping another by number.

front: What's the difference between `git stash apply` and `git stash pop`, and what happens to the stash if `pop` hits a merge conflict?
back:
Both re-apply a stash's changes to your working tree (the latest stash by default). `apply` keeps the stash in the list; `pop` removes it once it applies cleanly. If `pop` hits a conflict, Git keeps the stash so nothing is lost: resolve the conflict, then run `git stash drop` yourself.

```shell
git stash apply            # keep a copy, e.g. to apply on two branches
git stash pop              # apply the latest and remove it
git stash pop stash@{1}    # apply an older one and remove it
```

A stash isn't tied to its branch: you can apply it on a different branch, which is handy when you started work on the wrong one.

front: What does `git stash list` show, and which stash is `stash@{0}`?
back:
It lists every stash, newest first: `stash@{0}` is the most recent, and each older stash's number is one higher. Each line shows the stash ref, the branch it was made on, and its message.

```shell
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On fix-login: WIP: signup validation
# stash@{1}: WIP on main: 2b1e8a7 Add users table
```

`On <branch>: <message>` means the stash was made with `-m`; `WIP on <branch>: <commit>` is the automatic message naming the commit you were on. Numbers shift whenever you push or drop a stash, so label stashes with `-m` and re-check the list before popping one by number.

front: How do you completely remove a Git submodule from a repository, including the copy Git keeps inside `.git/`?
back:
Three steps, then commit: `git submodule deinit -f -- <path>` unregisters the submodule and empties its folder; `git rm -f <path>` deletes the folder, removes its `.gitmodules` entry and stages both; `rm -rf .git/modules/<name>` deletes the submodule's stored repository, which nothing else cleans up.

```shell
git submodule deinit -f -- vendor/ui-kit
git rm -f vendor/ui-kit
rm -rf .git/modules/vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Remove ui-kit submodule"
```

`<name>` is the name in `.gitmodules` (`[submodule "name"]`), usually the original path; it can differ from the current path after a `git mv`. Skipping the last step leaves a stale copy that gets in the way if you re-add a submodule at that path. In PowerShell, use `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force` instead of `rm -rf`.

front:
Finish removing the `vendor/ui-kit` submodule by deleting the copy of its repository that Git stores inside `.git/`.

```shell
git submodule deinit -f -- vendor/ui-kit
git rm -f vendor/ui-kit
____
git commit -m "Remove ui-kit submodule"
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
rm -rf .git/modules/vendor/ui-kit
```

`deinit` and `git rm` remove the submodule from your working tree and `.gitmodules`, but the submodule's own history stays in `.git/modules/<name>`. Deleting it finishes the cleanup and avoids a "git directory found locally" complaint if you later re-add a submodule at the same path. In PowerShell: `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .git/modules/vendor/ui-kit`.

front: You cloned a repo and its submodule folders are empty. Which command fetches and checks them out, and how could you have avoided this at clone time?
back:
`git submodule update --init --recursive`. `--init` registers the submodules listed in `.gitmodules`, `update` clones them and checks out the exact commit the parent repo recorded, and `--recursive` does the same for submodules nested inside them.

```shell
git submodule update --init --recursive

# or, at clone time:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/acme/shop.git
```

Submodules are checked out on a detached HEAD at the pinned commit, not on a branch. If you plan to commit inside one, switch it to a branch first (e.g. `git switch main`, if that is the submodule's branch). `git config --global submodule.recurse true` makes `pull` and `switch` keep submodules in sync automatically.

front: What does `git submodule update --remote` do differently from plain `git submodule update`, and what must you do afterwards?
back:
Plain `update` checks out the commit your repo has recorded for each submodule. `--remote` instead fetches each submodule and checks out the latest commit of its remote branch (the remote's default branch unless `.gitmodules` sets `branch`). That changes the recorded commit, so afterwards you commit the new pointer in the parent repo.

```shell
git submodule update --remote --recursive
git status            # modified: vendor/ui-kit (new commits)
git add vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Bump ui-kit submodule"
```

Until you commit and push that pointer, teammates still get the old version. Test before committing: `--remote` pulls in whatever changed upstream.

front: What does `git submodule add <url> <path>` create in your repo, and what actually gets committed?
back:
It clones the other repository into `<path>` and stages two things: a `.gitmodules` entry (URL and path) and a special entry for `<path>` that records one exact commit of the submodule. Your repo stores that pointer, not the submodule's files.

```shell
git submodule add https://github.com/acme/ui-kit.git vendor/ui-kit
git status -s
# A  .gitmodules
# A  vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Add ui-kit submodule"
```

Inside `vendor/ui-kit`, `.git` is a small file (`gitdir: ../../.git/modules/vendor/ui-kit`) pointing to where the submodule's history lives. It's a separate repo: new commits in it don't change what the parent records until you `git add vendor/ui-kit` in the parent and commit.

front:
Add the repository `https://github.com/acme/ui-kit.git` as a submodule in the folder `vendor/ui-kit`.

```shell
____
git status -s
# A  .gitmodules
# A  vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Add ui-kit submodule"
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git submodule add https://github.com/acme/ui-kit.git vendor/ui-kit
```

The first argument is the repository URL, the second the path inside your repo. Git clones it there and stages a `.gitmodules` entry plus a pointer to the submodule's current commit; committing records both.

front: How do you move or rename a submodule's folder so that `.gitmodules` stays correct?
back:
Use `git mv <old-path> <new-path>`. Git moves the folder, updates the submodule's `path` in `.gitmodules`, and stages both; then commit.

```shell
git mv vendor/lib vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Move ui-kit submodule"
```

Moving the folder with your file manager or plain `mv` does not update `.gitmodules`, so the submodule breaks. The submodule's name (`[submodule "vendor/lib"]`) stays the same; only its `path` changes.

front: Which modern command switches to an existing branch, and why is it safer than `git checkout` for this?
back:
`git switch <branch>` (Git 2.23+). It only switches branches, while `git checkout` also restores files: if no branch matches the name, `git checkout <name>` can treat it as a file and silently discard your uncommitted edits to it.

```shell
git switch fix-login        # existing branch
git switch -c fix-login     # create it and switch
git switch -                # back to the previous branch
```

If switching would overwrite uncommitted changes, Git refuses; commit or stash first. If `fix-login` exists only on the remote, `git switch fix-login` creates a local branch tracking `origin/fix-login`.

front: A bad commit is already on the shared `main` branch. How do you undo it without rewriting history?
back:
`git revert <commit>` creates a new commit that applies the exact inverse of that commit's changes. History only grows, so teammates who already pulled are unaffected and you push normally.

```shell
git revert 3050fc0
# [main 8e1f2a4] Revert "Add discount column"
git push
```

To revert a merge commit, add `-m 1` to say which parent is the mainline. If later commits changed the same lines, the revert can conflict: resolve it, then run `git revert --continue`.

front: What's the quickest way to undo your most recent commit when it's already pushed, and what does it leave in the history?
back:
`git revert HEAD`. `HEAD` is the commit you're on (the latest on your branch), and revert adds a new commit that reverses it, so both the original and the "Revert …" commit stay in the log.

```shell
git revert HEAD
git log --oneline -2
# 8e1f2a4 Revert "Add discount column"
# 3050fc0 Add discount column
```

If the commit is not pushed yet, `git reset --soft HEAD~1` is often cleaner: it removes the commit but keeps its changes staged so you can fix them and commit again.

front: You just committed with a typo in the message and haven't pushed yet. How do you fix only the message?
back:
`git commit --amend -m "New message"`. It replaces the last commit with a new one that has the same changes and the corrected message. Anything currently staged is added too, so check `git status` first.

```shell
git commit -m "Fix netwrok bug"
git commit --amend -m "Fix network bug"
```

Amending creates a new commit hash. That's harmless before pushing; after pushing you would need `git push --force-with-lease`, so only do it on a branch nobody else uses. Without `-m`, `--amend` opens your editor with the old message.

front: You committed but forgot to include one file. How do you add it to that last commit without changing the message?
back:
Stage the file, then run `git commit --amend --no-edit`. The last commit is replaced by one that includes everything now staged, and `--no-edit` keeps the existing message instead of opening the editor.

```shell
git commit -m "Add signup form"
git add src/validation.js      # the forgotten file
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

The result is a new commit with a new hash. Fine before pushing; if the commit is already pushed, it needs `git push --force-with-lease` and shouldn't be done on shared branches (make a new commit there instead).

front: How do you list the branches that exist on the remote, and why might that list be out of date?
back:
`git branch -r` lists your remote-tracking branches, such as `origin/main`. They are local snapshots of the remote, updated only when you fetch or pull, so run `git fetch --prune` first to add new branches and drop deleted ones.

```shell
git fetch --prune
git branch -r
#   origin/HEAD -> origin/main
#   origin/fix-login
#   origin/main
```

`git branch -a` shows local and remote-tracking branches together. `git ls-remote --heads origin` asks the server directly without updating anything locally.

front: What does plain `git branch` show, and how can you tell which branch you're on?
back:
It lists your local branches and marks the current one with `*`.

```shell
git branch
#   fix-login
# * main
#   old-experiment

git branch -vv          # plus last commit, upstream, ahead/behind
git branch --show-current
# main
```

It doesn't show remote branches (use `-r` or `-a`), and `git branch <name>` creates a branch instead of listing. `git status` also names the current branch on its first line.

front: How do you check which URL your `origin` remote points to?
back:
`git remote get-url origin` prints it. `git remote -v` lists every remote with its fetch and push URLs, and `git config --get remote.origin.url` reads the same value straight from the config.

```shell
git remote get-url origin
# https://github.com/acme/shop.git

git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/acme/shop.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/acme/shop.git (push)
```

`origin` is just the default name `git clone` gives the remote you cloned from; in a fork workflow you often add a second remote called `upstream` for the original project.

front:
Print only the URL that the `origin` remote points to.

```shell
____
# https://github.com/acme/shop.git
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git remote get-url origin
```

`git config --get remote.origin.url` gives the same result by reading the config value directly. `git remote -v` shows it too, but for every remote and twice (fetch and push).

front: Your repo moved, or you're switching from HTTPS to SSH. Which command points the existing `origin` remote at the new URL?
back:
`git remote set-url origin <new-url>`. It changes the URL of the existing remote in place, so your branches and their tracking setup keep working.

```shell
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:acme/shop.git
git remote -v    # confirm the fetch and push URLs
git fetch        # check that access works
```

Don't `git remote remove` and re-add it for this: removing a remote also deletes its remote-tracking branches and the upstream settings of your local branches.

front:
Switch the `origin` remote from HTTPS to the SSH URL `git@github.com:acme/shop.git`.

```shell
git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/acme/shop.git (fetch)
____
git remote -v
# origin  git@github.com:acme/shop.git (fetch)
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:acme/shop.git
```

`set-url` edits the existing remote's URL in place (both fetch and push), keeping your remote-tracking branches and upstream settings.

front: What does `git shortlog main..feature` show, and which commits does `main..feature` select?
back:
It lists the commits on `feature` that are not on `main`, grouped by author with a count, showing each commit's subject line. It summarizes who did what, not the code changes. `A..B` means "commits reachable from B but not from A", so the order matters.

```shell
git shortlog main..feature
# Ana Lopez (2):
#       Add signup form
#       Validate email format
#
# Sam Kim (1):
#       Fix password hint

git shortlog -sn v1.0..v2.0     # only commit counts per author
```

Any refs work: hashes, branches, tags. To see file changes between two points use `git diff --stat A B`; for plain release notes use `git log --oneline A..B`.

front:
Summarize, grouped by author, the commits made after the `v1.0` tag up to the `v2.0` tag.

```shell
____
# Ana Lopez (2):
#       Add signup form
#       Update dependencies
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git shortlog v1.0..v2.0
```

`v1.0..v2.0` selects commits reachable from `v2.0` but not from `v1.0`, i.e. everything added in that release. `git shortlog` groups their subject lines by author; add `-sn` for just the counts, sorted.

front: Which `git log` command draws a text graph of all branches and merges, with one line per commit?
back:
`git log --oneline --graph --all`. `--graph` draws branch and merge lines on the left, `--all` includes every branch instead of just the current one, and `--oneline` keeps each commit to a short hash plus subject. In a terminal, branch and tag names are shown next to commits by default (older guides add `--decorate` to force this).

```shell
git log --oneline --graph --all
# *   665318e (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'fix-login'
# |\
# | * 4af79a5 (fix-login) Fix login redirect
# * | 9ededda Update README
# |/
# * d82f06d Add login form
```

Save it as an alias with `git config --global alias.graph "log --oneline --graph --all"`, then run `git graph`.

front:
Show a graph of every branch in the repo, one line per commit.

```shell
____
# *   665318e (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'fix-login'
# |\
# | * 4af79a5 (fix-login) Fix login redirect
# * | 9ededda Update README
# |/
# * d82f06d Add login form
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --oneline --graph --all
```

`--graph` draws the branch lines, `--all` includes all refs rather than only `HEAD`, and `--oneline` gives the short hash and subject. The longer `git log --pretty=oneline --graph --decorate --all` is equivalent except that it prints full hashes.

front: How do you list only the commits written by a particular person, and what does `git log --author` actually match against?
back:
`git log --author=<pattern>`. The pattern is a regular expression matched against the author's `Name <email>`, so part of a name or an email address both work. Matching is case-sensitive unless you add `-i`.

```shell
git log --author="Ana" --oneline
git log --author="@acme.com" --oneline      # anyone with a company email
git log --author="Ana" --author="Sam"       # either person
```

Repeating `--author` means "any of these". It filters on who wrote the change; to filter on who created the commit object (e.g. after a rebase or a web-UI merge) use `--committer`.

front:
Show the full log entries of commits whose author is Duck Quacking.

```shell
____
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4
# Author: Duck Quacking <duck@example.com>
# Date:   Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --author="Duck Quacking"
```

`--author` takes a regex matched against `Name <email>`, so `--author=Duck` or `--author=duck@example.com` would also work. Quote the value when it contains spaces.

front: In Git, what's the difference between a commit's author and its committer, and how do you filter `git log` by committer?
back:
The author wrote the change; the committer created that commit object, for example by rebasing, cherry-picking, amending, or merging a pull request in a web UI. Filter with `git log --committer=<pattern>`, which matches `Name <email>` just like `--author`.

```shell
git log --committer="GitHub" --oneline   # commits created by GitHub's web UI
git log -1 --format='%an <%ae> | %cn <%ce>'
# Ana Lopez <ana@acme.com> | GitHub <noreply@github.com>
```

Usually author and committer are the same person. They differ when someone or something else applies your change, which is why `--author` is the right filter for "who wrote this".

front:
List the commits whose committer is GitHub (created by merging or squashing in GitHub's web UI).

```shell
____
# commit 8e1f2a4c9d0b...
# Author: Ana Lopez <ana@acme.com>
# Date:   Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --committer="GitHub"
```

`--committer` filters by who created the commit object, not who wrote the change. The default log output shows only the author; add `--format='%h %an | %cn'` to see both.

front: A function called `calculateTax` vanished from the codebase. Which `git log` option finds the commits that added or removed that string?
back:
`git log -S"calculateTax"` (the "pickaxe"). It lists commits that changed the number of occurrences of the string, meaning it was added or removed, not every commit that merely edited a line containing it.

```shell
git log -S"calculateTax" --oneline
# 81ea5bc Remove legacy tax helper
# 4b2c7d1 Add calculateTax

git log -S"calculateTax" -p -- src/billing/   # show diffs, only in that folder
```

Use `-G<regex>` instead to find commits whose added or removed lines match a regex, which also catches edits to a line that still contains the text. Combine with other filters such as `--since` or `--author`.

front: How do you list only the commits from the last two weeks, and what date formats does `git log --since` accept?
back:
`git log --since="2 weeks ago"`. `--since` (alias `--after`) keeps commits newer than the given date and accepts ISO dates such as `2025-04-01 09:00` or relative phrases like `yesterday`, `3 days ago` or `last monday`.

```shell
git log --since="2 weeks ago" --oneline
git log --since="last monday" --author="Ana" --oneline   # standup notes
```

It filters by committer date, while `git log` displays the author date by default, so a rebased or cherry-picked commit can show an older date than the filter suggests.

front:
List, one line each, the commits made in the last two weeks.

```shell
____
# 9c1d2e3 Add signup form
# 6d5c4b3 Fix login redirect
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --since="2 weeks ago" --oneline
```

`--since` (or `--after`) accepts relative phrases like `2 weeks ago` or an ISO date. `--oneline` gives the short hash and subject shown in the output.

front: What does `git log --until=<date>` do, and how would you find the last commit on `main` before a release date?
back:
`--until` (alias `--before`) keeps only commits older than the given date. Add `-1` to get just the newest of those.

```shell
git log --until="2025-03-31 23:59" --oneline
git log --until="2025-03-31 23:59" -1 --format=%h main
# 6d5c4b3
git switch --detach 6d5c4b3     # look at the code as it was
```

Like `--since`, it compares committer dates. A date without a time (`2025-03-31`) means that day at the current time of day, so add a time when the cut-off matters. `git switch main` takes you back.

front:
List, one line each, only the commits made before the end of March 31, 2025.

```shell
____
# 6d5c4b3 Fix login redirect
# 1f3e4d5 Initial commit
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --until="2025-03-31 23:59" --oneline
```

`--until` (or `--before`) drops commits newer than the date. Include the time: a bare `2025-03-31` is read as that day at the current time of day, which could cut the day in half.

front: How do you list the commits made from April 1 through April 4, 2025, and why should you include times of day?
back:
Combine both limits: `git log --since="2025-04-01 00:00" --until="2025-04-04 23:59"`. A bare date like `2025-04-01` is read as that day at the current time of day, so without explicit times you can miss commits at either end of the range.

```shell
git log --since="2025-04-01 00:00" --until="2025-04-04 23:59" --oneline
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Add login form
```

Relative forms also work (`yesterday`, `3 days ago`, `last monday`). Prefer ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` over `04/01/2025`, which readers can take as either April 1 or January 4.

front:
List, one line each, the commits made from April 1 through April 4, 2025 (whole days).

```shell
____
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Add login form
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --since="2025-04-01 00:00" --until="2025-04-04 23:59" --oneline
```

`--since` and `--until` can be combined to bound both ends. Explicit times matter: a bare date means that day at the current time of day.

front: Your `git log --oneline` is cluttered with "Merge pull request" commits. How do you hide them?
back:
Add `--no-merges`: it drops every commit with more than one parent, leaving only the commits that made actual changes.

```shell
git log --oneline --no-merges
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Initial commit

git log --oneline --merges        # the opposite: only merge commits
```

Handy for release notes, e.g. `git log --oneline --no-merges v1.0..main`. Teams that squash-merge or rebase-merge have no merge commits to hide in the first place.

front: What does `git log --oneline` print for each commit, and how long are the hashes it shows?
back:
One line per commit: an abbreviated hash plus the subject (first line) of the message. It is shorthand for `--pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit`.

```shell
git log --oneline -3
# d540ba1 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'fix-network'
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Initial commit
```

Hashes are shortened to at least 7 characters; in large repositories Git automatically uses more (often 10 to 12) so each short hash stays unique. You can pass a short hash to other commands, e.g. `git show 3050fc0`.

front: What do `git diff`, `git diff --staged` and `git diff HEAD` each compare?
back:
`git diff` compares your working tree with the staging area (index), so it shows only changes you have not staged yet. `git diff --staged` (same as `--cached`) compares the staging area with the last commit: exactly what `git commit` would record. `git diff HEAD` compares the working tree with the last commit, showing staged and unstaged changes together.

```shell
# after editing src/api.js and src/app.js:
git add src/api.js
git diff --name-only            # src/app.js  (unstaged)
git diff --staged --name-only   # src/api.js  (staged)
git diff HEAD --name-only       # both files
```

A common surprise: right after `git add`, plain `git diff` prints nothing, because the change is now staged. Review with `git diff --staged` before committing.

front: Which command shows the most recent commit's hash, author, date and message, and which one also shows its code changes?
back:
`git log -1` shows the latest commit's hash, author, date and message; `git show` shows the same plus its full diff. Both default to `HEAD` and accept any other commit or branch.

```shell
git log -1
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4 (HEAD -> main)
# Author: Ana Lopez <ana@acme.com>
# Date:   Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
#
#     Fix network bug

git show --stat        # latest commit + list of changed files
git log -1 --oneline   # c191f90 (HEAD -> main) Fix network bug
```

`-1` (or `-n 1`) limits any `git log` to that many commits, e.g. `git log -3 main`.

front: Before deleting old branches, how do you list the ones already merged into `main`, and what does adding `-a` change?
back:
Run `git branch --merged main` (or switch to `main` and run `git branch --merged`). It lists branches whose tip commit is already contained in `main`, so deleting them loses nothing. Adding `-a` also lists remote-tracking branches such as `remotes/origin/fix-login`.

```shell
git switch main
git pull
git branch --merged
#   fix-login
# * main
git branch -a --merged      # local + remote-tracking
git branch -d fix-login     # -d refuses if the branch isn't merged
```

Pitfall: branches merged with a squash or rebase merge (common on GitHub) usually don't appear, because their original commits never entered `main`. The list also includes `main` itself; don't delete that.

front: What does `git status -sb` show, and how do you read the `M`, `A` and `??` codes in its output?
back:
It's the short status (`-s`) plus a branch line (`-b`): first your branch, its upstream and ahead/behind counts, then one line per changed file with a two-letter code. The left letter is the staging area, the right letter the working tree.

```shell
git status -sb
# ## fix-login...origin/fix-login [ahead 1]
# M  src/api.js         <- modified, staged
#  M src/app.js         <- modified, not staged
# A  src/validate.js    <- new file, staged
# ?? notes.txt          <- untracked
```

`MM` means staged, then edited again. Plain `git status` gives the same information in long form, with hints for the next command to run.

front: A bad `git rebase` or `git reset` "lost" some of your commits. How does `git reflog` help you get them back?
back:
`git reflog` lists every position `HEAD` has had in your local repo (commits, checkouts, resets, rebase steps), newest first, including commits no branch points to anymore. Find the entry from before the mistake and point a branch at it.

```shell
git reflog
# 3ddf121 HEAD@{0}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/fix-login
# 5049dbb HEAD@{1}: rebase (pick): Fix network bug
# 4410b18 HEAD@{2}: rebase (start): checkout main
# b6a4f9d HEAD@{3}: commit: Add signup form

git branch rescue b6a4f9d    # safest: keep it on a new branch
git reset --hard b6a4f9d     # or move this branch back (discards uncommitted work)
```

The reflog is local only (never pushed or cloned) and entries expire, by default after 90 days, or 30 for commits no longer on any branch. Uncommitted changes never enter it, so it can't bring those back.

front: Beyond what the diff already shows, what should a pull-request description tell reviewers?
back:
The *why* and *how to check it*: which feature or bug this addresses (link the ticket), how you approached it and which decisions or trade-offs you made, known limitations, and how to verify it — reproduction steps, test notes, and screenshots for UI changes.

```text
What & why:
  Fixes #142 — saving a profile with an empty phone number returned 500.
How:
  Phone is now optional in the schema; the API returns 400 with a field error.
How to test:
  1. Open /profile, clear Phone, click Save
  2. Expect the inline error and no 500 in the network tab
```

The diff shows *what* changed. Reviewers can't see your intent, the alternatives you rejected, or how you tested unless you write them down.

front: Before asking for review, why rebase your feature branch onto the latest `main`, and what must you do after pushing a rebased branch?
back:
So your PR is tested against the current `main`: you resolve conflicts yourself, and reviewers don't see stale code or miss fixes that already landed. Rebasing rewrites your branch's commits, so you then update the remote branch with `git push --force-with-lease`.

```shell
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# on conflict: fix files, git add <file>, git rebase --continue
npm test
git push --force-with-lease
```

Only rebase a branch that is yours alone. If teammates have pushed to it, rebasing rewrites commits they already have — merge instead (`git merge origin/main`), which many teams prefer anyway.

front: Why do small, single-purpose pull requests get reviewed faster and better, and how do you keep a PR small?
back:
Reviewers can hold a small diff in their head, so they pick it up sooner and review it carefully; a 1,500-line PR tends to get a skim and a rubber stamp. Keep PRs small by giving each one a single purpose — e.g. a refactor in one PR and the feature that builds on it in the next — and make each commit one logical, well-described step.

```text
PR 1: Extract validateEmail() into utils   (refactor, no behavior change)
PR 2: Validate email on the signup form    (feature)
```

Mixing a 40-file rename with a behavior change hides the one change that actually needs scrutiny.

front: After review comments arrive on your PR, how should you push your fixes so reviewers can easily see what changed?
back:
Push the fixes as new commits — ideally `git commit --fixup <commit>` commits that point at the commit they correct — so reviewers can look at just the new changes. After approval, squash them in with an autosquash rebase (or let the platform squash-merge).

```shell
git add src/api/users.ts
git commit --fixup a1b2c3d      # "fixup! Add user endpoint"
git push

# after approval
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main
git push --force-with-lease
```

Also reply to every comment (fixed, or why not), ask when a request is unclear, and assume good intent. Rewriting and force-pushing mid-review makes it hard for reviewers to see what changed since their last look.

front: What should you check when you review your own pull request before requesting reviewers?
back:
Read the whole diff the way a reviewer would: leftover debug code (`console.log`, commented-out blocks), typos, unrelated changes that slipped in, missing tests, and any decision that needs a code comment or a line in the description.

```shell
git diff origin/main...HEAD          # everything this branch adds
git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD   # which files, how many lines
```

The hosting site's "Files changed" tab works too. Catching the easy stuff yourself lets reviewers spend their time on design and correctness, and explaining your choices to yourself shows which ones need explaining to others.

front: Which everyday Git commands are worth aliasing in `~/.gitconfig`, and what does a leading `!` in an alias mean?
back:
Alias the commands you type many times a day — status, switch, commit, rebase — under `[alias]`. A value starting with `!` runs as a shell command, which lets one alias chain several Git commands.

```ini
[alias]
  st = status -sb
  sw = switch
  swc = switch -c
  cm = commit -m
  amend = commit --amend --no-edit
  unstage = restore --staged
  undo = reset HEAD~1
  lg = log --oneline --graph --all
  pushf = push --force-with-lease
  rom = !git fetch && git rebase origin/main
```

Then `git st`, `git swc fix-login`, or `git undo` (removes the last commit but keeps its changes in your files). Avoid an alias for plain `push --force`: it overwrites teammates' work without checking, while `--force-with-lease` refuses if the remote moved.

front:
Git aliases: fill in the alias so `git unstage app.js` takes a file out of the staging area while keeping your edits.

```ini
[alias]
  st = status -sb
  sw = switch
  cm = commit -m
  ____
  undo = reset HEAD~1
  pushf = push --force-with-lease
```
back:
One solution:

```ini
  unstage = restore --staged
```

A plain alias expands to the text after `=`, so `git unstage app.js` runs `git restore --staged app.js`: the file leaves the index but your working-tree edits stay. Older configs use `unstage = reset HEAD --`, which does the same. Don't use `reset --soft HEAD^` — that undoes the last commit instead.

front: How do you create a Git alias from the command line, e.g. make `git cm "msg"` mean `git commit -m "msg"`?
back:
Run `git config --global alias.<name> "<command>"`, quoting the command if it has spaces. Git saves it in the `[alias]` section of `~/.gitconfig`.

```shell
git config --global alias.sw switch
git config --global alias.cm "commit -m"

git cm "Add login form"   # runs: git commit -m "Add login form"
```

For many aliases, or ones with tricky quoting, edit the file directly with `git config --global --edit`. Aliases can't replace built-in commands: an alias named `status` is ignored.

front:
Create a global alias so that `git sw main` runs `git switch main`.

```shell
# Syntax: git config --global alias.<alias> <command>
____

git config --global alias.cm "commit -m"   # git cm "msg" -> git commit -m "msg"
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global alias.sw switch
```

`alias.sw` creates the `sw` alias in `~/.gitconfig`; whatever you type after `git sw` is appended, so `git sw main` becomes `git switch main`. Quote the value when it contains spaces, as in the `cm` line.

front: How do you make Git automatically run the corrected command when you mistype one (e.g. `git sttaus`), and what does a number in `help.autocorrect` mean?
back:
Set `help.autocorrect` to a number greater than 1: it's a delay in **tenths of a second** before Git runs its single best guess, giving you time to press Ctrl+C.

```shell
git config --global help.autocorrect 10   # wait 1 second, then run the guess
git sttaus
# WARNING: You called a Git command named 'sttaus', which does not exist.
# Continuing in 1.0 seconds, assuming that you meant 'status'.
```

Gotcha: since Git 2.49, `1` means *true* (run immediately), not 0.1 s, and `0` (the default) only prints a suggestion. Autocorrect only runs when there is exactly one close match.

front:
Configure Git to wait 1 second, then run its corrected guess when you mistype a command.

```shell
# Syntax: git config [--global] help.autocorrect <value>
____
git sttaus   # "Continuing in 1.0 seconds, assuming that you meant 'status'."
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global help.autocorrect 10
```

Numbers above 1 are a delay in tenths of a second, so `10` = 1 second. Don't use `1` for "0.1 s": since Git 2.49 `1` means "run immediately", and `0` only shows the suggestion.

front: Which `help.autocorrect` keywords make Git run a typo's correction immediately, ask first, or stay completely silent?
back:
`immediate` runs the guess right away, `prompt` asks before running it, and `never` neither runs nor suggests anything. `show` (same as `0`, the default) just prints "The most similar command is …".

```shell
git config --global help.autocorrect prompt
git sttaus
# WARNING: You called a Git command named 'sttaus', which does not exist.
# Run 'status' instead [y/N]?
```

`prompt` is the safest automatic setting: a silent immediate guess could run a different command than you meant.

front:
Configure Git to run the corrected command for a typo immediately, with no delay.

```shell
# Syntax: git config [--global] help.autocorrect <value>
____
git sttaus   # runs `git status` right away

git config --global help.autocorrect prompt   # ask first instead
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global help.autocorrect immediate
```

`immediate` (or, since Git 2.49, `1`/`true`) runs the single best guess without waiting. `prompt` asks `Run 'status' instead [y/N]?`, and `never` disables both running and suggesting.

front: What does `push.autoSetupRemote` change about the first `git push` on a new branch?
back:
With `push.autoSetupRemote=true`, a plain `git push` on a branch with no upstream behaves like `git push -u origin <branch>`: it creates the same-named remote branch and records it as the upstream, instead of failing with "The current branch has no upstream branch".

```shell
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true

git switch -c fix-login
git commit -am "Fix login redirect"
git push        # creates origin/fix-login and tracks it
```

Needs Git 2.37+. It suits the usual workflow where local and remote branch names match. It does nothing for a branch that already tracks a differently named upstream (e.g. one created from `origin/main`).

front:
Make a plain `git push` create and track the remote branch the first time you push a new local branch.

```shell
____

git switch -c my-branch
git push        # pushes to origin/my-branch and sets it as upstream
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true
```

(`git config --global --add --bool push.autoSetupRemote true` is equivalent.) Without it, the first push needs `git push -u origin my-branch`. Requires Git 2.37+.

front: How do you list the branches that do NOT contain a given commit — e.g. to see which release branches still lack a hotfix?
back:
`git branch --no-contains <commit>` lists local branches whose history doesn't include that commit. Add `-r` for remote-tracking branches or `-a` for both.

```shell
git fetch
git branch -r --no-contains 3050fc0
#   origin/release-1.4
#   origin/release-1.5
```

Those branches still need the fix. Caveat: a cherry-picked copy has a different hash, so a branch that got the fix by cherry-pick still appears in this list.

front: A bug fix is commit `3050fc0`. How do you find which branches already include it?
back:
`git branch --contains 3050fc0` prints every local branch whose history includes that commit; add `-a` to include remote-tracking branches (fetch first so they're current).

```shell
git fetch
git branch -a --contains 3050fc0
#   main
# * fix-login
#   remotes/origin/main
```

For releases, `git tag --contains 3050fc0` tells you which tagged versions shipped the fix.

front: GitHub says a commit "does not belong to any branch on this repository". Why does `git cherry-pick <sha>` fail locally, and how do you get the commit?
back:
Your clone only has objects reachable from the branches and tags it fetched, so that commit isn't in your local repo. Fetch it explicitly by its **full** hash, then cherry-pick it.

```shell
git fetch origin 8776de5c1f0a4b2e9d3c7a6b5e4f3d2c1b0a9f8e
git cherry-pick FETCH_HEAD
```

An abbreviated hash fails (`couldn't find remote ref 8776de5`) because the server only matches full object IDs. Such commits usually come from force-pushed branches or pull requests from forks; for a PR you can also fetch `refs/pull/<number>/head`.

front: What does `git clone <url>` set up for you, and how do you clone into a folder with a different name?
back:
It creates a folder named after the repo, downloads the full history, registers the source as the remote `origin`, and checks out the default branch (usually `main`) with tracking set up. A second argument chooses the folder name.

```shell
git clone https://github.com/acme/shop-api.git
# -> ./shop-api

git clone https://github.com/acme/shop-api.git api
# -> ./api
cd api
git remote -v    # origin  https://github.com/acme/shop-api.git (fetch) / (push)
```

SSH URLs (`git@github.com:acme/shop-api.git`) work the same way and avoid password prompts once you've added an SSH key to your account.

front:
Clone the repository into a folder named `api` instead of the default `shop-api`.

```shell
git clone https://github.com/acme/shop-api.git
# -> clones into ./shop-api

____
# -> clones into ./api
cd api
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git clone https://github.com/acme/shop-api.git api
```

`git clone <url> [<directory>]`: the optional second argument is the target folder. Without it, Git uses the repo name minus `.git`. The folder must not exist or must be empty.

front: How do you set the name and email Git records on your commits — globally, and differently for one work repo?
back:
Use `git config --global user.name` / `user.email` for your default identity, and run the same commands without `--global` inside a repo to override them just there (saved in that repo's `.git/config`).

```shell
git config --global user.name "Sam Lee"
git config --global user.email "sam@example.com"

cd ~/work/shop-api
git config user.email "sam.lee@company.com"   # this repo only

git config user.email      # prints the value in effect here
```

Set it before your first commit: GitHub links commits to your account by that email, and fixing the author on pushed commits means rewriting history.

front:
Set the commit email for the current repository only, overriding your global one.

```shell
# Global default
git config --global user.name "Sam Lee"
git config --global user.email "sam@example.com"

# This repo only
cd ~/work/shop-api
____
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config user.email "sam.lee@company.com"
```

Without `--global`, `git config` writes to the current repo's `.git/config`, which takes precedence over `~/.gitconfig`. Check the effective value with `git config user.email`.

front: How do you make Git open VS Code for commit messages, and why does the command need `--wait`?
back:
Set `core.editor` to `"code --wait"`. `--wait` makes the `code` command block until you close the tab; without it `code` returns immediately, Git reads an empty message, and aborts the commit ("Aborting commit due to empty commit message").

```shell
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git commit      # opens the message in VS Code; save and close the tab to finish

git config --global core.editor "nano"   # terminal editors need no flag
```

The same editor is used for interactive-rebase todo lists, `git commit --amend`, and `git config --edit`.

front:
Make VS Code Git's editor, so that `git commit` waits until you close the message tab.

```shell
# Usage: git config --global core.editor <editor-command>
____

git config --global core.editor "vim"   # terminal editors block on their own
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
```

The quotes keep the command and its flag together. `--wait` is the key part: without it `code` exits immediately and Git aborts the commit because the message is empty. Sublime Text is similar: `"subl --wait"`.

front: How do you copy one file (or folder) from another branch into your current branch without merging or cherry-picking?
back:
Check out just that path from the other branch: `git restore --source=<branch> -- <path>` (or the older `git checkout <branch> -- <path>`). Only those paths change; nothing else on your branch is touched.

```shell
git switch feature-b
git restore --source=feature-a -- src/utils/date.ts
git restore --source=main -- 'src/config/*'

git add src/utils/date.ts src/config
git commit -m "Bring date utils over from feature-a"
```

Difference: `git checkout <branch> -- <path>` also stages the files; `git restore` only changes the working tree. Either way it overwrites your local copy of those files without asking.

front:
Copy `src/utils/date.ts` from the `feature-a` branch into your current branch (no merge, no cherry-pick).

```shell
git switch feature-b
____
git add src/utils/date.ts
git commit -m "Bring date utils over from feature-a"
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git restore --source=feature-a -- src/utils/date.ts
```

`git checkout feature-a -- src/utils/date.ts` also works (and stages the file for you). The path can be a folder or a quoted glob like `'src/*'`.

front: What's the modern command to create a new branch and switch to it in one step, and how do you make sure it starts from the latest `main`?
back:
`git switch -c <branch>` (older: `git checkout -b <branch>`) creates the branch at your current commit and switches to it. Update `main` first so the branch starts from the latest code.

```shell
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c fix-login

git switch review-123   # branch exists only on origin: creates a local
                        # branch that tracks origin/review-123
```

Gotcha: `git switch -c fix-login origin/main` also works but sets `origin/main` as the upstream, so a later plain `git push` fails with "upstream branch … does not match". Add `--no-track` if you branch that way.

front: How do you create a branch with no history at all (e.g. `gh-pages`), and how do `git switch --orphan` and `git checkout --orphan` differ?
back:
`git switch --orphan <branch>` starts a branch with no commits and removes all tracked files from the working tree. `git checkout --orphan <branch>` also has no history but keeps your current files, staged, ready to become the first commit.

```shell
git switch --orphan gh-pages
cp -r ../dist/* .
git add .
git commit -m "Initial gh-pages build"
```

The first commit on an orphan branch has no parent, so it shares no history with `main` — the point for deploy-only or docs branches. Untracked files (e.g. `node_modules`) stay put with either command.

front: What exactly does `git commit` record, and what happens if you leave off `-m`?
back:
It records only what's **staged** (added with `git add`), not every edit in your folder. Without `-m`, Git opens your configured editor for the message; saving an empty message aborts the commit.

```shell
git add src/LoginForm.tsx
git commit -m "Show error when login fails"   # only LoginForm.tsx goes in

git add .
git commit      # editor: subject line, blank line, details
```

The editor route suits anything non-trivial: a short subject (about 50 chars) plus a body explaining *why*. Run `git status` first to check nothing unintended is staged.

front: What does `git commit --no-verify` skip, and why is it risky to rely on?
back:
It skips the `pre-commit` and `commit-msg` hooks — local checks such as lint, formatting, tests, or message format that would otherwise block the commit. Short form: `-n`.

```shell
git commit --no-verify -m "WIP: save progress before switching tasks"
```

Use it sparingly, e.g. for a throwaway WIP commit. Hooks usually mirror rules CI enforces anyway, so skipping them locally just moves the failure to your pull request. If a hook is wrong or too slow, fix the hook.

front: How do you make a commit with no file changes, and when is that actually useful?
back:
`git commit --allow-empty -m "<message>"` — without `--allow-empty`, Git refuses with "nothing to commit". The common real use is re-triggering CI or a deploy without touching code.

```shell
git commit --allow-empty -m "Retrigger CI"
git push
```

It still adds a commit to history, so if your CI has a "re-run" button, prefer that on shared branches.

front: How can a `git fixup` alias let you pick the commit to fix from a searchable list instead of copying its hash?
back:
Pipe recent commits into `fzf` (a fuzzy-finder CLI), keep the chosen line's hash, and pass it to `git commit --fixup`. The leading `!` makes the alias run as a shell command.

```shell
# requires fzf (e.g. brew install fzf)
git config --global alias.fixup '!git log -n 50 --pretty=format:"%h %s" --no-merges | fzf | cut -d" " -f1 | xargs -o git commit --fixup'

git add src/api.ts
git fixup     # pick a commit -> creates "fixup! <its subject>"
```

`cut -d" " -f1` keeps the whole hash; cutting a fixed 7 characters breaks in repos where Git prints longer abbreviated hashes. `xargs -o` reattaches the terminal so `git commit` can run normally.

front:
Create a `git fixup` alias that lets you choose the target commit from an `fzf` list of the last 50 commits.

```shell
# Make sure fzf is installed (e.g. brew install fzf)
____

git fixup
# Pick a commit from the list; a "fixup! ..." commit is created for it
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global alias.fixup '!git log -n 50 --pretty=format:"%h %s" --no-merges | fzf | cut -d" " -f1 | xargs -o git commit --fixup'
```

`!` runs the alias in a shell: list commits as "hash subject", let `fzf` pick one, keep the first field (the hash), and hand it to `git commit --fixup`. Single quotes around the whole value keep the inner double quotes intact.

front: What does `git commit --fixup <commit>` create, and what step actually folds it into the target commit?
back:
It creates a commit titled `fixup! <target's subject>`. Nothing is combined until you rebase with `--autosquash`, which moves each fixup right after its target and squashes it in, dropping the fixup's message.

```shell
git add src/api/users.ts
git commit --fixup 3050fc0         # "fixup! Add user endpoint"

git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main
# todo list is pre-arranged: pick 3050fc0 / fixup 9e1d2a4 -> save and close
```

Since Git 2.44, `--autosquash` also works without `-i`. The rebase rewrites the branch, so push with `--force-with-lease`, and only on a branch nobody else is building on.

front: How would you create a `git fix <commit>` alias for fixup commits, and what happens to the argument you pass it?
back:
`git config --global alias.fix "commit --fixup"`. A non-`!` alias is plain text substitution: anything after `git fix` is appended, so `git fix 3050fc0` runs `git commit --fixup 3050fc0`.

```shell
git config --global alias.fix "commit --fixup"

git add .
git fix 3050fc0              # -> git commit --fixup 3050fc0
git fix ":/Add user endpoint" # newest commit whose message matches
```

The `:/text` form is standard revision syntax, so you don't have to look up the hash.

front:
Create an alias so `git fix 3050fc0` makes a fixup commit for `3050fc0`.

```shell
____

git add .
git fix 3050fc0   # creates "fixup! <subject of 3050fc0>"
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global alias.fix "commit --fixup"
```

Arguments after an alias are appended, so `git fix 3050fc0` becomes `git commit --fixup 3050fc0`. Squash the fixups later with `git rebase -i --autosquash <base>`.

front: What does `git init` actually create, and how do you make sure the first branch is named `main`?
back:
It creates a hidden `.git` folder (object database, refs, config) that turns the directory into a repository; nothing is tracked until you add and commit. Use `git init -b main`, or set `init.defaultBranch` once, to name the first branch.

```shell
mkdir todo-api && cd todo-api
git init -b main

git config --global init.defaultBranch main   # all future repos
git init my-app      # creates ./my-app with a repo inside
```

Re-running `git init` in an existing repo is harmless. Running it by accident in your home folder is not: that stray `.git` makes Git treat everything below it as one repo.

front: How do you print just the current branch name in a script, and what do you get in detached HEAD?
back:
`git branch --show-current` (Git 2.22+) prints the branch name, and prints nothing in detached HEAD. The older `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` prints the name, or literally `HEAD` when detached.

```shell
git switch fix-login
git branch --show-current          # fix-login
git push origin "$(git branch --show-current)"

git switch --detach HEAD~1
git branch --show-current          # (empty)
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD    # HEAD
```

CI jobs often check out a detached commit, so handle the empty / `HEAD` case before using the value.

front: What's the difference between `git diff main..feature` and `git diff main...feature` when reviewing a branch?
back:
`main..feature` (same as `git diff main feature`) compares the two branch tips, so anything that landed on `main` after you branched shows up as reversed changes. `main...feature` compares `feature` with the point where it left `main` — only what the branch adds, like a pull request's diff.

```shell
git diff main...feature                  # what the PR changes
git diff --stat main...feature           # files and line counts
git diff main...feature > feature.patch  # save as a patch (git apply feature.patch)
```

`git log` uses the same dots differently: there `main..feature` means "commits on feature that aren't on main".

front:
Save everything the `feature` branch adds since it branched off `main` into a patch file.

```shell
git diff patch-1..patch-2
# difference between the tips of patch-1 and patch-2

____
# writes feature's changes (since it left main) to feature.patch
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git diff main...feature > feature.patch
```

Three dots diff against the merge base, so only the branch's own changes are exported. `git diff main..feature` would also include reversed copies of anything merged into `main` since. Apply it elsewhere with `git apply feature.patch`.

front: How do you make `git merge` always create a merge commit, and what side effect does setting `merge.ff false` globally have on `git pull`?
back:
Set `merge.ff` to `false` (the config form of `--no-ff`): merges then create a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible. Side effect: `git pull` merges too, so a pull where you have no local commits creates a pointless "Merge branch 'main' of …" commit.

```shell
git config --global merge.ff false

# keep pulls clean:
git config --global pull.ff only       # or: pull.rebase true
```

Many people leave the default and type `git merge --no-ff feature` only when they want the merge commit.

front:
Globally stop `git merge` from fast-forwarding, so every merge creates a merge commit.

```shell
____

git switch main
git merge my-branch   # always creates a merge commit now
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global merge.ff false
```

Equivalent to always passing `--no-ff`. It also applies to the merge inside `git pull`, so pair it with `git config --global pull.ff only` to avoid "Merge branch 'main' of …" commits on every pull.

front: How do you throw away all uncommitted changes to tracked files and go back to the last commit — and what does that NOT remove?
back:
`git reset --hard HEAD` resets both the staging area and your tracked files to the last commit. The modern equivalent is `git restore --staged --worktree .`. Untracked (never-added) files are left alone; `git clean` removes those.

```shell
git status                 # see what you're about to lose
git reset --hard HEAD      # discard staged + unstaged edits to tracked files

git restore --staged --worktree .   # same effect, newer command
```

Changes that were never committed or stashed can't be recovered afterwards, not even from the reflog. If you're unsure, `git stash` first: it clears the working tree the same way but keeps a copy.

front: How do you delete untracked files and folders (e.g. leftover generated files) from your working tree, and how do you check what will go first?
back:
`git clean -fd` deletes untracked files (`-f`, required as a safety catch) and untracked directories (`-d`). Run it with `-n` first for a dry run that only lists what would be deleted.

```shell
git clean -nd     # Would remove tmp/
                  # Would remove src/debug-notes.txt
git clean -fd     # actually delete them
```

Ignored files (e.g. `node_modules`, `.env`) are kept unless you add `-x`, which is usually not what you want. Deleted untracked files aren't in Git, so they can't be recovered.

front: How do you open Git's config file in an editor instead of running many `git config` commands, and which file do you get with and without `--global`?
back:
`git config --global --edit` (short: `-e`) opens your user-wide `~/.gitconfig` in Git's editor; without `--global` it opens the current repo's `.git/config`, whose settings override the global ones for that repo.

```shell
git config --global --edit    # ~/.gitconfig: name, email, aliases...
git config --edit             # .git/config of this repo: remotes, branches

git config --list --show-origin   # every setting + the file it came from
```

`--show-origin` is the quickest way to answer "why is Git using this value?".

front: What does a non-fast-forward merge (`git merge --no-ff`) add to history compared with a fast-forward, and which does GitHub's default "Merge pull request" button do?
back:
It always creates a merge commit with two parents, even when Git could have just moved the branch pointer forward. The branch's commits stay visibly grouped, and the whole feature can be undone by reverting that one merge commit. GitHub's default "Create a merge commit" option behaves like `--no-ff`.

```shell
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature-login
git log --oneline --graph -4
# *   9f2c1ab Merge branch 'feature-login'
# |\
# | * 41d0e2c Add login form
# |/
# * 3050fc0 Previous main commit

git revert -m 1 9f2c1ab   # undo the whole feature
```

A fast-forward leaves no trace that a branch existed. GitHub also offers "Squash and merge" and "Rebase and merge".

front: What does `git fetch` change in your repository, and what does it leave alone?
back:
It downloads new commits from the remote and updates your **remote-tracking branches** (`origin/main`, `origin/fix-login`, …). It never touches your local branches or working files, so it's always safe to run.

```shell
git fetch            # or: git fetch --prune (also drop deleted remote branches)
git log --oneline main..origin/main   # commits you don't have yet
git merge origin/main                 # or rebase, when you're ready
```

`git pull` is `git fetch` followed by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch. Fetching first lets you see what's coming before it lands in your code.

front: How can `git bisect run` find the commit that broke your tests automatically, and how must the test command report its result?
back:
Start a bisect, mark one bad and one good commit, then `git bisect run <cmd>`: Git checks out commits in a binary search and runs the command on each. Exit code **0 means good**, **125 means skip** (can't test this commit), and any other code from 1 to 127 means bad.

```shell
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.4.0         # last known-good tag or hash
git bisect run npm test -- src/cart.test.ts
# ... "a1b2c3d is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset               # back to where you started
```

The test must exist in the old commits too; otherwise point `run` at a script stored outside the repo.

front: How does `git bisect` help you find the commit that introduced a bug, and what do you do at each step?
back:
It binary-searches the history between a known-good and a known-bad commit. At each step Git checks out a commit halfway between; you test it and answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`, halving the range until Git names the first bad commit. 1,000 commits take about 10 steps.

```shell
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # current commit has the bug
git bisect good v1.4.0      # this release didn't
# Git checks out a middle commit -> test it
git bisect good             # or: git bisect bad
# ... repeat until "abc1234 is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset            # return to your branch
```

Use `git bisect skip` for a commit you can't test (e.g. it doesn't build).

front: A dropped stash or lost commit isn't in `git reflog`. How can `git fsck --lost-found` help you recover it?
back:
It lists **dangling** objects — commits and file contents (blobs) that no branch, tag, or reflog entry points to — and copies them into `.git/lost-found/commit/` and `.git/lost-found/other/`. Inspect a candidate with `git show`, then give it a branch name to keep it.

```shell
git fsck --lost-found
# dangling commit d49248cfaf38...
# dangling blob 807e3fa41...

git show d49248c            # is this my stash / commit?
git branch rescued d49248c  # keep it
```

Try `git reflog` first — it's easier. Dangling objects are only kept until garbage collection prunes them (by default after about two weeks).

front: How do you limit a `git grep` search to certain file types, e.g. only `.js` and `.ts` files?
back:
Add pathspecs after `--`: `git grep "FIXME" -- '*.js' '*.ts'`, or one glob such as `'*.[jt]s'`. Quote them so Git, not your shell, expands the glob — then it matches in every subfolder.

```shell
git grep "FIXME" -- '*.js'
git grep "FIXME" -- '*.[jt]s'
# src/cart.js:  // FIXME rounding
# src/api.ts:   // FIXME retry
```

`git grep` prints each matching line prefixed by its file, and only searches files Git tracks, so `node_modules` and other ignored files are skipped automatically.

front:
Search only `.js` files for the word `FIXME` with `git grep`.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep <pattern> -- <pathspec>
____
# prints matching lines from .js files in any folder

git grep "FIXME" -- '*.[jt]s'   # .js and .ts files
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git grep "FIXME" -- '*.js'
```

Everything after `--` is a pathspec. Quoting the glob lets Git match it against every tracked path (including subfolders) instead of your shell expanding it in the current directory only.

front: How do you make `git grep` match lines containing either of two patterns, or both patterns on the same line?
back:
Give each pattern with `-e` and combine them: several `-e` patterns (or `--or`) match lines containing **either**; `--and` matches lines containing **both**. Results are lines, not whole files.

```shell
git grep -e "FIXME" -e "console.log"         # either (OR is the default)
git grep -e "FIXME" --or -e "console.log"    # same, explicit

git grep -e "FIXME" --and -e "console"       # both on the same line
```

Without `-e`, `git grep FIXME --or ...` fails with "option '--or' must come before non-option arguments". To find *files* containing both words on any lines, use `--all-match` with `-l`.

front: How do you get the number of matching lines per file from `git grep`?
back:
Add `-c`: each file with matches is printed as `path:count`.

```shell
git grep -c "FIXME"
# src/cart.js:2
# src/api.ts:1
# vendors/chart.js:1
```

The count is of matching **lines**: a line containing `FIXME` twice counts once. Combine with a pathspec (`-- src/`) to focus on your own code.

front: What are the main ways to narrow down `git grep` results?
back:
Restrict **where** it looks with pathspecs after `--` (a folder, a glob, or `:^path` to exclude), **what snapshot** by naming a branch/tag/commit, and **how** it matches with flags like `-i` (ignore case) and `-w` (whole word only).

```shell
git grep -w "user" -- src/ ':^src/generated/'
git grep -i "fixme" main -- '*.ts'
git grep -l "fetchUser"          # just file names
```

Pathspecs always go last, after `--`, so Git never mistakes them for branch names.

front: How do you search case-insensitively with `git grep`, so `fixme`, `FixMe`, and `FIXME` all match?
back:
Add `-i` (`--ignore-case`).

```shell
git grep -i "fixme"
# src/cart.js:// FIXME rounding
# src/api.ts:// fixme: retry on 503
```

`git grep` is case-sensitive by default. Pair `-i` with `-w` to match whole words only, so `-iw "id"` finds `id` and `ID` but not `userId` or `hidden`.

front: How do you make `git grep` search only one folder, or skip a folder like `vendors/`?
back:
Put the folder as a pathspec after `--`; to exclude one, prefix it with `:^` (or `:!`), and quote it.

```shell
git grep "FIXME" -- src/                 # only under src/
git grep "FIXME" -- ':^vendors/'         # everything except vendors/
git grep "FIXME" -- src/ ':^src/legacy/' # src/ minus a subfolder
```

The quotes matter: in many shells a bare `!` or `^` is special. An exclusion-only pathspec means "everything except".

front: How do you search the files as they are on another branch (say `main`) with `git grep`, without switching to it?
back:
Pass the branch (or any tag/commit) after the pattern: `git grep "FIXME" main`. Git searches that snapshot straight from the repository; your working tree isn't touched.

```shell
git grep "FIXME" main
# main:src/cart.js:// FIXME rounding

git grep "FIXME" origin/release-1.4 -- src/
```

Each line is prefixed with the revision name. Handy for checking whether a fix or a leftover `console.log` exists on a branch you don't have checked out.

front: How do you show line numbers in `git grep` output, and how do you make that the default?
back:
Add `-n`: the line number appears between the file name and the matched line. Set `grep.lineNumber` to get it every time.

```shell
git grep -n "FIXME"
# src/cart.js:14:  // FIXME rounding

git config --global grep.lineNumber true
```

Many editors and terminals make `path:line` clickable, so this takes you straight to the spot.

front: Does `git grep` accept regular expressions, and which flag do you need for `|` alternation like `console\.(log|debug)`?
back:
Yes. Patterns are **basic** regular expressions by default, where `(`, `|` and `+` are literal characters; add `-E` for extended regex syntax (similar to JavaScript's).

```shell
git grep -E "console\.(log|debug)"
# src/cart.js:console.log(total)
# src/api.ts:console.debug(res)

git grep "console\.(log|debug)"   # no -E: finds nothing
```

`-F` does the opposite: treats the pattern as a fixed string, so dots and brackets need no escaping.

front:
Find every `console.log` or `console.debug` call in tracked files with one `git grep` regex.

```shell
git grep "FIXME"
# plain search

____
# src/cart.js:console.log(total)
# src/api.ts:console.debug(res)
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git grep -E "console\.(log|debug)"
```

`-E` enables extended regex, so `( | )` group and alternate. Escape the dot, or it matches any character. Two `-e` patterns (`-e "console\.log" -e "console\.debug"`) also work.

front: Which `git grep` flags make long results easier to read?
back:
`--heading --break` print each file name once with a blank line between files, `-n` adds line numbers, and `-l` / `-c` shrink the output to file names or per-file counts.

```shell
git grep -n --heading --break "FIXME"
# src/cart.js
# 14:  // FIXME rounding
# 30:  // FIXME tax
#
# src/api.ts
# 8:  // FIXME retry
```

`-p` (`--show-function`) also shows the enclosing function's header line, which helps judge each match in context.

front: How do you get only the names of files that match a pattern from `git grep`, e.g. to open them all?
back:
Add `-l` (`--files-with-matches`): each matching file is printed once, with no line contents.

```shell
git grep -l "fetchUser"
# src/api/users.ts
# src/pages/Profile.tsx

code $(git grep -l "fetchUser")      # open them in VS Code
git grep -l "fetchUser" | wc -l      # how many files use it
```

`-L` is the inverse: files that do *not* match.

front: Given a commit hash, how can you find the merge commit (e.g. the merged pull request) that brought it into `main`?
back:
Find the first merge on `main`'s own line (first-parent) that has the commit as an ancestor. This alias intersects the two histories and prints that merge's hash:

```ini
[alias]
  find-merge = "!sh -c 'commit=$0 && branch=${1:-HEAD} && (git rev-list $commit..$branch --ancestry-path | cat -n; git rev-list $commit..$branch --first-parent | cat -n) | sort -k2 -s | uniq -f1 -d | sort -n | tail -1 | cut -f2'"
```

```shell
git switch main
git find-merge 3050fc0
# c2ec1385b47a4b9024bdde77c0978a34359480ac
git show --no-patch c2ec138      # "Merge pull request #142 from ..."
```

`--ancestry-path` lists commits that descend from the given one; `--first-parent` lists only `main`'s direct line. The oldest commit in both is the merge. A plain `git log --merges --ancestry-path` can instead return a "merge main into feature" commit from inside the branch.

front: Why prefer `git push --force-with-lease` over `git push --force`, and what can still defeat its safety check?
back:
`--force-with-lease` only overwrites the remote branch if it still points where your last fetch saw it (your `origin/<branch>`). If a teammate pushed since then, the push is rejected instead of silently deleting their commits. Plain `--force` overwrites unconditionally.

```shell
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease
# ! [rejected] ... (stale info)  <- someone pushed; fetch and look first
```

Pitfall: a background `git fetch` (many editors do this) updates `origin/<branch>` without you looking, so the lease passes anyway. Adding `--force-if-includes` (Git 2.30+, or `git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true`) also requires that you've actually integrated the remote commits.

front: After rebasing or amending commits you already pushed, why does `git push` get rejected, and how do you update the remote branch safely?
back:
The rewritten commits have new hashes, so your branch no longer contains the remote's commits and Git rejects the push as a non-fast-forward. Replace the remote branch with `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.

```shell
git switch patch-1
git fetch
git rebase origin/main
git push
# ! [rejected] patch-1 -> patch-1 (non-fast-forward)
git push --force-with-lease
```

Only do this on a branch that is yours. Anyone who pulled the old commits now has diverged history. Protected branches like `main` usually block force-pushes entirely — and should.

front: What must a `Co-authored-by:` trailer look like for GitHub to credit a co-author on a commit?
back:
Put it at the very end of the commit message, after one blank line, one line per person: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`. The email must be one linked to their GitHub account (their `ID+username@users.noreply.github.com` address works if they keep theirs private).

```shell
git commit -m "Add login form" \
  --trailer "Co-authored-by: Ana Ruiz <ana@example.com>"
# Add login form
#
# Co-authored-by: Ana Ruiz <ana@example.com>
```

`--trailer` (Git 2.32+) adds the blank line for you. If the email doesn't match an account, GitHub shows the trailer text but credits nobody.

front: What can you do to commits in `git rebase -i`, and how do you continue, abort, or re-edit the todo list mid-rebase?
back:
`git rebase -i <base>` opens a todo list of the commits after `<base>`. Change each line's word to `pick` (keep), `reword` (edit message), `edit` (stop to change it), `squash`/`fixup` (merge into the previous one) or `drop`, or reorder lines. Save and close to run it.

```shell
git rebase -i HEAD~5                 # last 5 commits
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main   # fixup! commits pre-arranged

git rebase --continue      # after fixing a conflict (git add first)
git rebase --abort         # give up, back to how it was
git rebase --edit-todo     # change the remaining plan
```

Every rewritten commit gets a new hash, so only rebase commits that aren't on a shared branch, and push with `--force-with-lease`.

front: A team mixes Windows and macOS and diffs show every line changed because of line endings. Why isn't `git config core.eol lf` a reliable fix, and what is?
back:
`core.eol` is a per-machine setting that only affects files Git already treats as text, and it's ignored when `core.autocrlf` is `true` or `input` (the Windows installer's default is `true`). Commit a `.gitattributes` file instead, so the rule travels with the repo and applies to everyone.

```text
# .gitattributes
* text=auto eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
```

```shell
git add .gitattributes
git add --renormalize .    # re-save existing files with the new rule
git commit -m "Normalize line endings"
```

`text=auto` lets Git detect text files; `eol=lf` checks them out with LF (`\n`) instead of Windows CRLF (`\r\n`).

front:
Line endings: fill in the `.gitattributes` rule that makes Git normalize all text files and check them out with LF endings on every machine.

```text
# .gitattributes (committed to the repo)
____
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
```
back:
One solution:

```text
* text=auto eol=lf
```

`*` matches every path, `text=auto` lets Git detect which files are text, and `eol=lf` checks those out with `\n`. Later lines override earlier ones, so `.bat` files still get CRLF. Unlike `git config core.eol lf`, this applies to every clone.

front: How do you list all your Git aliases and what they expand to?
back:
`git config --get-regexp '^alias\.'` prints every setting whose name starts with `alias.`, one per line as `name value`.

```shell
git config --get-regexp '^alias\.'
# alias.st status -sb
# alias.sw switch

git config --get-regexp '^alias\.' | sed 's/^alias\.//'
# st status -sb
# sw switch
```

The older `git config -l | grep alias` also catches unrelated settings whose value contains the word "alias". You can make this an alias itself: `git config --global alias.aliases "config --get-regexp ^alias\."`.

front:
List every Git alias you've defined, with its expansion.

```shell
____
# alias.st status -sb
# alias.sw switch
# alias.lg log --oneline --graph --all
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --get-regexp '^alias\.'
```

It matches config keys against the regex, so only `alias.*` entries print. Pipe to `sed 's/^alias\.//'` to drop the prefix.

front: How do you merge `patch-1` into `main` so that a merge commit is always created, with your own message?
back:
Switch to `main`, then run `git merge --no-ff -m "<message>" patch-1`. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible.

```shell
git switch main
git merge --no-ff -m "Merge patch-1: validate signup email" patch-1
```

The merge commit groups the branch's work under one commit, so it's easy to see in `git log --graph` and to undo as a unit with `git revert -m 1 <merge-hash>`.

front: To merge `patch-1` into `main`, which branch must you be on, and when does Git fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit?
back:
Be on the **target** (`main`) and name the source: `git merge patch-1`. Git fast-forwards — just moves `main` up to `patch-1` — only when `main` has no new commits since `patch-1` branched off. If both moved, it creates a merge commit with two parents.

```shell
git switch main
git pull
git merge patch-1
# "Fast-forward"  or  "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy."
```

On conflicts, Git stops: fix the marked files, `git add` them, then `git merge --continue` — or `git merge --abort` to back out completely.

front: What does `git gc --prune=now --aggressive` do, and why do you rarely need it?
back:
`git gc` packs loose objects into compressed packfiles and deletes unreachable ones. `--prune=now` deletes unreachable objects immediately instead of keeping them about two weeks, and `--aggressive` recompresses everything much harder (slow). Git already runs a lighter `git gc --auto` for you.

```shell
git count-objects -vH           # check size first
git gc --prune=now --aggressive
```
