Cost: `--prune=now` throws away dangling commits you might still want to recover, like a stash you dropped yesterday. And it won't shrink a repo whose history still contains a huge file; that needs a history rewrite (e.g. `git filter-repo`).

front:
Run a thorough garbage collection that recompresses everything and deletes unreachable objects right away.

```shell
git count-objects -vH   # size before
____
git count-objects -vH   # size after
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git gc --prune=now --aggressive
```

`--aggressive` spends much more time on compression; `--prune=now` removes unreachable objects now rather than after the ~2-week grace period, which also means dropped stashes and orphaned commits can no longer be recovered.

front: How do you copy one commit, several commits, or a range of commits onto your current branch with `git cherry-pick`, and does `A..B` include `A`?
back:
Pass hashes (`git cherry-pick <c1> <c2>`) or a range. `A..B` means "after A up to and including B", so **A is excluded**; write `A^..B` to include it. Each picked commit becomes a new commit (new hash) on your branch.

```shell
git switch release-1.5
git cherry-pick 3050fc0                # one commit
git cherry-pick 3050fc0 c191f90        # these two
git cherry-pick 3050fc0..c191f90       # after 3050fc0 .. c191f90
git cherry-pick 3050fc0^..c191f90      # 3050fc0 .. c191f90, inclusive
```

On a conflict: fix, `git add`, `git cherry-pick --continue` (or `--abort`). Add `-x` to note the original hash in the message, useful for backports.

front:
Cherry-pick the commits after `3050fc0de` up to and including `c191f90c7` (excluding `3050fc0de` itself).

```shell
git cherry-pick 3050fc0de             # one commit
git cherry-pick 3050fc0de c191f90c7   # exactly these two

____
# picks the range: 3050fc0de (excluded) .. c191f90c7 (included)

git cherry-pick 3050fc0de^..c191f90c7 # both ends included
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git cherry-pick 3050fc0de..c191f90c7
```

`A..B` is "commits reachable from B but not from A", which excludes A itself. Starting from `A^` (A's parent) pulls A into the range.

front: How do you get a local copy of a teammate's remote branch and keep it up to date, and what if you want a different local name?
back:
`git switch patch-1`: if no local `patch-1` exists but `origin/patch-1` does, Git creates a local branch that tracks it. After that, `git pull` fetches and merges new commits. For a different local name, create it with `--track`.

```shell
git fetch
git switch patch-1        # local patch-1 tracking origin/patch-1
git pull                  # later: bring in their new commits

git switch -c patch-one --track origin/patch-1   # custom local name
```

`git checkout patch-1` does the same auto-tracking. `git pull` is `git fetch` plus a merge (or a rebase with `--rebase` / `pull.rebase true`) into your current branch.

front: How do you push a new local branch and link it to its remote counterpart, so later `git push` and `git pull` need no arguments?
back:
`git push -u origin <branch>` (`-u` = `--set-upstream`): it creates the remote branch if needed and records it as your branch's upstream.

```shell
git switch -c patch-1
git commit -am "Fix cart total rounding"
git push -u origin patch-1
git push            # from now on, no arguments needed
```

`git branch -u origin/patch-1` only *links* to a remote branch that already exists — on a brand-new branch it fails with "the requested upstream branch 'origin/patch-1' does not exist". Set `push.autoSetupRemote true` to skip `-u` entirely.

front: What does `git rebase origin/main` do to your feature branch's commits, and how do you handle a conflict partway through?
back:
It sets your branch's commits aside, moves the branch to the tip of `origin/main`, and re-applies your commits one by one on top — as new commits with new hashes. The result reads as if you'd started your work from the latest `main`.

```shell
git switch patch-2
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# CONFLICT in src/cart.js
#   fix the file, then:
git add src/cart.js
git rebase --continue      # or: git rebase --abort
```

A conflict can stop the rebase once per commit being replayed. If the branch was already pushed, update it with `git push --force-with-lease`.

front: You committed `.env` by mistake (not pushed yet). How do you take it out of the last commit while keeping the file on disk?
back:
`git rm --cached .env` removes it from the index (not from disk), then `git commit --amend --no-edit` rewrites the last commit without it. Add it to `.gitignore` so it doesn't come back.

```shell
git rm --cached .env
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

If the commit was already pushed, amending means `git push --force-with-lease` (only on your own branch). Any secret that reached the remote must be rotated — it's in history and may already be copied.

front:
Remove `.env` from the last commit but keep the file in your working folder.

```shell
____
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git rm --cached .env
```

`--cached` removes the file from the staging area only, so the amended commit no longer contains it while your local copy stays. Without `--cached`, `git rm` would delete the file from disk too.

front: How do you rename a branch that has already been pushed, so the remote gets the new name too?
back:
Git can't rename a remote branch directly: rename it locally, push the new name with `-u`, then delete the old name on the remote.

```shell
git branch -m patch-1 patch-2          # rename locally
git push -u origin patch-2             # create + track the new one
git push origin --delete patch-1       # remove the old one
```

Teammates with the old branch must switch to the new one. On GitHub, deleting the old branch closes its open pull requests; renaming via the web UI ("Rename branch") keeps them.

front: How do you rename a local Git branch — both the one you're on and a different one?
back:
`git branch -m <new-name>` renames the current branch; `git branch -m <old-name> <new-name>` renames any branch.

```shell
git switch fix-lgoin
git branch -m fix-login              # rename current branch

git branch -m patch-1 cart-rounding  # rename another branch
```

`-m` refuses if the new name already exists; `-M` overwrites it. This only renames locally — a pushed branch also needs the new name pushed and the old one deleted.

front: Your local `main` has stray commits and you want it to exactly match `origin/main`. Which commands do that, and what do they destroy?
back:
Fetch, switch to `main`, and hard-reset it to the remote-tracking branch. This throws away `main`'s local-only commits and any uncommitted changes to tracked files; untracked files stay.

```shell
git fetch origin
git switch main
git branch backup-main          # optional safety net
git reset --hard origin/main
```

Works for any branch. Commits you reset away are recoverable for a while through `git reflog`, but uncommitted edits are not. If those stray commits are real work, move them to a new branch first (the `backup-main` line does exactly that).

front: A file was deleted in commit `3050fc0`. How do you bring it back, and why do you need the `^` in `3050fc0^`?
back:
Restore it from the commit *before* the deletion: `git restore --source=3050fc0^ -- <path>` (older: `git checkout 3050fc0^ -- <path>`). `^` means "parent of"; in `3050fc0` itself the file no longer exists.

```shell
git log --oneline --diff-filter=D -- src/api/client.js
# 3050fc0 Remove old API client

git restore --source=3050fc0^ -- src/api/client.js
git restore --source=3050fc0^ -- 'src/*.json'   # globs work, but also overwrite
                                                # json files that still exist
```

The file comes back as a new, uncommitted file; `git add` and commit it. `--diff-filter=D` shows only commits that deleted the path.

front:
Bring back `src/api/client.js`, which was deleted in commit `3050fc0de`.

```shell
git log --oneline --diff-filter=D -- src/api/client.js
# 3050fc0 Remove old API client

____
git add src/api/client.js
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git restore --source=3050fc0de^ -- src/api/client.js
```

`git checkout 3050fc0de^ -- src/api/client.js` also works. The `^` picks the deleting commit's parent — the last snapshot that still had the file.

front: What does `HEAD~3` refer to, and how do you use it to undo your last three commits but keep their changes?
back:
`HEAD~3` is the commit three steps back along the current branch (`HEAD~1` = the previous commit). `git reset HEAD~3` moves the branch there and leaves the undone commits' changes in your files as unstaged edits.

```shell
git reset HEAD~3           # undo 3 commits, keep the changes
git reset --soft HEAD~3    # same, but keep them staged (easy re-commit)
git reset --hard HEAD~3    # undo 3 commits AND discard their changes
```

A common use is squashing messy local commits: `git reset --soft HEAD~3` then one clean `git commit`. Only do this to commits you haven't pushed to a shared branch.

front: When you `git reset <commit>` to move your branch back, what happens to the undone changes with `--soft`, the default (`--mixed`), and `--hard`?
back:
All three move the branch to `<commit>`. `--soft` keeps the undone changes **staged**, the default `--mixed` keeps them as **unstaged edits**, and `--hard` **deletes** them from the staging area and your files.

```shell
git reset --soft 3050fc0    # changes staged, ready to re-commit
git reset 3050fc0           # changes kept, unstaged
git reset --hard 3050fc0    # changes gone
```

If `--hard` went wrong, `git reflog` still shows the old commit so you can `git reset --hard <old-hash>` back — but uncommitted edits it wiped are lost for good.

front: How would you write a `useToggler` custom hook that returns a boolean plus a `toggle` function whose identity stays the same on every render?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const toggleValue = useCallback(() => setValue(prev => !prev), []);
```

The functional updater `prev => !prev` reads the latest state from React, so the callback depends on nothing and `useCallback(..., [])` can return the same function forever. `setValue` itself is guaranteed stable, so it does not need to be a dependency either.

front: A branch `<select>` gets its options from an API after a delay, and should default to the first branch once they arrive. Instead of a `useDelayedState` hook whose effect copies `branches[0]` into state, what simpler pattern works?
How can a `useForm` hook let one `onChange` handler update every field of a login form, and why should that handler use the functional state updater?
Why doesn't calling `map.set(key, value)` on a `Map` stored in React state re-render the component, and how should a `useMap` hook's `set` action update it instead?

A counter increments inside `setTimeout`, and quick repeated clicks lose updates because each timeout captured an old `count`. How does a `useGetSet` hook (a ref plus a forced re-render) fix that, and what is the simpler built-in fix?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const [, update] = useReducer(x => x + 1, 0);
```

Writing to a ref never re-renders, so the hook needs a dispatch function that changes some state. A reducer that returns a new value each time (a counter, or `() => ({})`) always differs under `Object.is`, so every `update()` triggers a render that shows the new `state.current`.

front: How can a React component turn URLs inside a plain-text comment into clickable links without using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
i % 2 === 1
```

When the separator regex contains a capturing group, `split` puts each captured match between the surrounding text pieces, so the matches always land at odd indices, even when the text starts with a URL (index 0 is then `''`):

```js
'https://a.io and x'.split(/(https?:\/\/[^\s<]+)/g);
// → ['', 'https://a.io', ' and x']
```

An alternative is `URL_RE.test(part)`, but a `/g` regex keeps `lastIndex` between `test` calls and can give wrong answers, so the index check is simpler and safer.

front: A countdown timer keeps hours, minutes, seconds, and an `over` flag in four pieces of state and re-creates its `setInterval` on every render. What simpler state and effect make it correct?
How do you render an array of values as rows of a `<table>` in React, and what should each `<tr>` use as its `key`?
back:
`map` the array inside `` to one `` per item and give each row a `key` that identifies **that item**, ideally a stable ID from the data (`row.id`). Keys let React match rows between renders. ```jsx function DataTable({ rows }) { // rows: [{ id: 7, name: 'John' }, ...] return ( {rows.map(row => ( ))}
IDName
{row.id} {row.name}
); } ``` Pitfall: a key like `` `${i}_${val}` `` still contains the index, so it changes when rows are inserted, deleted, or sorted. React may then reuse the wrong row's DOM and state (e.g. a half-typed input moves to another row). Index keys are only safe for static lists that never reorder.

One solution:

```jsx
{users.map(user => (
```

JSX has no loop syntax, so you embed an expression with `{...}` and `map` each item to an element. Each `<tr>` gets `key={user.id}`: a stable, unique ID from the data, so React can keep the right row when the list is sorted or filtered.

front: How would a `DataList` component render an array of names as either a `<ul>` or an `<ol>`, depending on an `isOrdered` prop?

back:
One solution: ```jsx const items = data.map(name =>
  • {name}
    • ); ``` `map` turns each string into an `
  • `, and each element in an array needs a `key`. Because the names are unique, the name itself is a stable key. With real data, prefer an ID.

front: Given an array of user objects and a list of column names like `['name', 'email', 'age']`, how do you render only those columns as a React table?
A `useKeyPress('w')` hook defines its keydown and keyup handlers in the component body, then adds them in `useEffect(..., [])`. What bug does this create, and how do you fix it?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (e.key === targetKey) setPressed(true);
```

`KeyboardEvent.key` is the character or key name (`'w'`, `'Enter'`, `'Escape'`). The check filters out other keys. The handlers are created inside the effect, so they always see the current `targetKey`, and the cleanup removes those same functions.

front: Why does a `useEventListener(type, handler)` hook store `handler` in a ref instead of listing it in the dependencies of the effect that calls `addEventListener`?
How can a `useHover` hook attach mouse listeners to whatever element it's given through a callback ref, and what does React 19's ref cleanup function simplify?
What is the simplest way to lazy-load images in a React product list today, and when would you still reach for `IntersectionObserver`?
A `useComponentDidMount(fn)` hook wraps `useEffect(fn, [])`. What does the empty dependency array actually mean, and why does `fn` run twice in development?
A `useComponentDidUpdate` hook skips an effect's first run with a `mounted` ref that it sets to `true`. Why does that fire on mount under StrictMode, and what should you use instead?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (Object.is(prev.current, value)) return;
```

On mount `prev.current` already equals `value`, so both StrictMode setup runs return early. When `value` changes, the check fails, the ref is updated, and the callback runs once. A `mounted = true` flag would break here, because the ref keeps its value across StrictMode's extra setup, so the callback would fire on mount.

front: How do you run code when a component unmounts using hooks, and why might `useEffect(() => () => onUnmount(), [])` call an outdated version of `onUnmount`?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
return () => onUnmount();
```

Whatever function an effect returns is its **cleanup**. With `[]` dependencies, it runs only when the component unmounts (plus once right after mount in development StrictMode). Note that it keeps the `onUnmount` from the first render; store the callback in a ref if it must see current props.

front: A `TextArea` component copies its `value` prop into `useState` and renders that state. Why isn't that truly controlled, and what should the component do instead?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
onChange={e => onChange(e.target.value)}
```

React fires `onChange` on every keystroke (like the DOM `input` event). The component reads the new text from `e.target.value` and hands it up; the parent's state update re-renders the textarea with the new `value`. Without this, a `value` prop makes the field read-only.

front: How do you build a React textarea that stops accepting text after N words and shows "3/5 words", and why should the word count be derived rather than stored in state?
When would you make a textarea uncontrolled with `defaultValue`, and how can the parent still get its text?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
onChange={e => onValueChange(e.target.value)}
```

`defaultValue` is used only for the first render, and after that the browser owns the text, so there's no state and no `value` prop. `onChange` still fires on each edit, so the parent can observe the text without controlling it. Changing `defaultValue` later has no effect; remount with a new `key` if you need to reset it.

front: How do you limit a React textarea to 280 characters and show a live "12/280" counter?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
onChange={e => setText(e.target.value.slice(0, limit))}
```

`slice(0, limit)` keeps at most `limit` characters, so pasted text is clipped before it reaches state. Because the textarea is controlled, the DOM then shows exactly what's in state. The native `maxLength={limit}` attribute gives the same typing behavior in the browser; the `slice` also covers text you set from code.

front: How do you build a `mailto:` link in React that pre-fills the subject and body, and why use `encodeURIComponent` rather than `URLSearchParams` for them?

back: One solution: ```jsx return {children}; ``` The `mailto:` scheme opens the user's mail app with the address filled in; `?subject=...&body=...` pre-fills the rest. Encoding each value with `encodeURIComponent` keeps characters like `&` and spaces from breaking the URL (`'Hello & Welcome'` → `Hello%20%26%20Welcome`).

front: How do you make a phone number tappable on a phone in React, and what format should the `tel:` href use?

back: One solution: ```jsx return {children}; ``` The `tel:` scheme tells the device to start a call to that number. Stripping spaces and dashes (`'+30 210 123-4567'` → `'+302101234567'`) gives a clean, international number the dialer can use.

front: How would you build a group of checkboxes where the user can pick several options (e.g. interests on a profile form), and what should the component keep in state?
How does a "show password" toggle work in React, and which two details keep it from breaking the login form it sits in?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
type={shown ? 'text' : 'password'}
```

The browser masks characters only for `type="password"`; switching to `'text'` shows them, and the typed value is kept because it lives in state. The button needs `type="button"` so clicking it inside a form doesn't submit the form.

front: How does a `useLocalStorage(key, defaultValue)` hook read storage only once, and why should every read and write be wrapped in `try/catch`?
When persisting React state in the browser, how does `sessionStorage` differ from `localStorage`, and when would you choose `sessionStorage`?
PropTypes' `objectOf` described objects with unknown keys, like `{ [userId]: username }`. What is the TypeScript equivalent, and why won't `propTypes` validation help you in React 19?

back:
One solution:

```tsx
usernamesById: Record<string, string>;
```

`Record<K, V>` means "an object with keys of type `K`, each holding a `V`", which is what you want when the keys aren't known ahead of time. The index signature `{ [id: string]: string }` is equivalent. React 19 no longer runs `propTypes` checks, so TypeScript is the standard way to describe props now.

front: PropTypes' `shape()` described an object with known keys of different types, like a user with `name` and `age`. How do you type that prop in TypeScript, and how is it different from `Record<string, T>`?

back:
One solution:

```tsx
user: { name: string; surname: string; age: number };
```

An inline object type lists each known key with its own type. In real code you'd usually name it (`type User = { ... }`) and write `user: User`. Unlike `Record<string, T>`, it rejects unknown keys in object literals and lets each key have a different type.

front: Why replace hard-coded action type strings in a reducer with named constants, and what does Redux Toolkit's `createSlice` do about this today?

back:
One solution:

```js
case ACTION_TYPES.SET_NAME:
```

Referring to `ACTION_TYPES.SET_NAME` everywhere (reducer and `dispatch` calls) means the string is written once. The `default` branch must return the unchanged `state` so unknown actions don't wipe it out.

front: A reducer's `switch` grows with every new action, each action object has a different shape, and type strings are hard-coded. What conventions fix these three problems?
When a parent component re-renders, which of its child components re-render by default, and does that mean the DOM is updated?
Why does a Redux store update usually re-render fewer components than changing a large Context value, and what cost does every `useSelector` still pay on each dispatch?
Why does passing `value={{ user, setUser }}` to a context provider make every consumer re-render whenever the provider's component renders, and how do you fix it?
When do `useMemo` and `useCallback` actually prevent re-renders, and when are they wasted work?
A context provider sits in a component that re-renders often, and the whole subtree re-renders with it. How can you make only the components that read the context re-render?
Why is it safe for React to skip rendering a component whose props and state haven't changed, and what must your component code do for that to hold?
What does "rendering" mean in React, and what does React compare the result against to decide which DOM changes to make?

Components wrapped in React-Redux's `connect()` behave like `React.memo`, but components using `useSelector` don't. What does that mean for re-renders, and how do you get the same protection with hooks?
What happens in React's render phase versus its commit phase, and when do `useLayoutEffect` and `useEffect` run relative to them?
In a ripple-effect button, why is the ripple its own absolutely positioned `<span>`, and why is the label wrapped in a separate positioned `<span>`?
back: The ripple must be placed at the click point and clipped to the button, so it's an `position: absolute` child of a button with `position: relative; overflow: hidden`. The label gets its own `position: relative; z-index` so the text stays **above** the expanding circle instead of being covered by it. ```jsx ``` ```css .ripple-button { position: relative; overflow: hidden; } .ripple-button > .ripple { position: absolute; border-radius: 50%; } .ripple-button > .content { position: relative; z-index: 1; } ``` The ripple is decoration only, so `aria-hidden="true"` keeps screen readers from announcing an empty element; the button's accessible name still comes from its text.

front: A ripple button stores click coordinates and uses two chained `useEffect`s plus a `setTimeout` to show and hide the ripple. How can it work with no effects at all, and why must it measure `e.currentTarget` rather than `e.target`?
What CSS makes a ripple circle grow and fade out, and why does the animation need `animation-fill-mode: forwards`?

back:
One solution:

```css
animation: ripple-effect 0.9s ease forwards;
```

The `animation` shorthand takes the keyframes name, duration, timing function, and fill mode (it plays once by default). `forwards` keeps the `to` frame's `opacity: 0` after the animation ends, so the circle doesn't flash back into view.

front: How would you write a reusable React `Select` component that takes `[value, label]` pairs and preselects one of them, and when would you use `defaultValue` instead of `value`?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
defaultValue={selectedValue}
```

In React you set a select's choice on the `<select>` element, not with `selected` on an `<option>`. `defaultValue` applies only on the first render; afterwards the DOM keeps whatever the user picks, and `onChange` reports it. Use `value` instead if the parent must control the selection.

front: Why does React warn when you put `selected` on an `<option>`, and how do you choose the selected option instead?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
value={selected}
```

A controlled `<select>` shows the option whose `value` matches, so the parent's state decides the selection and `onChange` asks the parent to change it. Putting `selected={selected === value}` on each option instead triggers a React warning.

front: How would you build an accessible 5-star rating input in React that previews the rating on hover and saves it on click?
In a React Testing Library test, what does the warning "An update to X inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)" usually mean, and how do you fix it?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
expect(await screen.findByText('Saved')).toBeInTheDocument();
```

`findBy*` returns a promise that retries the query until the element appears (1 second by default), so the test waits for the async state update to finish. `getByText` would check immediately, fail, and leave the late update to trigger the act(...) warning. `await waitFor(() => expect(...))` is the general-purpose alternative.

front: How do you test a modal that renders through `createPortal` with React Testing Library, and why is mocking `createPortal` unnecessary?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
expect(screen.getByRole('dialog')).toHaveTextContent('Hello World!');
```

`screen` queries the entire document, so it finds elements rendered through a portal even though they aren't inside the test's `container`. Querying by role also checks that the dialog is exposed correctly to assistive technology. `toHaveTextContent` comes from `@testing-library/jest-dom`.

front: How do you render a Redux-connected component in a React Testing Library test with a chosen starting state, without repeating the `<Provider>` setup in every test?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const Wrapper = ({ children }) => <Provider store={store}>{children}</Provider>;
```

Testing Library's `wrapper` option renders your component as `children` of this component, so every connected component under test can reach the store. The store is created inside the helper, so each test starts from its own `preloadedState`.

front: A toggle switch hides its checkbox with `display: none` and colors the label green or red. What accessibility bug does that create, and how should a React toggle be built instead?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
aria-checked={on}
```

With `role="switch"`, assistive technology reads `aria-checked` to announce "on" or "off". React renders the boolean as `"true"`/`"false"`. Using a real `<button>` keeps keyboard support (Tab, Enter, Space) for free, unlike hiding a checkbox with `display: none`.

front: When a modal is open, how does a `useBodyScrollLock` hook stop the page behind it from scrolling, and what exactly must its cleanup restore?
How does a `useClickOutside(ref, onOutside)` hook detect clicks outside a dropdown, and why does it test `ref.current.contains(e.target)`?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (ref.current && !ref.current.contains(e.target)) {
```

`contains` returns `true` for the element itself and all of its descendants, so negating it means "somewhere else on the page". Checking `ref.current` first skips the moment before the element is attached (or after it's removed), when the ref is `null`.

front: A `useClickInside(ref, callback)` hook adds a document click listener and checks whether the click landed inside an element. Why is that usually unnecessary in React?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const button = e.target.closest('button[data-tag]');
```

`e.target` is the innermost element clicked (maybe text inside the button), so `closest` walks up to the nearest matching ancestor, or returns `null` for clicks elsewhere in the list. `dataset.tag` reads the `data-tag` attribute.

front: A `useEffectOnce(callback, when)` hook runs `callback` the first time `when` becomes true. How does a ref make that work, and when should the code go in an event handler instead?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (when && !hasRun.current) {
```

The effect runs whenever `when` changes, so the condition does the filtering: `when` must be true, and the ref must say it hasn't run yet. A ref (not state) is used because flipping the flag shouldn't cause a re-render.

front: Error boundaries don't catch errors thrown in event handlers or async code. How can a `useError` hook hand such an error to the nearest error boundary?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (error) throw error;
```

Error boundaries catch errors thrown while rendering, not in event handlers or promises. Storing the error in state triggers a re-render, and throwing it at that point moves it into the render phase, where the boundary can catch it and show its fallback.

front: A `useFetch(url)` hook fetches in `useEffect(..., [])` and stores the abort function in state. What bugs does that cause, and how should the effect handle URL changes, cancellation, and HTTP errors?
A `useSearchParam('post')` hook listens for `popstate`, `pushstate`, and `replacestate` events. Why doesn't it update when your code calls `history.pushState`, and what should you do instead?
How does a `useHash` hook keep React in sync with the URL's `#hash`, and why doesn't its setter need to call `setState`?
What's wrong with a `useIntersectionObserver` hook whose effect has `[]` dependencies and whose cleanup calls `observer.unobserve(ref.current)`, and how should it clean up?
In a `useInterval` hook, why is `setInterval` given a small `tick` wrapper that calls `savedCallback.current()`, instead of `savedCallback.current` itself?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
savedCallback.current();
```

`setInterval` holds on to `tick` forever, but `tick` looks up `savedCallback.current` each time it runs. The first effect points the ref at the newest `callback` after every render, so each tick sees current props and state.

front: Why must a React component start its `setInterval` inside `useEffect` with a cleanup, instead of calling it directly in the component body?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
return () => clearInterval(id);
```

The function an effect returns is its cleanup. React calls it on unmount (and before re-running the effect), so the interval doesn't keep calling `setNow` on a component that's gone. In development, StrictMode runs setup → cleanup → setup, which only works cleanly because this cleanup exists.

front: What does a complete `useInterval(callback, delay)` custom hook look like, and how does passing `delay = null` pause it?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (delay === null) return;
```

Returning early means no interval is created and there's nothing to clean up. When `delay` changes back to a number, the effect re-runs and starts a fresh interval; when it changes to `null`, the previous run's cleanup clears the old one. Use `=== null` rather than `!delay`, so a delay of `0` isn't treated as paused.

front: A counter uses `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])`. Why does it show 1 and then stop changing?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
setCount(c => c + 1);
```

The interval callback was created on the first render, so it would always see `count === 0`. A functional update doesn't read `count` from the closure at all: React passes the current value in as `c`, so each tick adds one to the real latest count.

front: A `useMutationObserver(ref, callback, options = { ... })` hook lists `callback` and `options` as effect dependencies. Why does it disconnect and re-create the observer on every render, and how do you fix it?

A `usePortal` hook builds a `Portal` component and removes it with `ReactDOM.unmountComponentAtNode`. Why does that fail in React 19, and what's the simpler way to render a modal into `document.body`?
How does a `useAnimationFrame(callback)` hook call `callback` once per frame with the time since the previous frame, and what must its cleanup cancel?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
if (last !== undefined) latest.current(time - last);
```

`requestAnimationFrame` passes a high-resolution timestamp to each frame. On the first frame there's no previous time, so the call is skipped; afterwards `time - last` is the frame's duration (about 16.7 ms at 60 Hz). Using the delta keeps animations the same speed on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens.

front: How can a custom hook show a readable label in React DevTools, and where is `useDebugValue` allowed to be called?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
useDebugValue(`${label}: ${value}`);
```

`useDebugValue` attaches a display value to the custom hook it's called in. DevTools strips the `use` prefix from the hook's name, so it shows `StateWithLabel: "counter: 0"` and updates as the state changes.

front: How does a `useTimeout(callback, delay)` hook differ from `useInterval`, and what happens to a pending timeout when the component unmounts or `delay` changes?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const id = setTimeout(() => savedCallback.current(), delay);
```

The arrow function reads the ref when the timer fires, so it runs whichever callback the component rendered last. Keeping `id` lets the cleanup cancel the timer if the component unmounts or `delay` changes first.

front: How do you set the browser tab's title from a React component in React 19, and what did the classic `useTitle` hook with `useEffect(..., [])` get wrong?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
document.title = title;
```

The effect lists `title` as a dependency, so a new title re-runs it (after the cleanup briefly restores the old one). Running in an effect keeps `document` access out of server rendering. In React 19 you can skip the hook and render `<title>{title}</title>` directly.

front: How can you force a React function component to re-render, and why is needing to do so usually a sign of a bug?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const [, forceUpdate] = useReducer(x => x + 1, 0);
```

React re-renders only when state changes by `Object.is`. A reducer that always returns a different value (a counter, or `() => ({})`) guarantees that. `useState` works too: `const [, set] = useState(0); () => set(n => n + 1)`. Before reaching for this, check whether the data should just be state.

front: Why does a `useWindowSize` hook start with `width` and `height` as `undefined` and read the real size in an effect, and when should you use CSS instead?
A `useSSR` hook returns `isBrowser` by checking `typeof window !== 'undefined'` during render. Why can that cause a hydration mismatch, and how do you safely render browser-only content?
How do you warn a user before they close or reload a tab with an unsaved form, and why can't the `beforeunload` handler show your own `confirm()` dialog?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
e.preventDefault();
```

Canceling the `beforeunload` event tells the browser to show its built-in confirmation; the text can't be customized. Because the effect depends on `isDirty`, the listener is removed as soon as the form is saved, so users can leave freely again.

front: How does a `useOnline` hook track whether the browser is online, and what does `navigator.onLine === true` **not** guarantee?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => navigator.onLine, () => true);
```

`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` calls `subscribe` once with a `notify` function, re-reads `getSnapshot` whenever `notify` fires, and re-renders if the value changed. The third argument is used on the server and during hydration. Keep `subscribe` outside the component so it isn't recreated each render.

front: A `useMediaQuery` hook returns early when `window.matchMedia` is missing (before calling `useState`), and subscribes with `mql.addListener` in `useEffect(..., [])`. What's wrong, and how should it be written?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
mql.addEventListener('change', notify);
```

A `MediaQueryList` fires `change` whenever `matches` flips. The older `mql.addListener(fn)` still works but is deprecated. The cleanup must remove the same `notify` function, which `useSyncExternalStore` gives you for each subscription.

front: What problem did the `useIsomorphicLayoutEffect` pattern (`typeof window !== 'undefined' ? useLayoutEffect : useEffect`) solve, and is it still needed in React 19?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
typeof window !== 'undefined' ? useLayoutEffect : useEffect;
```

`typeof window` is safe even where `window` doesn't exist (it returns `'undefined'` instead of throwing). The choice is made once, at module load, so hook order stays the same on every render. This mainly silenced React 18's server warning about `useLayoutEffect`; React 19 dropped that warning.

front: A `useOnWindowResize` hook stores the result of `window.addEventListener('resize', callback)` in a ref and later removes `listener.current`. Why does it leak listeners, and what's the fix?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', handler);
```

`removeEventListener` only works when given the **same function reference** that was added, which is why `handler` is a named constant inside the effect. `addEventListener` returns `undefined`, so storing its return value (as older versions of this hook did) gives you nothing to remove.

front: What is the danger of running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a production UPDATE?
How should an application respond to a serialization failure?
back: **Retry the whole transaction from the start**, with a small bounded number of attempts. A serialization failure (PostgreSQL error code `40001`) happens under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE isolation when concurrent transactions conflict; the database aborts one. Its earlier reads may now be outdated, so re-running only the last statement is wrong. Side effects outside the database (emails, HTTP calls) need their own idempotency.

front: Why is Math.random unsuitable for generating authentication tokens?
back: **`Math.random` is predictable**: it is not cryptographically secure, so an attacker may guess tokens. Use a crypto source: `crypto.randomUUID()` or `crypto.getRandomValues()` in browsers/Node, `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')` in Node, `secrets.token_urlsafe()` in Python.

front: What does the satisfies operator help you check while preserving inference?
Why should CI use a lockfile when installing dependencies?
back: **So every CI run installs the exact same dependency versions.** Without the lockfile, a fresh install can pick up newer versions and break (or fix) the build for reasons unrelated to your change. Use `npm ci`, which installs strictly from `package-lock.json` and fails if it is out of sync with `package.json`.

front: What is the difference between a value and an expression?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A value is a piece of data, such as the number 7 or the text "hello". An expression is a piece of code that produces a value. The computer evaluates an expression by doing its operations and obtaining a result. A single value can also be an expression.

## A worked example

```js
2 + 3       // 5
"hi"        // "hi"
10 > 4      // true
```

Read each line as "what value does this produce?" Addition produces a number. Quoted text produces a string. A comparison produces a yes-or-no value called a boolean.

## Picture it another way

Think of a calculator. The keys you press, `2 + 3`, are the expression: an instruction to compute something. The 5 on the display is the value it produces. Typing just `5` is also an expression; it simply produces itself.

## A common mistake

Not every piece of code is an expression. A statement such as an `if` block or a `let` declaration does work but does not produce a value you can store. `const x = if (ok) 1;` is a syntax error, while `const x = ok ? 1 : 2;` works because `? :` is an expression.

## Try a small exercise

What value does `(2 + 3) * 4` produce, and why?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It produces **20**. Parentheses make the computer evaluate 2 + 3 first, giving 5. It then multiplies 5 by 4. Without the parentheses, multiplication normally happens before addition.

front: Why do programmers put quotation marks around text?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Quotation marks tell the language that the enclosed characters are text, called a string. Without quotes, a word usually names a variable or has a special meaning in the language. The quotes mark where the string starts and ends; they are not normally part of its contents.

## A worked example

```js
const name = "Ada";
console.log("Hello " + name); // Hello Ada
console.log("name");         // name
```

The first log combines two pieces of text. The second uses the literal letters n-a-m-e rather than looking up the name variable.

## Picture it another way

Compare "Say your name" with "Say 'your name'". The first means look up your name and say it; the second means say the literal words "your name". Quotes in code work the same way: `name` looks up a variable, while `"name"` is just those four letters.

## A common mistake

The plus sign can join strings instead of doing arithmetic. `"2" + 3` produces the string "23" in JavaScript. Convert input deliberately when you intend to calculate with numbers.

## Try a small exercise

What does `"cat".toUpperCase()` produce? Does the original string change?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It produces a **new string, "CAT"**. JavaScript strings are immutable: this method returns different text rather than changing the original string in place. Save the returned value if you need it later.

front: What does a data type tell you about a value?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A type describes the kind of data and what operations make sense for it. Numbers support arithmetic, strings represent text, and booleans represent true or false. JavaScript can convert between types automatically in some operations, which is why knowing the input types matters.

## A worked example

```js
typeof 7       // "number"
typeof "7"     // "string"
typeof true    // "boolean"
Number("7") + 2 // 9
```

The digit inside quotes is text. Number explicitly asks for a numeric conversion before addition.

## Picture it another way

A phone number and a price are both written with digits, but you add prices and never add phone numbers. The type tells the program which operations make sense for a value. It is a clue about behavior, not a guarantee the value is valid for your task.

## A common mistake

A value can have the right type and still be invalid. A negative age is a number, but probably not a valid age. Validate the rules of your application as well as the basic type.

## Try a small exercise

A form gives you the string "12". Why might `input + 1` produce "121"?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Because input is text, JavaScript uses string concatenation here. Convert it to a number first and check that conversion succeeded. `Number("12") + 1` produces 13; not every string can be converted to a useful number.

front: What is a callback, without the jargon?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A callback is a function you give to another function so that it can call yours when needed. You provide a little piece of behavior, while the other function controls when to use it. A callback may run immediately during a loop or later after an event; the word alone does not mean asynchronous.

## A worked example

```js
const numbers = [1, 2, 3];
const doubled = numbers.map(n => n * 2);
// [2, 4, 6]
```

The small function n => n * 2 is passed to map. map calls it once for each item and collects the returned values into a new array.

## Picture it another way

You leave a set of instructions with a helper: "For every parcel, write its address here." The helper decides when each parcel is ready, then follows your instructions. The instructions are the callback.

## A common mistake

Do not confuse passing a callback with invoking it yourself. `onClick={handleClick}` gives React a function to call later. `onClick={handleClick()}` runs it during rendering and passes its result instead.

## Try a small exercise

Is every callback asynchronous?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The callback given to array map normally runs synchronously while map is working. A timer callback runs later. You must look at the API receiving the callback to understand the timing.

front: A save function receives a blank task title. Where should you handle that?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Check the input before saving anything. A guard clause is an early return for a case that cannot continue. It keeps the normal save path easy to read and prevents an invalid value from reaching the write operation. The server must also validate requests because a browser check can be bypassed.

## A worked example

```js
function saveTask(title) {
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") {
    return { ok: false, error: "Enter a title" }; // guard: stop here
  }
  // Only valid titles reach this line.
  return db.insertTask({ title: title.trim() });
}
```

The early return is the guard clause. A missing or blank title never reaches the insert, and the normal save path below it stays uncluttered.

## Picture it another way

A receptionist checks that a form has a name before passing it to the filing desk. An incomplete form goes back for correction immediately.

## A common mistake

Do not show an error and then keep executing the save. Reporting an error and stopping the operation are separate steps. Do not assume this one check validates every field.

## Try a small exercise

A handler displays "Title required" but still calls saveTask afterward. What is missing?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Stop that path with an early return, or put the save in the valid-input branch. Showing a message alone does not stop the rest of the handler from running.

front: What does array map do in plain English?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

map builds a new list by transforming each item in an existing list. You supply a small function describing the transformation. For each item, map uses the value your function returns as the matching item in the new list. The original array is left unchanged.

## A worked example

```js
const prices = [2, 5, 8];
const doubled = prices.map(price => price * 2);
// doubled: [4, 10, 16]
// prices:  [2, 5, 8]
```

Follow the first item: 2 goes into the small function, which returns 4. Then 5 becomes 10, and 8 becomes 16.

## Picture it another way

Imagine a conveyor belt passing plain mugs through a painting station. Each incoming mug produces one painted mug. map is good when you want one transformed result per item; it is not the tool for deciding which mugs to throw away.

## A common mistake

The callback must return the new value. With braces, write an explicit return. `prices.map(p => { p * 2; })` produces undefined entries. map creates a new array, but your callback can still mutate objects if you write it that way.

## Try a small exercise

What does `[1, 3, 5].map(n => n + 1)` produce?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**[2, 4, 6].** Each number is transformed independently by adding one. The result has one item for every item in the original array, in the same order.

front: What is the accumulator in a reduce operation?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The accumulator is the result you are building as you walk through a list. Each step receives that running result and the current item, then returns the running result for the next step. You choose an initial value that makes sense, such as zero for a sum.

## A worked example

```js
[2, 3, 4].reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
// 9
```

Start with total = 0. Add 2 to get 2. Add 3 to get 5. Add 4 to get 9. The final running result becomes the return value.

## Picture it another way

A cashier adds prices to a running total. The running total is the accumulator. After each item, the updated total is handed to the next step. The accumulator can also be an object or another collection, not only a number.

## A common mistake

If you omit the initial value, JavaScript uses the first item as the starting result and the callback starts at the second item. On an empty array with no initial value, reduce throws a TypeError. Pass an initial value, such as 0 for a sum, unless you have a clear reason not to.

## Try a small exercise

What does `[2, 3].reduce((total, n) => total + n, 10)` return?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**15.** The starting accumulator is 10, not zero. The first step adds 2, producing 12. The second adds 3, producing 15.

front: Why can changing an object through one variable affect another variable?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Two variables can refer to the same object. Assigning one object variable to another usually copies the reference, not all the object contents. A change through either reference changes the one shared object, so both variables can observe it.

## A worked example

```js
const first = { score: 1 };
const second = first;
second.score = 9;
console.log(first.score); // 9
```

There is one object and two names referring to it. No new object was created by the second line.

## Picture it another way

Two people can have the same shared document bookmarked. Changing the document through one bookmark changes what the other person sees. Copying the bookmark is not the same as copying the document.

## A common mistake

Copying the outer object does not copy nested objects. `{...first}` is a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared. When you need fully independent nested data, use a deep copy such as `structuredClone(first)`, which works for plain data but not for functions.

## Try a small exercise

What does this print?

```js
const a = { n: 1 };
const b = { n: 1 };
console.log(a === b);
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**false.** a and b refer to two different objects. Their properties happen to contain equal numbers, but strict equality on objects checks identity rather than comparing every property.

front: When is a Set useful?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A Set stores each distinct value at most once. It is useful when you care about membership or uniqueness, such as whether an ID has already been seen. You can add values, test whether they are present, and remove them.

## A worked example

```js
const seen = new Set(["a", "b", "a"]);
seen.size;     // 2
seen.has("a"); // true
[...seen];     // ["a", "b"]
```

The repeated string "a" does not become a second entry. Spreading the Set creates an array of its values.

## Picture it another way

Imagine a guest list where each name is checked off only once. Adding the same entry again does not create another seat. For objects, JavaScript distinguishes separate object identities, even if their visible contents look the same.

## A common mistake

A Set does not merge objects with equal-looking properties. Two separately created `{id: 1}` objects are different identities, so both stay in the Set. To deduplicate records, track their IDs instead, for example with a Set of ids or a Map keyed by id.

## Try a small exercise

How many values are in `new Set([1, 1, 2, 2, 3])`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Three.** The distinct values are 1, 2, and 3. Repeated additions of those same numeric values do not increase the Set's size.

front: Why does JavaScript sometimes need a comparison function to sort numbers?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

By default, array sort converts values to strings and compares them character by character. "10" starts with "1", so 10 lands before 2. A comparison function tells sort which of two values comes first: return a negative number to put a before b, positive to put a after b, and zero if they are equal.

## A worked example

```js
const numbers = [10, 2, 1];
numbers.sort((a, b) => a - b);
// [1, 2, 10]
```

For a = 2 and b = 10, a - b is negative, so 2 belongs before 10. The function compares pairs; it does not directly return the whole sorted array.

## Picture it another way

Alphabetizing labels reading "10" and "2" is different from arranging quantities from small to large. A comparison function tells the sorter which kind of ordering you actually intend.

## A common mistake

sort changes the array it is called on. If the original order must stay available, use `numbers.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` (ES2023), which returns a sorted copy, or sort a copy with `[...numbers].sort(...)`.

## Try a small exercise

What is the result of `[3, 12, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b)`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**[1, 3, 12].** Subtracting b from a gives the comparison rule for ascending numeric order. Using b - a would reverse the direction.

Alphabetizing labels reading "10" and "2" is different from arranging quantities from small to large. A comparison function tells the sorter which kind of ordering you actually intend.

## A common mistake

sort changes the array it is called on. If the original order must stay available, use `numbers.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` (ES2023), which returns a sorted copy, or sort a copy with `[...numbers].sort(...)`.

## Explain it in your own words

Why does JavaScript sometimes need a comparison function to sort numbers?

<!-- recall:solution -->

By default, array sort converts values to strings and compares them character by character. "10" starts with "1", so 10 lands before 2. A comparison function tells sort which of two values comes first: return a negative number to put a before b, positive to put a after b, and zero if they are equal.

front: What do try and catch help a program do?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A try block contains work that might throw an exception. If it does, execution jumps to the matching catch block, where you can handle the failure. This lets you respond deliberately instead of continuing as if the operation succeeded.

## A worked example

```js
try {
  JSON.parse("not valid JSON");
} catch (error) {
  console.log("Please check the input");
}
```

Parsing fails, so control moves to catch. Code after the failing expression inside the try block would be skipped.

## Picture it another way

Imagine a normal route through a building with an emergency exit. An exception takes the emergency route. The catch block decides what happens next. It should not quietly pretend the destination was reached if the work actually failed.

## A common mistake

A catch block that does nothing can hide bugs and leave callers believing an operation succeeded. Recover meaningfully, report the failure, or rethrow it. Async failures need to be awaited or handled through the Promise chain.

## Try a small exercise

Will this try/catch catch a network failure from fetch?

```js
try {
  fetch("/data");
} catch (error) {
  showError();
}
```

**No.** fetch returns a Promise immediately, so the try block finishes before the request fails. The later rejection is not caught here. Write `await fetch("/data")` inside an async function's try block, or attach a `.catch()` handler to the Promise.

front: What is a useful automated test?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A test supplies a known situation, performs an action, and checks an expected outcome. It turns an example of correct behavior into something the computer can repeat. A useful test fails when an important behavior is wrong, not merely when internal formatting changes.

## A worked example

```js
import { test, expect } from "vitest";

test("adds two numbers", () => {
  expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5);
});
```

Known input (2 and 3), action (call add), expected result (5). Then add examples at real boundaries, such as zero or negative values, if those are allowed inputs.

## Picture it another way

A test is like a small checklist a machine can carry out exactly. The checklist needs an actual expected result. "Turn the machine on" checks less than "turn it on and verify that the light becomes green."

## A common mistake

A test that repeats the same formula as the implementation can repeat the same mistake. Use independently understandable examples or meaningful properties. Do not mock away the very behavior you intend to verify.

## Try a small exercise

A discount starts at 100. Which three totals make a useful boundary test?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**99, 100, and 101.** They check below the cutoff, exactly at the cutoff, and above it. The expected result at 100 must match whether the rule means "at least 100" or "more than 100."

front: How does a CSS rule decide which elements to style?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A rule has a selector and declarations. The selector describes which elements match. The declarations set visual properties for those matches, such as color or spacing. When several rules set the same property on the same element, the cascade picks a winner: mainly the more specific selector wins, and if they tie, the rule written later wins.

## A worked example

```css
.notice {
  color: green;
  padding: 12px;
}
```

The dot means a class selector. Elements with class="notice" receive the matching styles. Padding adds space inside the element around its content.

## Picture it another way

Imagine an instruction saying "give everyone wearing a blue badge a green folder." The badge description is the selector; the green-folder instruction is the declaration. CSS rules can overlap, so there must also be rules for resolving competing instructions.

## A common mistake

Do not immediately add !important whenever a style loses. Inspect which rule is winning and why. Repeated overrides make later changes difficult to predict.

## Try a small exercise

What does the selector `.warning` match: an element named warning, or elements with class="warning"?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It matches **elements with the warning class**. A dot introduces a class selector. A selector written simply as `warning` would target elements with that tag name.

front: What does React context help you avoid?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Context lets a component read a value from an appropriate provider above it without passing that value through every intermediate component as a prop. It is useful for shared concerns such as a theme. It does not automatically manage state or remove the need to think about updates.

## A worked example

```jsx
const ThemeContext = React.createContext("light");

function App() {
  return (
    <ThemeContext value="dark">
      <Layout />
    </ThemeContext>
  );
}

function SaveButton() {
  const theme = React.useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <button className={theme}>Save</button>;
}
```

SaveButton, nested somewhere inside Layout, reads "dark" directly. Layout never has to accept or pass a theme prop. (React 19 lets you render the context itself as the provider.)

## Picture it another way

A building-wide noticeboard can make information available without every person forwarding the same message down a chain. The noticeboard still needs an owner, and changing it may affect everyone who reads it.

## A common mistake

Putting all application data into one frequently changing context can cause broad updates and make ownership unclear. Keep related concerns separate and use simpler props when they communicate the relationship clearly.

## Try a small exercise

Does creating a context automatically make its value persistent across browser reloads?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Context distributes a value within the component tree. Persistence requires a separate storage mechanism, such as a server or browser storage, plus code to restore the value.

front: What happens when you type a command into a terminal?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The terminal displays a text interface to a shell. The shell interprets your command and runs a built-in action or a program. The command usually has a program name and arguments that tell it what to do. Its working directory helps determine which files it uses.

## A worked example

In PowerShell, `Get-Location` shows your current directory and `Get-ChildItem` lists its contents. `Set-Location src` moves into the src child directory if it exists. In Unix shells such as bash, the commands are `pwd`, `ls`, and `cd src`; PowerShell on Windows also accepts those three short names as aliases.

## Picture it another way

Think of giving written instructions to an assistant who is currently standing in one room. “List the files here” depends on which room they are in. The shell has a current directory, and different commands can change or use it.

## A common mistake

Commands differ across shells and operating systems. Read what a command does before pasting it, particularly when it deletes files, changes permissions, or downloads and executes code.

## Try a small exercise

A tool says it cannot find package.json, but the file exists inside your project. What simple thing should you check first?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Check your **current working directory**. You may be running the tool from the parent folder or a different project. Move to the intended project directory and verify the file is there.

front: How do parameterized queries help prevent SQL injection?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A parameterized query supplies SQL instructions separately from user-provided values. The database driver binds those values as data, so characters in a name do not become new SQL syntax. You should use the driver's parameter mechanism rather than constructing SQL by joining raw input strings.

## A worked example

```js
// Unsafe: user input becomes part of the SQL text
db.query("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'");

// Safe: SQL text and value travel separately
db.query("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);
```

The $1 placeholder (node-postgres style) is filled by the driver as data. Placeholder syntax differs across drivers, such as ? or @email.

## Picture it another way

A form has separate boxes for an instruction and a customer's name. Writing instruction-like words in the name box should still produce a name, not change what the office is asked to do.

## A common mistake

Parameters generally represent values, not arbitrary table names, column names, or sort directions. Dynamic identifiers need a controlled allowlist or an appropriate safe API. Validation alone is not a substitute for parameterization.

## Try a small exercise

A search accepts a name containing an apostrophe. Should you manually paste that name into the SQL query string?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Pass the name as a bound parameter through the database driver. Apostrophes and other characters then remain part of the data rather than changing the SQL structure.

front: What problem does a generic type parameter solve in a reusable function?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A generic lets a function describe a relationship between types without choosing one specific type in advance. For example, the first item of a list should have that list's item type. A generic preserves that connection for each call.

## A worked example

```ts
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}
const name = first(["Ada", "Lin"]);
```

T becomes string for this call. The result is string or undefined because the list might be empty.

## Picture it another way

A coat-check ticket links your particular coat to the one returned later. The service works for many coats while preserving each handover relationship.

## A common mistake

Using any for the result loses the useful connection and allows callers to assume unsupported operations. A generic also does not make empty input impossible.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a generic first-item function include undefined in its return type?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An empty list has no first item, so the return type should make callers handle that case. TypeScript will not add it for you: by default `items[0]` is typed as plain `T` even for `[]`, unless you write `T | undefined` or enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. The alternative is to require a non-empty input or throw deliberately for empty lists.

front: Why give each member of a TypeScript union a different kind field?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A shared field with different literal values identifies which shape is present. Checking that tag lets the compiler narrow to the matching fields. This is useful when a result can succeed with data or fail with an error, but should not have contradictory combinations.

## A worked example

```ts
type Result =
  | { kind: "ok"; value: number }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };
function describe(r: Result) {
  return r.kind === "ok" ? String(r.value) : r.message;
}
```

The tag decides which field is safe to read.

## Picture it another way

A form marked pickup asks for a collection time; one marked delivery asks for an address. The form type determines the required details.

## A common mistake

Several optional fields can accidentally allow impossible states, such as no result and no error. A tagged union expresses the intended alternatives more clearly.

## Try a small exercise

For this union, should code read message before checking kind?

```ts
type Result =
  | { kind: "ok"; value: number }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** TypeScript rejects `r.message` before the check ("Property 'message' does not exist on type 'Result'"), because an ok result has `value` instead. Check `r.kind` first; inside the `"error"` branch, `message` is guaranteed by the declared shape.

front: How can Record help describe a TypeScript object whose keys come from a known set?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Record<Key, Value> describes properties for each allowed key with a chosen value type. When Key is a finite union, the compiler can check that each required entry exists. It is useful for small complete lookup tables such as labels for every status.

## A worked example

```ts
type Status = "open" | "closed";
const labels: Record<Status, string> = {
  open: "Still working",
  closed: "Finished",
};
```

Both statuses need text labels. Adding another status prompts you to consider its label too.

## Picture it another way

A checklist of two required rooms needs a label for each room. A complete lookup table is that checklist expressed as data.

## A common mistake

With `Record<string, T>`, TypeScript types every lookup as `T`, even for a key that was never stored, so `labels[userInput]` can be `undefined` at runtime without a compiler warning. Declare `Record<string, T | undefined>` (or enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) and check the result.

## Try a small exercise

A label table uses `Record<Status, string>`, where `Status` is `"open" | "closed"`. If Status gains `"paused"`, what must the table add?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Add a paused label. With Record<Status, string>, TypeScript reports the missing required key, helping keep the table aligned with the states your program supports.

front: How do the start and stop positions in a Python list slice work?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A slice such as items[start:stop] returns a new list containing positions from start up to, but excluding, stop. Leaving out start means begin at the beginning. Leaving out stop means continue to the end. The elements themselves are not deep-copied.

## A worked example

```python
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
print(letters[1:3])  # ['b', 'c']
print(letters[:2])   # ['a', 'b']
```

Positions 1 and 2 belong to the first slice. Position 3 is the excluded boundary.

## Picture it another way

Imagine cutting a strip between two ruler marks. The marks define its edges; the right-hand edge does not add another item.

## A common mistake

A new outer list can still contain references to the same nested objects. Changing a nested dictionary through the slice can affect the original list's contents.

## Try a small exercise

For `[10, 20, 30, 40]`, what does the slice `[-2:]` return?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**[30, 40]**. A negative position counts backward from the end. Start two items before the end and continue through the remaining items.

front: How does Python dictionary get differ from square-bracket lookup?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Square-bracket lookup requires the key to exist and raises KeyError if it does not. get returns a default for a missing key, using None when no default is given. Choose based on whether missing data is expected or represents a bug.

## A worked example

```python
counts = {"apple": 2}
print(counts.get("pear", 0))  # 0
print(counts)  # {'apple': 2}
```

front: Why can a Python function with a default argument of [] remember earlier calls?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Default argument values are evaluated when the function definition runs, not freshly for each call. If the default is a mutable list, calls that omit the argument use that same list. Mutating it can unexpectedly carry data into later calls.

## A worked example

```python
def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag("a"))  # ['a']
print(add_tag("b"))  # ['a', 'b']  same list reused
```

The `[]` was created once, when `def` ran, so the second call sees the first call's data. The fix is `tags=None` plus `if tags is None: tags = []` inside the function, which builds a fresh list per call.

## Picture it another way

A shared scratchpad left at a service counter keeps earlier notes. Handing out a fresh sheet for each visitor prevents accidental carryover.

## A common mistake

Replacing the list default with another mutable object, such as {}, has the same issue. Choose a sentinel and create the object inside the function.

## Try a small exercise

Do `collect("a")` and then `collect("b")` return one growing list here?

```python
def collect(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** They return ["a"] and ["b"] separately. Each omitted bucket begins as None and gets a fresh list inside that call.

front: How does reducing a failing example help locate a bug?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Remove unrelated inputs and steps while checking that the failure still occurs. A smaller case leaves fewer possible causes and makes the important relationship easier to see. Keep the original reproduction too, because a fix should eventually work there as well.

## A worked example

A table fails with 500 records. Try a small copied set, then reduce it until one record with a missing city still fails. The investigation can now focus on handling that missing field instead of table size.

## Picture it another way

If one ingredient spoils a recipe, reducing the recipe helps isolate which ingredient matters. The reduced version must still produce the same bad result.

## A common mistake

If simplifying makes the bug disappear, you may have removed an essential condition. Restore that part and reduce somewhere else.

## Try a small exercise

While shrinking a failing bug example down to a minimal case, why rerun it after each simplification?

<!-- recall:solution -->

To prove the simplified example still represents the same issue. Otherwise you can end up explaining a different problem, or a case that does not fail at all.

front: Why state a debugging hypothesis before changing several things?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A hypothesis is a specific possible cause with a prediction you can check. Testing one change against that prediction teaches you whether the explanation fits the evidence. Several simultaneous edits may remove the symptom while leaving you unsure what mattered.

## A worked example

Hypothesis: the page reads count as text from storage. Prediction: inspecting typeof count before addition shows string. If the value is already a number, investigate another cause rather than adding an unnecessary conversion.

## Picture it another way

A mechanic tests whether a battery is flat before replacing several unrelated parts. Each test should distinguish possible explanations.

## A common mistake

A passing result after one edit is evidence, not proof of every assumption. Recheck the original failing case and nearby valid cases.

## Try a small exercise

What is a useful prediction for "this request runs twice because the handler is registered twice"?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Prediction: one click produces two handler calls, for example a log or breakpoint in the handler fires twice and the Network panel shows two identical requests. Then confirm where the handler is registered. If the handler runs only once per click, the hypothesis is wrong and the duplicate comes from elsewhere in the request path.

front: When a page shows no data, what should you inspect in the browser Network panel?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Check whether a request was sent, its destination, method, status, and response body. Compare those observations with what the UI expected. This separates cases such as no request, a rejected request, an unexpected response shape, and a successful response that the UI mishandles.

## A worked example

A list is empty. The Network panel shows 200 and `{ "items": [...] }`, but the component reads response.results. The transport succeeded; the response contract and UI code disagree about the field name.

## Picture it another way

Checking the delivery receipt and opening the parcel tells you more than staring at an empty shelf. Sending, receiving, and displaying are separate steps.

## A common mistake

A 200 status does not prove the response contains valid application data. Inspect the body and remember that debug payloads can contain sensitive information.

## Try a small exercise

The expected request does not appear at all. Should your first investigation be a database query?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** If the request never appears, the server was never reached. Start earlier: check whether the event handler ran, whether validation stopped the submission, or whether a client-side error was thrown before the request was sent.

front: How can passing a clock into code make time-based behavior easier to test?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A controllable clock lets the test choose the current time instead of depending on the real date or waiting for time to pass. You can check exact expiration boundaries and scheduling behavior quickly and repeatably.

## A worked example

```js
function isExpired(expiresAt, now = Date.now()) {
  return now >= expiresAt;
}
expect(isExpired(1000, 999)).toBe(false);
expect(isExpired(1000, 1000)).toBe(true);
```

Production callers omit `now` and get the real time; the test passes its own time, so both sides of the comparison are fixed and repeatable. All values use the same unit (milliseconds).

## Picture it another way

A rehearsal clock can jump directly to midnight so you can practice what happens then without staying awake until the real midnight.

## A common mistake

Replacing the current date may not also advance timers. Understand whether your test controls wall-clock readings, scheduled callbacks, or both.

## Try a small exercise

Why can a test using the real current date fail only around midnight?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Its setup and assertion may cross a date boundary or depend on a local timezone. Fix the reference time and test the intended boundary explicitly.

front: Where should keyboard focus go when a modal dialog opens and closes?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Opening a modal should move focus into an appropriate place in the dialog, and keyboard interaction should remain within the active modal. Closing normally returns focus to the control that opened it, if that control still exists. This keeps the user's location understandable.

## A worked example

A Rename button opens a dialog. Focus enters the name field; Tab moves among the dialog controls. Cancel closes the dialog and focus returns to Rename. A user can complete the flow without hunting through the background page.

## Picture it another way

Entering a service booth moves your conversation inside it. When you leave, you return to the place in the queue where you started.

## A common mistake

Adding aria-modal alone does not move focus or block the background page. Prefer the native `<dialog>` element opened with `showModal()`: browsers move focus into it, make the rest of the page inert, close it on Escape, and restore focus on close. Still test the real behavior.

## Try a small exercise

After closing a dialog, why is sending focus to the top of the page usually unhelpful?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It loses the user's working position and forces extra navigation. Return focus to the opener or another logical next control if the opener was removed by the completed action.

front: What different jobs do an HTTP request's method, URL, headers, and body perform?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The method expresses the kind of operation, and the URL identifies the target. Headers carry metadata such as accepted formats or credentials. A body can carry submitted data. Reading these parts separately helps you diagnose a request and describe its contract clearly.

## A worked example

```http
POST /notes HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{ "text": "Review closures" }
```

POST is the operation, /notes names the target collection, the headers say the body is JSON and who is calling, and the body carries the new note's data.

## Picture it another way

A parcel has a destination, handling instructions, and contents. Confusing the label with the contents makes delivery harder to reason about.

## A common mistake

A body is not automatically JSON merely because the client sent text that resembles an object. The content type and server parsing rules need to agree.

## Try a small exercise

If a server expects JSON but receives an unparseable body, which parts of the request should you inspect?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Inspect the Content-Type header and the actual transmitted body. Confirm valid JSON encoding and the field shape the endpoint expects, instead of assuming the client's original object was sent correctly.
