front: Why should a GET endpoint avoid performing an action such as deleting a record?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

GET has safe semantics: the caller is asking to retrieve information, not requesting a state-changing action. Browsers, crawlers, and intermediaries may fetch or repeat such requests. Encoding deletion in a GET URL makes ordinary retrieval behavior dangerous.

## A worked example

```http
GET /notes/7      -> show note 7 (safe to repeat, prefetch, or crawl)
DELETE /notes/7   -> delete note 7 (authorized, CSRF-protected)
```

A crawler or link prefetcher following the GET should never delete anything. The deletion lives on a separate method the browser will not send just by visiting a link.

## Picture it another way

Opening a product catalog should not place an order. Looking and acting are different commitments even if both involve the same product.

## A common mistake

Safe does not mean nothing whatsoever changes internally: access logging may occur. The distinction is whether the client requested a meaningful mutation through the operation.

## Try a small exercise

Why is a GET link such as `/account/delete` a poor deletion design?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A browser or automated fetcher may visit it as an ordinary retrieval. Deletion needs an explicit mutation operation, authorization, and appropriate protections against unintended requests.

front: What broad difference separates HTTP 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx responses?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

2xx indicates successful handling at the HTTP level. 4xx indicates a problem with the request in relation to the resource or its rules. 5xx indicates the server could not fulfill an apparently valid request because of a server-side failure. Specific codes refine those meanings.

## A worked example

A successful retrieval might return 200. An unknown resource might return 404. A temporary service failure might return 503. The response body can add application details, but clients should not have to treat every outcome as an indistinguishable 200.

## Picture it another way

A service desk can say completed, please correct the request, or our equipment is unavailable. Those categories suggest different next steps.

## A common mistake

The broad category does not determine a safe retry policy by itself. Some failures need corrected input, some may be transient, and repeated mutations may duplicate effects.

## Try a small exercise

If a client sends a required field in the wrong format, is a generic 500 usually the clearest response?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Return a 4xx client error, typically 400 Bad Request or 422 Unprocessable Content, with a message naming the invalid field. A 500 wrongly signals an unexpected server failure instead of a request the client can correct.

front: Why can response.json() fail even after an HTTP request succeeds?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

json() parses the body as JSON. A success status does not guarantee that the body contains JSON; it could be empty, HTML, or another format. The client and server need an agreed response contract, including cases that intentionally return no body.

## A worked example

```js
const res = await fetch(`/api/notes/${id}`, { method: "DELETE" });
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Delete failed: ${res.status}`);
// 204 No Content: there is no body, so do not call res.json()
// (it would throw SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input)
if (res.status !== 204) console.log(await res.json());
```

The delete succeeded; the client just has nothing to parse.

## Picture it another way

A delivered envelope may intentionally be empty. Receiving it successfully does not mean there is a letter inside to read.

## A common mistake

A proxy or login redirect can produce HTML where your API client expected JSON. Inspect status, final response details, and content type when parsing unexpectedly fails.

## Try a small exercise

After a documented 204 response, should the client require a JSON object before showing success?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** 204 means there is no response content. Treat the documented outcome as success without JSON parsing, while handling other status cases according to the endpoint contract.

front: Before writing an aggregate query, why define what one output row should represent?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A row might represent an order, a customer, or a customer-month. That level of detail determines grouping and which joins are appropriate. Stating it first helps avoid combining unrelated quantities or accidentally returning several rows when the caller expects one.

## A worked example

```sql
-- one row per customer
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

Adding order_id to the SELECT and GROUP BY would silently change the grain to one row per order, so you would no longer get one total per customer.

## Picture it another way

A school report can have one row per student or one per class. Mixing those meanings makes averages and totals hard to interpret.

## A common mistake

Do not select extra grouping columns just to make a SQL error disappear. Each extra column may change what a row means.

## Try a small exercise

If a report needs one row per day, what happens if you also group by individual event ID?

<!-- recall:solution -->

You split each day into separate event groups, losing the intended daily total. Group at the requested level and aggregate the event values that belong to each day.

GROUP BY customer_id;

Adding order_id to the SELECT and GROUP BY would silently change the grain to one row per order, so you would no longer get one total per customer.

## Picture it another way

A school report can have one row per student or one per class. Mixing those meanings makes averages and totals hard to interpret.

## A common mistake

Do not select extra grouping columns just to make a SQL error disappear. Each extra column may change what a row means.

## Explain it in your own words

Before writing an aggregate query, why define what one output row should represent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A row might represent an order, a customer, or a customer-month. That level of detail determines grouping and which joins are appropriate. Stating it first helps avoid combining unrelated quantities or accidentally returning several rows when the caller expects one.

front: Why can a WHERE condition on the right table remove unmatched rows from a LEFT JOIN?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A left join keeps left-side rows without a match by filling right-side columns with NULL. A later WHERE condition keeps only rows where its condition is true. If that condition rejects the NULL-filled rows, those unmatched left rows disappear.

## A worked example

```sql
-- every customer, plus their paid orders if any
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid';
```

Customers with no paid orders still appear with order_id NULL. Moving `o.status = 'paid'` into WHERE would drop them, because `NULL = 'paid'` is not true.

## Picture it another way

A guest list first includes everyone, even those without meal orders. A later rule saying "keep only people with a vegetarian order" removes guests with no order.

## A common mistake

Moving a condition changes meaning. Decide whether you want to filter possible matches or filter final result rows; neither placement is always correct for every question.

## Try a small exercise

To retain customers with no orders while matching only shipped orders, where should the shipped condition usually go?

<!-- recall:solution -->

In the **ON condition** for the LEFT JOIN. It limits which orders match while preserving each customer even when no shipped order is found.

front: How does a SQL window function differ from grouping rows with GROUP BY?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A window function computes across a related set of rows while retaining the individual result rows. GROUP BY normally collapses rows into groups. Window functions help when you need both each item and a comparison or calculation over its peers.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT name, team_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_size
FROM members;
```

Each member still gets a row. team_size repeats the count for that member's team beside their name.

## Picture it another way

Each student keeps an individual report card with the class size written beside their own information. You did not replace the class with one summary card.

## A common mistake

Adding ORDER BY inside OVER changes the default frame to "start of the partition up to the current row" (plus ties), so `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY created_at)` becomes a running total, not the team total. Know which frame you are getting.

## Try a small exercise

Five members belong to one team. How many rows does this query return for that team?

```sql
SELECT name, team_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_size
FROM members;
```

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Five rows**, each showing team_size as 5. A grouped team-count query would instead usually return one summary row for that team.

front: Why is checking that a user is signed in insufficient before returning a private note by ID?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Signing in establishes identity, but the server must also check whether that identity may access this particular note. A caller can change an ID in a request. Restrict the lookup by the authenticated user's permissions or ownership rules before returning private data.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT id, title, body
FROM notes
WHERE id = $1          -- note ID from the URL
  AND owner_id = $2;   -- user ID from the verified session
```

No row means "not found" for this user. Never take owner_id from the request body or query string. Shared notes need an explicit sharing rule instead.

## Picture it another way

A building pass proves who you are; it does not give you permission to open every tenant's mailbox.

## A common mistake

Hiding an Edit button is useful UI behavior but does not enforce server permissions. Direct requests can bypass the page entirely.

## Try a small exercise

If note IDs are long random strings, can the API skip checking ownership?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Hard-to-guess identifiers can reduce guessing but do not grant permission. A leaked or shared ID must still be subject to the server's authorization rules.

front: Why is a server API secret unsafe when bundled into frontend JavaScript?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Code and configuration delivered to a browser can be inspected by the person using it. A private credential included in that bundle is therefore exposed. Keep server secrets in an appropriate server environment and have the browser use an authorized server API.

## A worked example

A weather-provider secret used for billed server requests belongs behind your backend. The browser calls your endpoint, which enforces its own access and request limits. A public publishable key is different only when the provider explicitly designed it to be public.

## Picture it another way

Writing a safe combination on a customer receipt does not keep it secret just because the receipt was printed by trusted staff.

## A common mistake

An environment variable is not automatically secret. Bundlers inline variables with public prefixes such as `VITE_` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_` into the browser bundle. Check what actually ships and follow the provider's key model.

## Try a small exercise

Does minifying JavaScript protect a private API key embedded in it?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Minification changes presentation, not access. Anyone receiving the bundle can recover its values; move the private credential to the proper server boundary and rotate it if exposed.

front: Why should a server use a dedicated password-hashing algorithm rather than plain text or a fast general hash?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

If the database leaks, a password verifier should make offline guessing slow and expensive. Dedicated password-hashing algorithms add a unique salt per password and a tunable work factor. OWASP currently recommends Argon2id first, then scrypt; bcrypt for legacy systems; PBKDF2 where FIPS compliance is required. Use a maintained library with current parameters rather than inventing a scheme.

## A worked example

At registration, the password library produces a stored verifier including algorithm settings and salt information. At login, its verify operation checks the submitted password against that verifier. The server does not need to recover the original password.

## Picture it another way

The system keeps a way to check the answer, not a readable copy of the answer. The checking process is intentionally costly enough to slow mass guessing.

## A common mistake

A fast hash such as plain SHA-256 (even salted) is not a password-storage scheme; GPUs can try billions per second. Also note bcrypt ignores input beyond 72 bytes. Hashing does not replace rate limits, HTTPS, or a safe reset flow.

## Try a small exercise

Should a password-reset feature email the user their existing password?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The system should not be able to retrieve it from a proper verifier. Use a secure, time-limited reset process that allows the user to choose a new password.

front: Why is a focused pull request easier to review than several unrelated changes together?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A focused change gives the reviewer one concrete problem and a connected solution to assess. It is easier to understand its behavior, choose useful checks, and identify regressions. Large changes are sometimes necessary, but unrelated cleanup can obscure the part that changes user behavior.

## A worked example

A bug fix for saved filters includes the URL initialization change and a regression test. A broad restyling of every button would make that review harder without helping establish whether filters survive refresh.

## Picture it another way

Proofreading one revised paragraph is easier than finding it among pages of unrelated formatting edits. The important change should remain visible.

## A common mistake

Splitting code into tiny commits does not automatically create a coherent review. Keep pieces together when they are necessary to understand and safely apply one behavior change.

## Try a small exercise

You fixed a bug where a list's saved filters reset when the page is refreshed. What should the pull-request description tell the reviewer first?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The trigger and the fix: "Filters were lost on refresh because they were not read from the URL on load; now they are." Then how you verified it (e.g. the regression test). That lets the reviewer judge the code against a clear intended outcome.

front: Two people edit the same customer record. How can the second save avoid overwriting the first?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Include a version from the record the form loaded. The server updates only if the stored version still matches. If another save has changed it, report a conflict and let the user reload or reconcile their edits. The version check and write must be one coordinated database operation.

## A worked example

```sql
UPDATE customers
SET name = $1, version = version + 1
WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3;  -- version the form loaded
```

If the update affects 0 rows, the record changed (or was deleted) since the form loaded: return 409 Conflict and keep the user's draft on screen.

## Picture it another way

A checkout slip records which edition you borrowed. You cannot silently replace the current edition with handwritten changes based on an older one.

## A common mistake

Checking the version in one request and updating unconditionally afterward leaves a race between the two steps. Put the condition in the write or use your database's concurrency mechanism.

## Try a small exercise

An edit form loaded version 7, but the server now has version 8. Should it automatically overwrite version 8?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Show a conflict and help the user compare or reload. Blindly retrying the stale draft removes the protection and can discard the other person's changes.

front: Two registration requests both check that an email is unused, then both insert it. What prevents duplicates?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A pre-check can improve feedback, but it cannot guarantee uniqueness while requests overlap. Define the intended uniqueness rule and enforce it with a database constraint or unique index. Catch the constraint failure and translate it into an appropriate, understandable application response.

## A worked example

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique ON users (lower(email));
```

Both requests can pass the availability check, but the second INSERT fails with a unique violation (PostgreSQL error code 23505). Catch that and return a friendly "email already registered" (e.g. 409).

## Picture it another way

Two clerks can both see an empty seat on an old printout. A central reservation system must decide who actually gets the seat at the moment of booking.

## A common mistake

Be explicit about normalization and scope. Unique within one organization differs from unique across the entire application. Do not assume every email comparison rule is interchangeable.

## Try a small exercise

Can a "Check availability" endpoint replace a database uniqueness rule?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Another request can claim the value after the check. Treat the check as feedback and the database constraint as the final enforcement at write time.

front: A user types "cat", then "caterer", but the screen ends up showing results for "cat". Why?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Requests can finish in a different order from the order they started. The earlier search may be slower and arrive last. Associate results with the active query or request generation and apply only the current result. Cancel obsolete requests where supported to avoid unnecessary work.

## A worked example

```js
let controller;
async function search(q) {
  controller?.abort(); // cancel the previous request
  const current = (controller = new AbortController());
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, { signal: current.signal });
    const data = await res.json();
    if (current === controller) showResults(data); // only the latest wins
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name !== "AbortError") throw err;
  }
}
```

Loading and error state should also belong to the active request, so an old one cannot clear the new spinner.

## Picture it another way

You ask two assistants for different reports. The report delivered last is not necessarily the report you requested most recently.

## A common mistake

Debouncing reduces how often requests start; it does not guarantee their completion order. An old in-flight request can still finish after the latest one.

## Try a small exercise

Does waiting 300 milliseconds before issuing each search fully prevent stale results?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It reduces request volume but does not order responses. Use cancellation and/or a current-request check before updating results, errors, and loading state.

front: Why is saving every property from a profile request into the user row dangerous?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An incoming object can contain fields that the form never offered. Build an update command from explicitly allowed fields and validate each one. Sensitive fields such as owner IDs, account roles, and approval status must come from trusted logic or separate authorized operations.

## A worked example

```js
const ALLOWED = ["displayName", "bio"];
const update = Object.fromEntries(
  ALLOWED.filter((k) => Object.hasOwn(body, k)).map((k) => [k, body[k]])
);
// body   { displayName: "Ada", bio: "hi", isAdmin: true }
// update { displayName: "Ada", bio: "hi" }
```

Only allowlisted fields reach the database update; isAdmin is dropped. Validate each allowed value too.

## Picture it another way

A change-of-address form authorizes changing an address. Writing "make me the manager" in the margin should not grant the clerk authority to change your job title.

## A common mistake

Hiding a field in the interface is not a defense: callers can construct JSON directly. Likewise, a broad Partial<User> type is not a runtime allowlist.

## Try a small exercise

The browser sends ownerId along with a new note. Which value should determine ownership?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Derive ownership from the authenticated server context or an explicitly authorized sharing workflow. Do not let an arbitrary request body choose whose data the note belongs to.

front: In a partial profile update, how can an omitted phone field differ from phone: null?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A partial-update contract can define omission as leaving a value unchanged and explicit null as clearing it. The server must preserve that distinction when validating and building its update. An empty string is a third input whose meaning should also be defined rather than guessed.

## A worked example

```js
const update = {};
if (Object.hasOwn(body, "phone")) update.phone = body.phone; // null clears it
// { displayName: "Ada" } -> update {} : phone unchanged
// { phone: null }         -> update { phone: null } : phone cleared
```

Check whether the key is present, not whether its value is truthy or non-null. Clearing is allowed only if the column is nullable and the API permits it.

## Picture it another way

Leaving an instruction box blank can mean "do nothing to this field." Writing "erase this value" is a separate instruction with a different result.

## A common mistake

Using incoming.phone ?? existing.phone treats null like omission and prevents clearing. Conversely, filling every missing property with null can erase values the user never intended to change.

## Try a small exercise

A PATCH request changes only a biography, but the server clears the address too. What may be wrong?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The server likely converted omitted fields into empty or null values. Apply only supplied, permitted fields and handle explicit clearing according to the update contract.

front: A PATCH request changes only a biography, but the server clears the address too. What may be wrong?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer, explained

The server likely converted omitted fields into empty or null values. Apply only supplied, permitted fields and handle explicit clearing according to the update contract.

### Why this happens

A partial-update contract can define omission as leaving a value unchanged and explicit null as clearing it. The server must preserve that distinction when validating and building its update. An empty string is a third input whose meaning should also be defined rather than guessed.

## A worked example

```js
const update = {};
if (Object.hasOwn(body, "phone")) update.phone = body.phone; // null clears it
// { displayName: "Ada" } -> update {} : phone unchanged
// { phone: null }         -> update { phone: null } : phone cleared
```

Check whether the key is present, not whether its value is truthy or non-null. Clearing is allowed only if the column is nullable and the API permits it.

## Picture it another way

Leaving an instruction box blank can mean "do nothing to this field." Writing "erase this value" is a separate instruction with a different result.

## A common mistake

Using incoming.phone ?? existing.phone treats null like omission and prevents clearing. Conversely, filling every missing property with null can erase values the user never intended to change.

## Explain it in your own words

In a partial profile update, how can an omitted phone field differ from phone: null?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A partial-update contract can define omission as leaving a value unchanged and explicit null as clearing it. The server must preserve that distinction when validating and building its update. An empty string is a third input whose meaning should also be defined rather than guessed.

front: The API saved a task successfully, but the task list still shows the old title. What should you check?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The screen may be showing a cached copy that was never updated or invalidated. Decide which views depend on the changed record. Use the saved response to update those copies, or mark the relevant queries stale and fetch them again. Include filters and sort order when deciding where the record belongs.

## A worked example

A task changes from open to completed. Remove it from an open-only list or refetch that list after success. Also update its detail view and counts if they are displayed. Replacing just the title in one unrelated list is not enough.

## Picture it another way

Changing the master address book does not automatically update every printed contact sheet. Each copy needs to be replaced or refreshed.

## A common mistake

Do not indiscriminately clear all application data after every save. Target the records and queries affected by the mutation, and handle refetch failures without claiming the save failed.

## Try a small exercise

A completed task still appears under the "Open" filter after a successful save. Is changing its checkbox enough?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Its membership in the filtered list changed too. Remove it from the "Open" list or refetch that list with the active filter, and refresh any affected counts.

front: A table accepts sort=title from the URL. How should the API use it in a database query?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Map public sort options to a small set of trusted query expressions. Bind ordinary filter values using the database driver. A parameter placeholder usually represents a value, so it does not automatically make arbitrary table names, column names, or sort directions safe.

## A worked example

```js
const SORTS = {
  title: "title ASC, id ASC",
  newest: "created_at DESC, id DESC",
};
const sort = req.query.sort;
const orderBy = Object.hasOwn(SORTS, sort) ? SORTS[sort] : SORTS.newest; // unknown -> default
const sql = `SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${orderBy}`;
```

Only fixed strings from the map reach the SQL; the user's text never does. The id tie-breaker keeps equal titles in a stable order across pages.

## Picture it another way

A restaurant lets you choose from a menu. It does not let the text you write in the order box become instructions for rewiring the kitchen.

## A common mistake

Do not append a raw sort string to SQL. Also specify a stable tie breaker so records with equal titles do not jump unpredictably between pages.

## Try a small exercise

Does putting a user-provided column name in a value parameter select that SQL column?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Parameters bind data values, not SQL identifiers, so `ORDER BY $1` is treated as a constant value (or rejected), never as the named column. Choose the column through an allowlist or a query builder that enforces allowed options.

front: Does var make a C# variable dynamically change its type?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

No. var asks the compiler to infer the variable's type from its initial value. Once inferred, that variable follows the normal type rules. An int inferred from a whole number does not become a string just because you later try to assign text.

## A worked example

```csharp
var attempts = 2;
attempts += 1;
Console.WriteLine(attempts); // 3
// attempts = "three"; // compile-time error
```

The compiler infers int on the first line. var saves typing the obvious type; it does not disable checking.

## Picture it another way

An unlabeled box can be identified from its contents. Once the label is inferred, the same storage rules still apply.

## A common mistake

Do not confuse var with dynamic. dynamic defers certain operations until runtime, which changes when mistakes are detected and is unnecessary for ordinary typed application code.

## Try a small exercise

After `var enabled = true;`, can ordinary C# code assign `enabled = "yes";`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** `enabled` was inferred as `bool` on the first line, so assigning the string "yes" is a compile-time error. Assign `true` or `false`, or declare a different type if the value really needs more than two states.

front: What does the dollar sign before a C# string let you do?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An interpolated string allows expressions inside braces to contribute text. It is useful for readable labels and messages. The braces evaluate expressions; they do not automatically validate input or make text safe for every destination such as SQL or HTML.

## A worked example

```csharp
string name = "Ada";
int count = 3;
Console.WriteLine($"{name} has {count} notes.");
```

The output combines literal text with the current values of name and count. A normal string without the dollar sign does not evaluate those braces.

## Picture it another way

A mail-merge template fills labeled spaces with the recipient's information. The template remains readable while values vary.

## A common mistake

Do not build SQL by pasting user input into a string: `"... WHERE Title = '" + title + "'"` or an interpolated `$"... {title}"` passed to a raw-SQL API are both injection risks. Use parameters. EF Core's `FromSql($"... {title}")` is a special case: it takes a FormattableString and turns each hole into a SQL parameter.

## Try a small exercise

What does `Console.WriteLine("Total: {2 + 3}");` print without a dollar sign?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It prints **Total: {2 + 3}** literally. `$"Total: {2 + 3}"` instead evaluates the expression and produces Total: 5.

front: What does a C# method declaration such as `int Add(int left, int right)` tell its caller?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It names the operation, lists the input parameters with their types, and declares the return type. A non-void return gives the caller a result to use. Parameter names explain each value's role; parameter types restrict which values can be passed. Strictly, C# calls only the name and parameter list the "signature", which is why you cannot overload two methods by return type alone.

## A worked example

```csharp
int Add(int left, int right)
{
    return left + right;
}
Console.WriteLine(Add(2, 4)); // 6
```

This local function accepts two integers and returns an integer. The caller receives the result rather than merely observing a console message inside the function.

## Picture it another way

A service menu describes what you order and what you receive. The method body explains how the service performs the work.

## A common mistake

Console.WriteLine is not a replacement for return when another method needs the result. Printing is an output side effect, while return passes data back to the caller.

## Try a small exercise

If a method is declared `bool IsAvailable(int stock)`, what kind of value should its normal return paths provide?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A **bool**, such as the result of `stock > 0`. The int is the input type; bool is the output type promised to callers.

front: Why is int.TryParse useful for text entered in a web form?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

TryParse reports success as a boolean and supplies the parsed value through an out parameter. Invalid user input is an expected possibility, so it can take a normal validation path. Parsing establishes a number; a separate check establishes whether the number is acceptable for your feature.

## A worked example

```csharp
string input = "12";
if (int.TryParse(input, out int quantity) && quantity > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine(quantity); // 12
}
```

The second check runs only if parsing succeeds. A parsed negative number still fails the business rule.

## Picture it another way

First check whether a ticket can be read, then check whether it is valid for this trip. Readability and eligibility are different checks.

## A common mistake

When TryParse returns false, the out variable is set to 0, not to anything the user typed. Only use it inside the success branch. For decimals and dates, also decide which culture and formats you accept, since "1,5" and "1.5" parse differently by culture.

## Try a small exercise

If int.TryParse successfully parses "-3", does that prove the value is a valid order quantity?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Parsing proves it is representable as an int. Apply a separate rule such as quantity > 0 and any upper limit required by the application.

front: Why are C# records useful for small request or response data types?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Records provide concise data declarations and generated value-based equality over their members. They can make an API data shape easy to read. A record does not automatically validate data, deeply freeze nested objects, or replace a thoughtful boundary between storage and public responses.

## A worked example

```csharp
var a = new NoteDto(7, "LINQ");
var b = new NoteDto(7, "LINQ");
Console.WriteLine(a == b); // True
record NoteDto(int Id, string Title);
```

The generated equality compares Id and Title. With an ordinary `class Note` holding the same values, `a == b` would print False, because classes compare references by default.

## Picture it another way

Two printed labels can represent the same information even though they are different sheets of paper. A data record makes that comparison convenient.

## A common mistake

A record containing a `List<string>` is not deeply immutable: callers can still add to the list. Equality also uses the list's own equality, which is by reference, so two records with separate lists holding the same items are **not** equal.

## Try a small exercise

Does putting a List<string> inside a C# record automatically prevent callers from adding items to that list?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Record syntax does not recursively freeze referenced objects. Choose an appropriate representation and ownership policy when data must remain unchanged.

front: When is a C# Dictionary a useful alternative to scanning a list?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A dictionary maps keys to values and supports efficient lookup by key in typical use. It fits tasks such as finding a count by category. Keys are unique within the dictionary, while different keys may map to equal values.

## A worked example

```csharp
var counts = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["api"] = 3 };
if (counts.TryGetValue("api", out int count))
{
    Console.WriteLine(count); // 3
}
```

TryGetValue separates the found case from a missing key. Reading a missing key with the indexer, `counts["sql"]`, throws KeyNotFoundException instead.

## Picture it another way

A labeled cabinet lets you go directly to a folder name instead of inspecting every folder in a pile.

## A common mistake

A normal Dictionary is not a general solution for simultaneous mutation from multiple threads. Choose suitable synchronization or a concurrent collection when state is actually shared.

## Try a small exercise

Why use TryGetValue when a dictionary key may legitimately be absent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It reports absence through a boolean so you can take a normal fallback path. This avoids treating an expected missing key as a successful lookup or relying on an exception for that case.

front: Why avoid Task.Result and Wait in an ASP.NET Core request path?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

They block the calling thread while it waits. Under load, many blocked request threads reduce capacity and can cause thread-pool starvation, so the server slows down or stops responding. Await asynchronous I/O all the way up the call chain instead. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so the classic `.Result` deadlock from old ASP.NET and UI apps does not happen there; the cost is starvation, not deadlock.

## A worked example

In an async endpoint, use `await service.LoadAsync(cancellationToken)` and return a Task-based result. Calling `.Result` on that task turns the wait into a blocked thread without making the remote work finish sooner.

## Picture it another way

Every waiter standing motionless at the kitchen door leaves fewer waiters available to serve other tables. Waiting efficiently matters when many requests overlap.

## A common mistake

Wrapping every blocking call in Task.Run does not remove its resource cost. Use genuinely asynchronous APIs for I/O where available and bound expensive background work.

## Try a small exercise

A server has hundreds of requests blocked on databaseTask.Result. Does adding async to the method declaration alone fix the blocking?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Replace the blocking wait with await and propagate the asynchronous return through callers. The keyword alone does not change what Result does.

front: Why should ordinary asynchronous C# service methods return Task rather than async void?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A Task lets callers await completion and catch failures. async void returns nothing to await, so the caller cannot know when the work ends, and an exception thrown inside it cannot be caught by the caller: it is rethrown on the thread pool and crashes the process. async void exists for event-handler signatures, not for request handlers or service methods.

## A worked example

Define `Task SaveNoteAsync(...)` so the endpoint can await it before returning success. If the method were async void, the endpoint could finish its response while the save was still running or later failed.

## Picture it another way

A claim ticket lets you check when a job finishes. Handing off work without any completion signal leaves the caller guessing.

## A common mistake

Ignoring a returned Task can cause similar problems even when the signature is correct. Decide who owns and observes the operation through completion.

## Try a small exercise

Why can an endpoint that calls an async void save method return 200 too early?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It has no returned Task to await, so it cannot reliably wait for the save. Return and await Task so the response can reflect completion or an appropriate failure.

front: Why is IHttpClientFactory useful in an ASP.NET Core service?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The factory hands out HttpClient instances while pooling and recycling the underlying handlers. That avoids two classic bugs: creating a new HttpClient per request can exhaust sockets, and one client kept forever can miss DNS changes. Named or typed clients also keep each API's base address, timeout, and message handlers in one registration.

## A worked example

front: What do CreateBuilder, Build, MapGet, and Run do in a small ASP.NET Core app?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

CreateBuilder prepares configuration and service registration. Build creates the web application. MapGet associates a GET route with a handler. Run starts the host so it can accept requests. Services are normally registered on the builder before Build.

## A worked example

In Program.cs of a .NET 10 web project:

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapGet("/hello", () => "Hello from C#");
app.Run();
```

A GET to /hello invokes the lambda and receives the text response. Declaring the route is separate from receiving a request.

## Picture it another way

Prepare a service desk, assign a station to a request type, then open the doors. Customers cannot arrive until the host is running.

## A common mistake

Register all services on builder.Services before calling Build. Adding a service afterwards is not quietly ignored: it throws InvalidOperationException ("The service collection cannot be modified because it is read-only").

## Try a small exercise

In a Minimal API, does writing app.MapGet call the handler immediately for a real HTTP request?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It registers how matching requests will be handled. The handler runs later when the running application receives a suitable request.

front: What does a request DTO help ASP.NET Core understand about a JSON body?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It provides a typed shape for deserializing accepted fields. Successful binding means the data could be represented in that shape, not that every business rule passed. Required content, maximum lengths, and permissions still need the appropriate validation and authorization.

## A worked example

Endpoint excerpt; declare the record after top-level statements:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/notes", (CreateNote request) =>
    Results.Ok(new { request.Title }));
// Type declaration goes after app.Run() in Program.cs:
record CreateNote(string Title);
```

This only echoes input to demonstrate binding. It does not persist a note.

## Picture it another way

A form gives each answer a named box. Filling those boxes is separate from approving whether the answers are acceptable.

## A common mistake

A non-nullable `string Title` is not a runtime check. If the JSON omits title, binding still succeeds and Title is null. In .NET 10, call `builder.Services.AddValidation()` and annotate the DTO (for example `[Required, MaxLength(200)]`) to get automatic 400 responses, or check the request explicitly.

## Try a small exercise

If JSON successfully deserializes into a C# request DTO, does that prove its Title is acceptable for storage?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Validate rules such as nonblank content and allowed length, then enforce authorization and persistence constraints. Deserialization is only one step.

front: What does dependency injection do for an ASP.NET Core handler?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The application registers how required services are created. A handler or class declares its dependencies, and the container supplies them according to those registrations and lifetimes. This separates the work a feature performs from the details of constructing every collaborator.

## A worked example

Register `builder.Services.AddScoped<NoteService>()` before Build. A Minimal API handler can then declare a NoteService parameter, which the framework resolves from services. NoteService must be a real application type with dependencies the container can also resolve.

## Picture it another way

A workshop supplies tools to a worker at the start of a job. The worker can focus on the task instead of manufacturing every tool.

## A common mistake

Do not call BuildServiceProvider ad hoc during normal registration to get another provider. That can create duplicate singleton instances and confusing ownership.

## Try a small exercise

If a handler requests a service whose constructor needs an unregistered dependency, what should you investigate?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Check the registration chain. Every constructor parameter of the requested service must itself be registered with a compatible lifetime. The typical error is InvalidOperationException: "Unable to resolve service for type 'X' while attempting to activate 'Y'", which names the missing dependency X. Register it; the container never invents an implementation.

front: Why should a singleton not directly keep a request-scoped DbContext?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The singleton lives for the whole app, while a scoped service is meant to live for one request. Capturing the scoped dependency stretches it beyond that lifetime and shares non-thread-safe state such as a DbContext across requests. Scope validation, on by default in the Development environment, throws at startup when it detects this; turning it off hides the bug rather than fixing it.

## A worked example

A hosted worker is long-lived. For one job, it can create a service scope, resolve the scoped service there, await the work, and dispose the scope. Alternatively, use an appropriate context factory for the unit of work.

## Picture it another way

Keeping a visitor's temporary desk key forever does not make it a valid building-wide key. The owner and lifetime still matter.

## A common mistake

Do not resolve a scoped service once at startup and reuse it for every background job. Create a valid lifetime boundary for each unit of work.

## Try a small exercise

A BackgroundService needs EF Core for each queued job. Should it normally capture one injected request-scoped context forever?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Resolve a context through a suitable per-job scope or factory, then dispose it after that job. Avoid shared concurrent access to one context.

front: What does the options pattern add to reading unrelated configuration strings everywhere?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It binds a configuration section to one typed class that services request, instead of scattering string-key lookups. Validation can fail at startup instead of mid-request. Pick the interface by update needs: IOptions<T> reads once and never changes, IOptionsSnapshot<T> rereads per request (scoped), and IOptionsMonitor<T> notifies on changes and works in singletons.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOptions<MailOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Mail")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

class MailOptions
{
    [Required] public string Host { get; set; } = "";
}
```

A MailService then takes `IOptions<MailOptions>` and reads `options.Value.Host`. If Mail:Host is missing, the app refuses to start with an OptionsValidationException.

## Picture it another way

A labeled settings sheet groups all the controls for one machine. That is easier to review than loose scraps containing unrelated values.

## A common mistake

Binding an options object does not automatically prove every property is valid. Register the appropriate validation and decide when invalid configuration should fail.

## Try a small exercise

Why might validating essential options at startup be preferable to discovering a missing value during the first real request?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It makes a broken deployment fail clearly before serving misleading partial behavior. The error can be fixed at the configuration boundary instead of appearing as a confusing downstream failure.

front: What do .NET development user secrets protect you from, and what do they not guarantee?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

User secrets help keep development settings out of the project repository. They are a development convenience, not an encrypted production vault. Use appropriate production secret storage and access controls, and avoid logging or returning secret values.

## A worked example

```bash
dotnet user-secrets init
dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:Notes" "Host=localhost;..."
```

The value is stored as plain JSON in your user profile, outside the repo, and is loaded automatically only when the environment is Development. Production gets its credential from the platform's secret store instead.

## Picture it another way

Keeping a spare key out of the public noticeboard helps, but a nearby drawer is not automatically a high-security safe.

## A common mistake

Do not copy the development secrets file into a container image or publish output. The fact that a tool calls them secrets does not make every later handling safe.

## Try a small exercise

Are .NET user secrets a substitute for a production secret manager?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** They help avoid checking development values into source control. Production needs the appropriate protected storage, access policy, rotation, and handling for its environment.

front: What job does an EF Core DbContext perform during a typical request?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A DbContext is one unit of work: it runs queries, tracks the entities they return, and turns changes to those entities into INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements when you call SaveChangesAsync. `AddDbContext` registers it as scoped, so each HTTP request gets its own short-lived instance. It is not thread-safe; Blazor Server components and background services should create their own contexts with `IDbContextFactory`.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDb>(o => o.UseSqlite("Data Source=notes.db"));

app.MapPut("/notes/{id:int}", async (int id, RenameNote dto, AppDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    var note = await db.Notes.FindAsync([id], ct);   // tracked
    if (note is null) return Results.NotFound();
    note.Title = dto.Title;                          // change recorded
    await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);                   // UPDATE sent here
    return Results.NoContent();
});
```

The `AppDb` injected here lives only for this request and is disposed afterwards. It is not an app-wide cache of every user's notes.

## Picture it another way

A clerk opens a worksheet for one transaction, records its edits, submits them, and closes the worksheet. Sharing one worksheet across every customer would mix unrelated work.

## A common mistake

Do not start a second operation on the same context before awaiting the first. Using async does not make DbContext safe for simultaneous calls.

## Try a small exercise

Can two queries safely run in parallel through the same DbContext simply because both use ToListAsync?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** A DbContext supports only one operation at a time. When EF Core detects overlap it throws `InvalidOperationException` ("A second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed"). Await the queries one after another, or give each parallel task its own context.

front: What is an EF Core entity, and why does its key matter?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An entity is a type included in the persistence model. Its key identifies a record so the context and database can distinguish updates and relationships. Not every response object needs to be an entity; public DTOs can describe a narrower external contract.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class Note
{
    public int Id { get; set; }            // primary key by convention
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
}
```

By convention EF Core treats a property named `Id` (or `NoteId`) as the primary key, and for an `int` key the database generates the value on insert. Add `DbSet<Note> Notes` to your context to include the type in the model.

## Picture it another way

A library inventory number distinguishes two copies with the same title. The title alone is not a dependable record identity.

## A common mistake

Do not assume C# types capture every database rule. A non-nullable `string Title` becomes a NOT NULL column, but it gets no length limit unless you add `[MaxLength(100)]` or `HasMaxLength`, and uniqueness needs an explicit unique index. Read the generated migration to see the real schema.

## Try a small exercise

Why is a note's title usually a poor replacement for a stable primary key?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Titles can change or repeat. A stable key lets references and updates identify the same record independently of its current display text.

front: When is AsNoTracking useful in an EF Core query?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Use `AsNoTracking` for read-only queries, such as a list you will serialize straight into a response. EF Core then skips the change-tracking snapshot for each returned entity, which saves memory and CPU. Keep tracking (the default) when you plan to modify the loaded entities and let SaveChanges detect the edits. Queries that project into DTOs with `Select` are not tracked anyway.

## A worked example

```csharp
var notes = await db.Notes
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(n => n.OwnerId == userId)
    .OrderByDescending(n => n.UpdatedAt)
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

The result goes straight into a JSON response, so nothing will be edited and nothing needs tracking.

## Picture it another way

Reading a reference copy does not require opening an editing worksheet for every line. Tracking is useful when changes are part of the intended job.

## A common mistake

Editing an untracked object and calling SaveChanges saves nothing. The quick fix `db.Update(note)` marks every property as modified, including fields the client should not control. Prefer loading a tracked entity and copying only the allowed fields onto it.

## Try a small exercise

Will changing a property on an AsNoTracking result necessarily be saved by a later SaveChanges call?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The context is not tracking that object, so SaveChanges finds nothing to save and returns 0. Load a tracked entity and change it, or attach it deliberately and mark only the properties you intend to update.

front: Why must an EF Core create operation call SaveChangesAsync after Add?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Add tells the context to track an entity as something to insert. SaveChangesAsync sends the pending changes to the database. Until the save completes successfully, the application should not claim that the new row is durably stored.

## A worked example

```csharp
var note = new Note { Title = "Transactions" };
db.Notes.Add(note);                 // state: Added, note.Id is still 0
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);      // INSERT runs, note.Id is now set
```

Until SaveChangesAsync completes, the row exists only in the context's memory. Another connection querying the table will not see it.

## Picture it another way

front: What is the purpose of an EF Core database migration?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A migration is a generated C# file describing how to change the database schema from one model version to the next (add a column, create an index, and so on). Changing an entity class alone never changes the deployed database; you generate a migration, review it, and apply it. Migrations are kept in source control, so every environment can be brought to the same schema version.

## A worked example

```bash
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef   # one-time setup
dotnet ef migrations add AddNoteTitleLimit
dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -o migrate.sql
```

Read the generated `Up` method before applying it. Existing rows longer than the new limit may need cleanup first. A reviewed SQL script (or `dotnet ef database update` in development) then applies the change.

## Picture it another way

Changing a building plan does not move the walls. A migration is the planned construction work that brings the real building into line with the plan.

## A common mistake

Do not casually apply destructive migrations to production or assume every application instance should race to migrate the database at startup. Plan ownership, compatibility, and recovery.

## Try a small exercise

Why inspect an EF Core migration after renaming a property?

<!-- recall:solution -->

EF Core often scaffolds a proper `RenameColumn` for a simple property rename, but when it cannot match the old and new columns (for example, a rename combined with a type or length change) it generates `DropColumn` + `AddColumn`, which deletes that column's data. Inspect the migration and edit it into a rename if needed.

front: What does an N+1 query problem look like in an EF Core web page?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The page loads a list with one query, then triggers another query for each item's related data. As the list grows, database round trips grow too. A deliberate projection, suitable eager loading, or another measured query design can fetch the needed data more efficiently.

## A worked example

```csharp
// N+1: 1 query for orders, then 1 per order (lazy loading enabled)
var orders = await db.Orders.ToListAsync(ct);
foreach (var o in orders) names.Add(o.Customer.Name);

// 1 query: project only what the page shows
var rows = await db.Orders
    .Select(o => new { o.Id, o.Total, CustomerName = o.Customer.Name })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

With 50 orders the first version can send up to 51 queries (one per distinct customer not yet loaded). The projection becomes a single SQL JOIN. Turn on EF Core command logging to count the queries.

## Picture it another way

Walking back to the store for one ingredient at a time is slower than planning a suitable shopping trip.

## A common mistake

Loading every relationship eagerly can create a different performance problem, such as duplicated rows and very large result sets. Fetch what the screen actually needs and measure.

## Try a small exercise

Why might enabling lazy loading hide a performance issue until the list gets large?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Each property access can trigger additional database work. Small examples hide the accumulated round-trip cost; inspect query counts under realistic list sizes.

front: What transaction guarantee does one EF Core SaveChanges call normally provide with a supporting provider?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

With relational providers such as SQL Server, PostgreSQL and SQLite, all changes in one SaveChanges call run inside a single transaction, so they all commit or all roll back. A workflow spanning several SaveChanges calls needs an explicit transaction. No database transaction covers outside effects such as sending an email or calling an HTTP API.

## A worked example

```csharp
await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
order.Status = OrderStatus.Paid;
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
db.AuditRows.Add(new AuditRow { OrderId = order.Id, Action = "paid" });
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
await tx.CommitAsync(ct);   // both saves commit together
```

If the method throws before `CommitAsync`, disposing `tx` rolls both saves back. Sending the receipt email is a separate step; use an outbox table if it must reliably follow the commit.

## Picture it another way

A clerk can submit a bundle of forms to one records office atomically. That does not automatically control a separate courier company delivering a message.

## A common mistake

A transaction alone does not eliminate every race in a read-then-write rule. Isolation, constraints, conditional updates, and retry design may still matter.

## Try a small exercise

If an email was sent and the later database transaction rolls back, is the email automatically unsent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The external effect is outside the database transaction. Design the ordering, durable intent, idempotency, and recovery behavior explicitly.

front: How can an EF Core concurrency token help prevent silently overwriting another edit?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A concurrency token is a column (such as a version number) that EF Core adds to the WHERE clause of UPDATE and DELETE statements, using the value you originally read. If another writer changed the row in the meantime, no row matches and SaveChanges throws `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` instead of silently overwriting. Your code then decides whether to reject, reload, or merge.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class Note
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    [Timestamp] public byte[] Version { get; set; } = []; // SQL Server rowversion
}

try { await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct); }
catch (DbUpdateConcurrencyException) { return Results.Conflict(); }
```

Two users open the same note; the first save changes the version, so the second save fails with a 409 Conflict. `[ConcurrencyCheck]` on an app-managed `int Version` works on any provider.

## Picture it another way

A document checkout slip records the edition you edited. The clerk notices if a newer edition was filed before accepting your changes.

## A common mistake

Do not silently retry every stale edit by overwriting the new data. That can erase the very change the concurrency check was meant to protect.

## Try a small exercise

Is SQL Server rowversion a portable wall-clock timestamp you can assume every EF Core provider supports?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** SQL Server `rowversion` is not a date or time at all: it is an 8-byte counter the database bumps on every change, and it is specific to SQL Server. Other providers use other mechanisms (PostgreSQL via Npgsql commonly uses its `xmin` system column), or you manage a version column yourself with `[ConcurrencyCheck]`.

front: Do validation attributes on a Minimal API DTO always run automatically without configuration?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

No. Minimal APIs ignore attributes like `[Required]` unless you call `builder.Services.AddValidation()` (new in .NET 10; no extra package is needed in a web project). With it registered, invalid input is rejected with a 400 validation Problem Details response before your handler runs. Controllers marked `[ApiController]` do this automatically. Neither replaces authorization or business-rule checks.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddValidation();
var app = builder.Build();

app.MapPost("/notes", (CreateNote input) => Results.Ok(input));

public record CreateNote([Required, MaxLength(100)] string Title);
```

Posting `{ "title": "" }` now returns 400 with `errors.Title`. Remove the `AddValidation()` line and the same request reaches the handler.

## Picture it another way

Writing rules on a form does not guarantee anyone checks them. The processing desk must actually run the checks before accepting the form.

## A common mistake

Do not copy `[ApiController]` assumptions into Minimal APIs, or assume a non-nullable `string` property rejects blank input. Verify the behavior by sending an invalid HTTP request.

## Try a small exercise

How can you verify that a required-title rule really runs in a .NET endpoint?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Send an actual request with a missing or invalid title through the endpoint and assert the documented validation error. A test that only constructs the DTO does not exercise the request validation path.

front: Why use a consistent Problem Details response shape for API failures?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Problem Details (RFC 9457, content type `application/problem+json`) is a standard JSON error shape with fields such as `type`, `title`, `status` and, for validation, `errors`. With one predictable shape, clients can handle every failure the same way instead of parsing ad-hoc messages. ASP.NET Core can produce it for exceptions, empty error status codes and validation failures.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();
var app = builder.Build();
app.UseExceptionHandler();   // unhandled exception -> 500 problem+json
app.UseStatusCodePages();    // bare 404 etc. -> problem+json

app.MapGet("/fail", () => Results.ValidationProblem(
    new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["Title"] = ["Title is required."] }));
```

An unhandled exception now returns a generic 500 body with a `traceId`, while the details go to the server log.

## Picture it another way

A standard repair form has familiar fields for the issue and reference number. Every failure need not arrive in a completely different format.

## A common mistake

Do not include exception stack traces or private database details in public production errors. A standard envelope is still unsafe if you put sensitive content inside it.

## Try a small exercise

Should a production Problem Details response normally expose the database password to explain a connection failure?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Return safe public context and keep necessary diagnostics in protected logs with secrets redacted. The error format does not justify revealing credentials.

front: How are authentication and authorization different in ASP.NET Core?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Authentication establishes an identity from a configured mechanism such as a session cookie or a validated token. Authorization checks whether that identity may perform an action. Knowing a user's name does not establish permission to read every note or administer the app.

## A worked example

```csharp
app.MapGet("/notes/{id:int}", (int id, ClaimsPrincipal user) =>
{
    // Filled in by the authentication handler from a verified cookie or token
    var userId = user.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier);
    // Authorization question: may userId read note id?
    return Results.Ok();
}).RequireAuthorization();
```

Authentication produces `user`. `RequireAuthorization` then rejects anonymous callers (401 with bearer tokens; cookie auth on a page app redirects to the login page instead), and a signed-in user who fails a policy gets 403.

## Picture it another way

Showing a library card identifies a member. It does not make that member a librarian with permission to change everyone's account.

## A common mistake

Do not trust a user ID in a request body as authenticated identity. The server derives trusted identity from its configured, verified authentication process.

## Try a small exercise

If a browser sends `{ "userId": "admin" }`, has it authenticated as an administrator?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** That is untrusted input. Authentication must validate the configured credential or session, and authorization must enforce the relevant permissions.

front: What does an ASP.NET Core authorization policy help an endpoint express?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A policy names a set of requirements that the caller must satisfy. Endpoints can reference it so permission rules are explicit and reusable. A policy can involve roles, claims, or custom requirements, but it only protects routes where the authorization path is actually applied.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("CanExport", p => p.RequireRole("admin"))
    .SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder()
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build());

app.MapGet("/export", ExportNotes).RequireAuthorization("CanExport");
```

The fallback policy covers every endpoint that declares no policy of its own; mark public ones with `AllowAnonymous()`. The export handler must still limit rows to data the caller may see.

## Picture it another way

A venue has a named access rule for backstage. Each backstage entrance must enforce the rule, and a badge's scope still matters.

## A common mistake

Do not treat a claim sent by the browser as trusted just because it has a useful name. Claims are meaningful only within a correctly verified identity and issuance policy.

## Try a small exercise

Does putting RequireAuthorization on one endpoint automatically protect every other endpoint in the app?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** `RequireAuthorization` protects only the endpoint (or route group) it is applied to. To make "signed in" the default, set a fallback policy, then opt public endpoints out with `AllowAnonymous()`, and review new routes against that default.

front: Why must a .NET notes API check ownership or sharing rules after accepting a note ID?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Signing in proves who the caller is, not that they may see note 8. Any user can type another ID into a URL, a bug known as IDOR (insecure direct object reference). So scope each lookup to the verified caller, or run a resource authorization check. Apply the same rule to reads, updates, deletes, downloads and background jobs that touch private records.

## A worked example

```csharp
var userId = user.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier);
var note = await db.Notes.FirstOrDefaultAsync(
    n => n.Id == id && n.OwnerId == userId, ct);
return note is null
    ? Results.NotFound()
    : Results.Ok(new NoteDto(note.Id, note.Title));
```

Another user's note looks exactly like a missing note, so the API does not even confirm it exists. Shared notes need an explicit membership check.

## Picture it another way

A hotel guest can know another room number without being allowed to open its door. The requested number and permission are separate facts.

## A common mistake

Do not accept OwnerId from the request as proof that the caller owns the record. Derive or validate the authority on the server.

## Try a small exercise

A user changes /notes/7 to /notes/8 manually. Which server check should prevent leaking another user's note?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A lookup scoped to the verified caller, such as `WHERE Id = 8 AND OwnerId = <caller's ID from the auth claims>`, returning 404 (or 403) when nothing matches. Route parsing and a successful sign-in alone do not prove access to note 8.

front: A user changes /notes/7 to /notes/8 manually. Which server check should prevent leaking another user's note?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## The answer, explained

A lookup scoped to the verified caller, such as `WHERE Id = 8 AND OwnerId = <caller's ID from the auth claims>`, returning 404 (or 403) when nothing matches. Route parsing and a successful sign-in alone do not prove access to note 8.

### Why this happens

Signing in proves who the caller is, not that they may see note 8. Any user can type another ID into a URL, a bug known as IDOR (insecure direct object reference). So scope each lookup to the verified caller, or run a resource authorization check. Apply the same rule to reads, updates, deletes, downloads and background jobs that touch private records.

## A worked example

```csharp
var userId = user.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier);
var note = await db.Notes.FirstOrDefaultAsync(
    n => n.Id == id && n.OwnerId == userId, ct);
return note is null
    ? Results.NotFound()
    : Results.Ok(new NoteDto(note.Id, note.Title));
```

Another user's note looks exactly like a missing note, so the API does not even confirm it exists. Shared notes need an explicit membership check.

## Picture it another way

A hotel guest can know another room number without being allowed to open its door. The requested number and permission are separate facts.

## A common mistake

Do not accept OwnerId from the request as proof that the caller owns the record. Derive or validate the authority on the server.

## Explain it in your own words

Why must a .NET notes API check ownership or sharing rules after accepting a note ID?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Signing in proves who the caller is, not that they may see note 8. Any user can type another ID into a URL, a bug known as IDOR (insecure direct object reference). So scope each lookup to the verified caller, or run a resource authorization check. Apply the same rule to reads, updates, deletes, downloads and background jobs that touch private records.

front: Why use a maintained identity system instead of inventing password and session handling for a .NET web app?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Identity features involve password verification, recovery, session behavior, lockout, and many edge cases. ASP.NET Core Identity or an appropriate external identity provider can supply established components. You still need correct integration, secure configuration, and application-specific authorization.

## A worked example

ASP.NET Core Identity stores salted PBKDF2 password hashes, supports lockout after failed attempts, and generates password-reset and email-confirmation tokens. You configure it, then add your own rule that each user sees only their notes. Never store plaintext passwords or invent your own token signature format, even in a demo.

## Picture it another way

Use a tested lock mechanism and install it correctly. Buying a reliable lock does not automatically decide who should receive which key.

## A common mistake

Choosing an identity library does not make every endpoint private. Registration, login, recovery, and protected routes all need deliberate behavior and verification.

## Try a small exercise

Does using ASP.NET Core Identity remove the need to check which records a signed-in user may access?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It supplies identity-related capabilities. Your application must still enforce resource and action permissions for its own data.

front: Why do cookie-authenticated .NET forms need the appropriate antiforgery protection?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Browsers can attach your session cookie to a request that another page started. SameSite cookie settings reduce this but do not cover every case, so a malicious page may submit a form to your app that looks legitimate. This is cross-site request forgery (CSRF). An antiforgery token is a secret value embedded in your own form and checked on submit; another site cannot read it, so it cannot forge the request.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddAntiforgery();
var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAntiforgery();

// Form-bound Minimal API endpoints now require a valid token
app.MapPost("/notes/form", ([FromForm] string title) => Results.Ok(title));
```

Razor Pages validate the token on POST automatically, and the form tag helper and Blazor `EditForm` emit it. MVC needs `[ValidateAntiForgeryToken]` or a global filter. A form post without the token is rejected.

## Picture it another way

A familiar courier badge does not prove you approved every form the courier carries. The instruction needs an appropriate authenticity check too.

## A common mistake

Do not assume CORS is a complete antiforgery defense or that every Minimal API request automatically has identical form protections. Verify the actual configured endpoint behavior.

## Try a small exercise

If a request includes a valid session cookie, does that alone prove the user intentionally submitted a change?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Cookies can accompany induced browser requests. Apply the appropriate antiforgery and origin-related defenses for the application's credential and form model.

front: What are the main roles of a controller and a view in ASP.NET Core MVC?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A controller action handles a request, coordinates application work, and chooses a result. A view renders HTML using an appropriate model. Keep important business and persistence rules in suitable services rather than hiding all of them inside markup.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class NotesController(INoteService notes) : Controller
{
    public async Task<IActionResult> Index(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var summaries = await notes.ListForUserAsync(User, ct); // only allowed rows
        return View(summaries);   // renders Views/Notes/Index.cshtml
    }
}
```

The view just loops over `summaries` to render links. It never receives the DbContext, so it cannot decide access rules.

## Picture it another way

A coordinator gathers the right information; a presenter lays it out for the audience. Those responsibilities cooperate without being identical.

## A common mistake

An API controller returning JSON and an MVC controller returning a view have different response purposes. Naming something Controller alone does not determine the client contract.

## Try a small exercise

Should a Razor view independently decide which private database records the caller is allowed to read?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The controller (or a service it calls) should retrieve only records the caller may read, before rendering. The view should receive data the user is already allowed to see and only decide how to display it.

front: How do OnGet and OnPost handlers fit a Razor Pages feature?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The page model can use OnGet to prepare a page and OnPost to process a submitted form. Async variants support awaited work. Bound properties carry input, and the handler checks validity and permissions before making changes.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class CreateModel(AppDb db) : PageModel
{
    [BindProperty] public NoteInput Input { get; set; } = new();

    public void OnGet() { }                 // just show the empty form

    public async Task<IActionResult> OnPostAsync()
    {
        if (!ModelState.IsValid) return Page(); // redisplay with errors
        var userId = User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)!;
        db.Notes.Add(new Note { Title = Input.Title, OwnerId = userId });
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        return RedirectToPage("Index");
    }
}
```

## Picture it another way

A service form has a display step and a submission step. Showing the form should not itself create a record.

## A common mistake

Do not mutate important state merely because OnGet ran. Links, refreshes, and automated retrieval should not unexpectedly submit a form action.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a Razor Pages OnPost handler check ModelState.IsValid before persisting ordinary form input?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It tells you whether model binding and validation succeeded, for example that a `[Required]` title was actually supplied. If it is false, return `Page()` so the form shows its errors instead of saving bad data. The handler still needs authorization and business-rule checks.

front: How does the post-redirect-get pattern help a successful server-rendered form?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

After processing the POST, the server redirects the browser to a GET page. Refreshing that destination then retrieves the page instead of resubmitting the same POST in the usual flow. This improves navigation, but does not provide complete duplicate-action protection by itself.

## A worked example

```csharp
public async Task<IActionResult> OnPostAsync()
{
    if (!ModelState.IsValid) return Page();       // no redirect on errors
    db.Notes.Add(note);
    await db.SaveChangesAsync();
    return RedirectToPage("Details", new { id = note.Id }); // 302 -> GET
}
```

The address bar ends on `/Details?id=42`, so refreshing re-reads the note instead of re-posting the form.

## Picture it another way

After handing in an order, the clerk sends you to the receipt desk. Looking at the receipt again should not place the order again.

## A common mistake

A user can still submit twice, retry after a timeout, or use multiple tabs. Important mutation workflows may need idempotency or uniqueness protections in addition to this navigation pattern.

## Try a small exercise

Does post-redirect-get guarantee that two rapid POST requests cannot create duplicate records?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It changes the browser's normal post-success navigation. Server-side duplicate handling and concurrent request rules remain separate requirements.

Their interactive behavior depends on the rendering mode and hosting configuration. ## A worked example ```razor @* NoteCard.razor *@

@Title

@code { [Parameter] public int Id { get; set; } [Parameter] public string Title { get; set; } = ""; [Parameter] public EventCallback OnDelete { get; set; } } ``` The parent owns the list of notes and passes a handler to `OnDelete`.
