front: How do Interactive Server and Interactive WebAssembly differ in a Blazor Web App?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Interactive Server runs component code on the server and sends UI updates to the browser over a live SignalR connection (a "circuit"). Interactive WebAssembly downloads the .NET runtime and your component code, then runs them in the browser itself. Static server rendering sends plain HTML with no interactivity. You pick a mode per component or app with `@rendermode`.

## A worked example

```razor
@page "/counter"
@rendermode InteractiveServer   @* or InteractiveWebAssembly / InteractiveAuto *@

<button @onclick="() => count++">Clicked @count times</button>

@code { int count; }
```

With Server, each click is a round trip to the server, so a dropped connection stops the page. With WebAssembly, clicks run locally, but data still comes from server APIs that must enforce authorization.

## Picture it another way

One remote control sends each action to a central operator; another device can perform some actions locally. Their connection and download needs differ.

## A common mistake

Do not ship server secrets into WebAssembly assets. Code and configuration delivered to the browser can be inspected by the person running it.

## Try a small exercise

Can a Blazor WebAssembly client safely contain a private database connection string because its source language is C#?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Client-delivered code and settings are inspectable. Keep private credentials and authoritative data access on an appropriate server boundary.

front: Why should a Blazor child component usually notify its parent when parent-owned data needs to change?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The parent is the authoritative owner of that state. Parameters pass data downward, while callbacks communicate intended changes upward. This avoids confusing competing copies and keeps rerendering behavior easier to understand.

## A worked example

```razor
@* NoteEditor.razor *@
<input @bind="draft" />
<button @onclick="() => OnSave.InvokeAsync(draft)">Save</button>

@code {
    [Parameter] public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    [Parameter] public EventCallback<string> OnSave { get; set; }
    string draft = "";
    protected override void OnInitialized() => draft = Title;
}
```

The child edits a local `draft`, never the `Title` parameter. The parent saves, then updates its list only if the save succeeded.

## Picture it another way

A branch office proposes an update to the central register instead of editing an unofficial duplicate and assuming every other office saw it.

## A common mistake

Blindly mutating a parameter inside a child can be overwritten by the parent's next render. Distinguish local draft state from the committed parent value.

## Try a small exercise

If a child edits a private draft, should the parent assume it was durably saved merely because the textbox changed?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** A draft and a saved result are different states. Use an explicit save interaction and communicate the confirmed result or error through the intended contract.

front: What role do EditForm and validation components play in a Blazor form?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

EditForm coordinates an edit model or edit context and submission events. Suitable validation components can show field errors and determine valid submission behavior. Server-side operations must still validate untrusted input and authorize the action, even when the browser displayed a valid form.

## A worked example

```razor
<EditForm Model="input" OnValidSubmit="SaveAsync">
    <DataAnnotationsValidator />
    <InputText @bind-Value="input.Title" />
    <ValidationMessage For="() => input.Title" />
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
</EditForm>
```

`SaveAsync` runs only when the `[Required]`/`[MaxLength]` attributes on `input` pass. This improves the editing experience; the API that finally stores the note must validate and authorize again.

## Picture it another way

Checking a parcel before leaving home is helpful, but the receiving office still verifies that it meets the real acceptance rules.

## A common mistake

Do not assume a disabled submit button or client-side validation protects the backend. A caller can bypass the component and send a request directly.

## Try a small exercise

If a Blazor client reports that its form is valid, can the API skip validation and authorization?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The server must independently enforce the accepted input and permissions. Client checks improve usability but do not establish trust in a remote caller.

EditForm coordinates an edit model or edit context and submission events. Suitable validation components can show field errors and determine valid submission behavior. Server-side operations must still validate untrusted input and authorize the action, even when the browser displayed a valid form.

front: What should a small C# unit test establish about a business rule?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It should set up a meaningful input, run the rule, and check an independently reasoned result. Focus on behavior rather than private helper calls. Boundary and invalid-input cases often reveal more than many nearly identical happy-path examples.

## A worked example

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Title_of_101_chars_is_rejected() =>
    Assert.False(TitleRule.IsValid(new string('a', 101)));

[Fact]
public void Title_of_100_chars_is_accepted() =>
    Assert.True(TitleRule.IsValid(new string('a', 100)));
```

The expected results come from the requirement ("up to 100 characters"), not from calling the implementation again. Also test blank input if it is forbidden.

## Picture it another way

A measuring jig checks whether a part fits a known requirement. Measuring it with the same faulty ruler used to cut it can hide the mistake.

## A common mistake

A unit test that bypasses HTTP does not establish route binding, middleware, authentication, or database-provider behavior. Use the right test level for those boundaries.

## Try a small exercise

If a pure title-validation unit test passes, has it proven that ASP.NET Core invokes that validation during a real POST?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It proves the rule itself under the tested inputs. An endpoint test must verify that the HTTP request path actually runs and responds to that rule.

front: Why use parameterized tests for a C# validation rule?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

They let the same behavioral assertion run against a visible table of inputs and expected results. Frameworks such as xUnit, NUnit, and MSTest provide their own mechanisms. Keep cases readable so a failing input clearly explains the requirement that was violated.

## A worked example

```csharp
[Theory]
[InlineData(0, false)]
[InlineData(1, true)]
[InlineData(100, true)]
[InlineData(101, false)]
public void Quantity_must_be_1_to_100(int qty, bool expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, QuantityRule.IsValid(qty));
```

xUnit runs and reports each row separately, so a failure names the exact input. NUnit uses `[TestCase]` and MSTest uses `[DataRow]` for the same idea.

## Picture it another way

A checklist table applies the same inspection to several representative parts while preserving which part produced each result.

## A common mistake

Avoid a huge generated list that makes the expected behavior impossible to review. Choose clear partitions and boundaries, then add broader property tests where they help.

## Try a small exercise

For a C# rule accepting values from 1 through 10 inclusive, why include both 1 and 10 as accepted test cases?

<!-- recall:solution -->

They establish that the boundaries themselves are included. Tests only using 2 and 9 would not catch accidentally excluding one of the endpoints.

front: What does WebApplicationFactory help an ASP.NET Core integration test exercise?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`WebApplicationFactory<Program>` (package Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing) boots your real app in memory and gives you an `HttpClient` wired to it. Each test request passes through routing, model binding, validation, middleware, auth and your handler, just like production, without opening a network port. Override services in the factory to point at test databases and fake external APIs.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class NotesApiTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Blank_title_returns_400()
    {
        var client = factory.CreateClient();
        var res = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/notes", new { title = "" });
        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest, res.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

In .NET 10 a top-level `Program` is usable from the test project without adding `public partial class Program`.

## Picture it another way

A rehearsal opens the whole service counter to a test customer instead of inspecting only the clerk's private checklist.

## A common mistake

A test host is not a full browser. It does not by itself prove that JavaScript interactions, CSS layout, or client rendering work.

## Try a small exercise

Does a passing HTTP test using WebApplicationFactory prove that a Blazor button is reachable by keyboard in a browser?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** That requires appropriate browser or component interaction checks. The test host verifies the exercised server HTTP behavior, not the whole rendered user experience.

front: Why can EF Core's InMemory provider miss defects in a relational production query?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The InMemory provider is not a database: it does not translate LINQ to SQL and does not enforce relational rules such as unique indexes or foreign keys. A query that works against it can fail or behave differently on SQL Server or PostgreSQL. Use it only for simple logic; test queries and constraints against the real database engine.

## A worked example

In a quick EF Core 10 check, the InMemory provider saved two notes with the same value in a unique `Slug` column, while SQLite rejected them with `DbUpdateException`. Tools such as Testcontainers can start a throwaway PostgreSQL or SQL Server container for tests. SQLite is closer, but still differs from those engines.

## Picture it another way

Practicing on a painted cardboard lock does not establish that a real metal lock will turn the same way.

## A common mistake

Do not call a test a production-query check when it mocks away the query or replaces the provider with different semantics. State which boundary it actually exercises.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a test for a database UNIQUE constraint run against a provider that actually enforces the intended constraint?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Otherwise the test can pass while production fails. For example, EF Core's InMemory provider happily stores duplicate values in a unique-indexed column. Only a database that enforces the constraint can show that your code handles the rejection (a `DbUpdateException`) correctly.

front: How can you narrow down a .NET endpoint that returns an unexpected result?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Start with a reproducible request, including method, path, headers, and safe representative data. Inspect whether the expected endpoint runs, what values were bound, and which response path was taken. Follow one value across boundaries instead of changing unrelated code at random.

## A worked example

A title arrives as blank. First inspect the actual JSON body and bound DTO. Then check validation, mapping, and the saved entity. The first point where the value differs from expectation identifies a smaller area to investigate.

## Picture it another way

Inspect a parcel at each handoff to find the first place its contents changed. The final damaged box alone cannot identify the responsible handoff.

## A common mistake

Do not paste live bearer tokens or private request bodies into public bug reports. Use redacted context and synthetic reproduction data.

## Try a small exercise

If a breakpoint in the intended endpoint is never reached, what should you inspect before its database code?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Check what happens before the handler: the URL and HTTP method (route match), earlier middleware, authentication and authorization (401/403), and model binding (a 400 before the handler runs). Setting the `Microsoft.AspNetCore` log category to `Debug` logs which endpoint matched and why binding failed.

front: How can a TimeProvider dependency help test an expiring web token or deadline?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`TimeProvider` (built into .NET 8+) is an abstraction over "what time is it now?". Production code asks `clock.GetUtcNow()` instead of reading `DateTime.UtcNow`, and the app registers `TimeProvider.System`. Tests pass a `FakeTimeProvider` set to a chosen instant and can move it forward with `Advance`, so expiry boundaries are checked instantly and repeatably.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class TokenService(TimeProvider clock)
{
    public bool IsExpired(DateTimeOffset expiresAt) => clock.GetUtcNow() >= expiresAt;
}

// Test (package Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing)
var clock = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
var svc = new TokenService(clock);
var expiresAt = clock.GetUtcNow().AddMinutes(30);
clock.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(29));
Assert.False(svc.IsExpired(expiresAt));
clock.Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1));
Assert.True(svc.IsExpired(expiresAt));   // exactly at the boundary
```

## Picture it another way

A rehearsal clock can jump to closing time so you can check the closing procedure without waiting all afternoon.

## A common mistake

Do not mix local wall-clock strings with UTC instants without an explicit timezone policy. A testable clock does not repair inconsistent time representations.

## Try a small exercise

Why can reading DateTime.UtcNow directly in many helpers make expiry tests harder to control?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Each helper independently reads the real clock. A shared time abstraction gives the test a consistent chosen instant and makes boundary behavior repeatable.

front: A .NET note API lost whitespace-only title validation after a refactor. What should its regression test assert?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Send the failing request through the relevant endpoint and assert that it produces the documented validation error without creating a row. Keep a valid-title case too so the repair does not reject every request. The test should detect the old broken behavior.

## A worked example

Post `{ "title": "   " }` to an isolated test app and assert a 400 validation response and an unchanged note count. Then post a normal title and assert 201. (With .NET 10 `AddValidation()`, `[Required]` already rejects whitespace-only strings, so the test also guards against someone removing that attribute.)

## Picture it another way

After fixing a leak, add that exact seam to the inspection checklist and check that water still flows through the intended pipe.

## A common mistake

A test that only verifies a validator mock was called may pass while the endpoint ignores its result. Assert the observable outcome and persistence effect.

## Try a small exercise

Why should the whitespace-title regression test check that no note was stored?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Returning an error after already saving would still violate the requirement. The test needs to establish that invalid input cannot create the record, not just that an error message appears.

front: What are three useful limits for a .NET API that lists a growing table?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Limit the number of rows, project only necessary fields, and use an appropriate indexed filtering and ordering strategy. These choices reduce transfer, memory, and database work. Validate client-provided limits and measure the actual query plan under representative data.

## A worked example

```csharp
var page = await db.Notes
    .Where(n => n.OwnerId == userId && (before == null || n.Id < before))
    .OrderByDescending(n => n.Id)
    .Select(n => new NoteSummary(n.Id, n.Title, n.UpdatedAt))
    .Take(Math.Clamp(limit, 1, 50))
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

Rows are limited by `Take` (clamped, so a client cannot ask for a million), columns by `Select`, and `before` is a cursor for the next page. An index on `(OwnerId, Id)` supports the filter and order.

## Picture it another way

A catalog page lists short descriptions, not every warehouse item and its full manual. Fetch detail when the reader asks for it.

## A common mistake

ToListAsync is still capable of loading an enormous result. Async avoids blocking the wait; it does not automatically limit data volume or memory consumption.

## Try a small exercise

Does switching ToList to ToListAsync fix an endpoint that loads a million unnecessary rows?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It changes waiting behavior, not the amount of requested data. Add appropriate filtering, projection, paging, and limits.

front: Why must a cache key for private .NET API data account for the caller's access scope?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A cached response may be reused without rerunning the original computation. If the key ignores ownership or tenant boundaries, one caller can receive another's data. Some responses should not be cached at all; others require explicit scope and invalidation rules.

## A worked example

```csharp
var notes = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"notes:{userId}", async entry =>
{
    entry.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
    return await LoadNotesAsync(userId, ct);
});
```

A key of just `"notes"` would serve the first user's list to everyone. The key must include every input that changes the result: user or tenant, filters and page.

## Picture it another way

A shared coat-check number cannot safely identify every customer's coat. The lookup must preserve the boundary between owners.

## A common mistake

Do not assume IMemoryCache is shared across all server instances. Each process has its own memory cache, which affects consistency and invalidation.

## Try a small exercise

If an app runs on three instances, does removing a key from one instance's IMemoryCache automatically clear the other two?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Each instance has its own in-process `IMemoryCache`. Use a shared distributed cache such as Redis via `IDistributedCache`, or keep expiry times short enough that brief staleness is acceptable. (`HybridCache` adds a shared Redis layer, but each instance still keeps its own in-memory copy until it expires.)

front: What should a .NET outbound HTTP retry policy consider before repeating a request?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Decide which failures are transient, how much total time and load retries may add, and whether the operation is safe to repeat. Use bounded delays with suitable backoff. Resilience libraries supply mechanisms, but your application supplies the operation's correctness rules.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<PaymentsClient>()
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler(o =>
        o.Retry.DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()); // no auto-retry of POST/PUT/DELETE…
```

The standard handler (package Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience) adds bounded retries with exponential backoff, timeouts and a circuit breaker. A read can be retried safely; a create-payment POST should retry only with an idempotency key.

## Picture it another way

Repeating a question can help if the line dropped. Repeating an order can create two deliveries if the first order already reached the shop.

## A common mistake

Independent retry loops at several service layers can multiply the number of attempts. Account for the whole request chain and honor cancellation.

## Try a small exercise

A payment request times out after the server may have processed it. Is a blind repeat automatically safe?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Use the provider's idempotency and outcome-reconciliation contract. A timeout does not prove that the first attempt had no effect.

```csharp
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler(o =>
        o.Retry.DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()); // no auto-retry of POST/PUT/DELETE…
```

The standard handler (package Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience) adds bounded retries with exponential backoff, timeouts and a circuit breaker. A read can be retried safely; a create-payment POST should retry only with an idempotency key.

## Picture it another way

Repeating a question can help if the line dropped. Repeating an order can create two deliveries if the first order already reached the shop.

## A common mistake

Independent retry loops at several service layers can multiply the number of attempts. Account for the whole request chain and honor cancellation.

## Explain it in your own words

What should a .NET outbound HTTP retry policy consider before repeating a request?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Decide which failures are transient, how much total time and load retries may add, and whether the operation is safe to repeat. Use bounded delays with suitable backoff. Resilience libraries supply mechanisms, but your application supplies the operation's correctness rules.

front: Why can a .NET service need different liveness and readiness checks?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Liveness asks whether the process should be considered alive or restarted. Readiness asks whether it should receive traffic now. Startup, required initialization, and dependency conditions can make those answers differ. Design checks around the hosting platform's actual actions.

## A worked example

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck("warmup", () => cacheReady
        ? HealthCheckResult.Healthy() : HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy(), tags: ["ready"]);

app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz/live", new() { Predicate = _ => false });
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz/ready", new() { Predicate = c => c.Tags.Contains("ready") });
```

Liveness runs no checks: it answers 200 if the process can respond. Readiness returns 503 until warm-up finishes, so the load balancer holds traffic without restarting the instance.

## Picture it another way

A restaurant can have staff inside while the kitchen is not ready to accept orders. Turning the lights on and opening for service are different milestones.

## A common mistake

A health endpoint that always returns OK cannot establish that every important dependency or feature works. Define what it checks and keep expensive checks bounded.

## Try a small exercise

Does a 200 response from a basic liveness endpoint prove that an authenticated note save works?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It establishes only the liveness conditions implemented there. Readiness, integration checks, and operation-level monitoring cover other aspects of service behavior.

front: How does publishing a .NET app differ from simply having its source files?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Publishing creates deployable output for the selected target and settings. Framework-dependent output expects a compatible runtime on the host. Self-contained output includes the needed runtime for its target, but the application owner must still rebuild and deploy runtime updates.

## A worked example

```bash
dotnet publish                                   # framework-dependent
dotnet publish -r linux-x64 --self-contained     # bundles the runtime
```

Since .NET 8, `dotnet publish` uses the Release configuration by default, so `-c Release` is optional. Output lands in `bin/Release/net10.0/publish/` (plus a runtime folder when `-r` is set).

## Picture it another way

A recipe is source code; a packaged meal ready for delivery is publish output. The packaging still needs to match its destination.

## A common mistake

Do not assume self-contained means maintenance-free or cross-platform for every output. Runtime identifier, architecture, native dependencies, and patching still matter.

## Try a small exercise

If you deploy framework-dependent .NET output, what must the server normally provide?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A compatible installed runtime, along with the application's required configuration and hosting environment. The SDK used to build the app is not usually required merely to run published output.

front: Why use separate build and runtime stages for a .NET container?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The build stage needs the SDK to restore and publish. The final stage can use a suitable smaller runtime image and copy the publish output. This separates tooling from the running service while keeping the target runtime compatible with the app.

## A worked example

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish -o /app

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Notes.dll"]
```

The final image has no SDK. .NET 8+ images listen on port 8080 by default, and `dotnet publish /t:PublishContainer` can build an image without a Dockerfile.

## Picture it another way

A bakery uses large manufacturing equipment, but the delivered cake does not include the oven. The final package contains what the consumer needs.

## A common mistake

Do not assume deleting a secret in a later image layer removes it from earlier layers. Keep secrets out of the build context and image history through the appropriate secret mechanisms.

## Try a small exercise

Why does an ASP.NET Core app commonly need an ASP.NET runtime image rather than only the basic .NET runtime image?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A framework-dependent web app relies on the ASP.NET Core shared framework as well as the .NET runtime. Choose an image that supplies the application's actual framework requirements.

front: What should a .NET background worker consider when the host is shutting down?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Observe the shutdown signal, stop accepting new work as appropriate, and complete or safely release in-progress work within the allowed time. Important jobs need recovery if the process ends before completion. A graceful-stop opportunity is useful but not guaranteed for every failure.

## A worked example

```csharp
public class QueueWorker(IJobQueue queue) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            var job = await queue.DequeueAsync(stoppingToken);
            await job.RunAsync(stoppingToken);
            await queue.AckAsync(job);   // acknowledge only after success
        }
    }
}
```

`stoppingToken` is cancelled as soon as shutdown begins; the host then waits up to 30 seconds by default (`HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout`) for the worker to finish. An unacknowledged job goes back to the queue for another worker, so jobs must be safe to run twice.

## Picture it another way

At closing time, stop taking new orders and account for each unfinished ticket. A fire alarm may still force an earlier exit.

## A common mistake

Do not rely on a finally block as the only durability strategy. Abrupt termination, machine failure, and forced shutdown can prevent cleanup from completing.

## Try a small exercise

Does a graceful-shutdown handler guarantee that every queued job survives a power failure?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Durable storage and recoverable processing handle abrupt failure. Graceful shutdown only helps when the process receives time to cooperate.

front: How can logs, metrics, and traces complement each other in a .NET service?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Metrics show aggregate trends such as error rates and latency. Logs record specific events and context. Traces connect work across operations and services. Correlation lets you move from a detected problem to an example request and its relevant path.

## A worked example

```csharp
logger.LogWarning("Note save failed for {NoteId} after {ElapsedMs} ms", id, elapsed);
```

A rising error-rate metric shows that saves are failing. A trace (carrying a trace ID across services) shows the time going into one dependency call. Structured logs like the one above, filtered by that trace ID, give the specific failure. Log IDs, not note bodies or tokens.

## Picture it another way

A dashboard shows traffic congestion, a route map shows the affected journey, and an incident note explains one blockage.

## A common mistake

Averages can hide slow experiences for some users. Use appropriate distributions and avoid unbounded metric labels such as unique request IDs that create excessive cardinality.

## Try a small exercise

Why is a unique request ID often useful in logs but a poor label for an aggregate metric?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It helps correlate a particular event, but each unique metric label creates another time series. High-cardinality labels can make metrics expensive and hard to use.

front: What sequence should a .NET create-note endpoint establish before returning a created response?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Bind the allowed request, validate its content, establish the caller's rights, construct the entity with server-owned fields, and await persistence. Then return an appropriate public response and location. Each step establishes something the next step relies on.

## A worked example

```csharp
app.MapPost("/notes", async (CreateNote input, ClaimsPrincipal user, AppDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    var note = new Note
    {
        Title = input.Title.Trim(),                               // client field
        OwnerId = user.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)!, // server-owned
        CreatedAt = DateTime.UtcNow                               // server-owned
    };
    db.Notes.Add(note);
    await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    return Results.Created($"/notes/{note.Id}", new NoteDto(note.Id, note.Title));
}).RequireAuthorization();
```

`AddValidation()` rejects a bad `CreateNote` before this runs. A failed save throws, so no 201 is ever sent for a note that was not stored.

## Picture it another way

An official receipt is issued after the records office accepts a valid form, not while the form is still being checked.

## A common mistake

Do not allow the client to submit arbitrary internal entity fields or return a database object containing information outside the public API contract.

## Try a small exercise

Should a create-note response claim a saved ID before the awaited persistence step completes successfully?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Report completed creation only after its required save succeeds. If the design merely accepts a background job, use a distinct documented job-status contract.

front: What should a .NET note-edit flow do when the stored note changed after the user opened it?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Detect the stale version when the feature requires conflict protection, then give a defined outcome such as a conflict response and a reload or merge path. Preserve the user's draft where practical. Silently overwriting the newer data can lose another person's work.

## A worked example

```csharp
var note = await db.Notes.FirstOrDefaultAsync(n => n.Id == id && n.OwnerId == userId, ct);
if (note is null) return Results.NotFound();
db.Entry(note).Property(n => n.Version).OriginalValue = input.Version; // version the user read
note.Title = input.Title;
note.Version++;                   // [ConcurrencyCheck] int Version
try { await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct); }
catch (DbUpdateConcurrencyException) { return Results.Conflict(); }
return Results.NoContent();
```

Setting `OriginalValue` makes EF check the client's version, not the one just loaded. On 409 the UI keeps the draft and asks the user to reconcile.

## Picture it another way

Two editors submit changes to the same manuscript edition. The publisher needs to notice that the edition changed rather than blindly replacing the latest draft.

## A common mistake

A disabled Save button only reduces duplicate clicks in one page. It does not coordinate other tabs, other users, or another server instance.

## Try a small exercise

Why keep the unsaved draft visible after an edit conflict instead of clearing the form?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The draft may contain valuable work the user needs to compare or reapply. A conflict means the base version is stale, not that the user's intended changes should be discarded.

front: What decisions belong in a .NET delete-note endpoint contract?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Define who may delete the record, whether deletion is permanent or logical, what happens to related data, and the response when the record is already absent. Clients may retry a request after losing its response, so repeated attempts need an understandable policy.

## A worked example

```csharp
var deleted = await db.Notes
    .Where(n => n.Id == id && n.OwnerId == userId)
    .ExecuteDeleteAsync(ct);   // one DELETE statement, returns row count
return deleted == 0 ? Results.NotFound() : Results.NoContent();
```

The first call returns 204; a retry returns 404, yet the end state is the same. For soft delete, set an `IsDeleted` flag and add `HasQueryFilter(n => !n.IsDeleted)` so normal queries skip deleted rows.

## Picture it another way

Canceling a reservation needs a policy for both the first request and a caller asking again because they never received the confirmation.

## A common mistake

Soft deletion is not automatically privacy erasure or complete protection from accidental exposure. Retention, backups, access rules, and all query paths still need deliberate behavior.

## Try a small exercise

Does returning a different status for an already-deleted record necessarily mean DELETE cannot be idempotent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Idempotency (RFC 9110) is about the effect on the server: after one DELETE or five, the note is gone. A first 204 followed by 404 on retry is still idempotent. Document which statuses callers should expect.

front: What should a .NET note-search feature define before adding a database filter?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Specify which fields are searchable, how case and whitespace are handled, allowed query length, access scope, ordering, and result limits. Database collation and search capabilities affect behavior and performance. A simple C# string method does not automatically express every database search requirement.

## A worked example

```csharp
var q = query.Trim();
if (q.Length is 0 or > 100) return Results.BadRequest();
var hits = await db.Notes
    .Where(n => n.OwnerId == userId && EF.Functions.Like(n.Title, $"%{q}%"))
    .OrderByDescending(n => n.UpdatedAt)
    .Take(20)
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

The query stays scoped to the caller and bounded. Whether it is case-insensitive depends on the database: SQL Server's default collation is, PostgreSQL is not (use `EF.Functions.ILike` with Npgsql).

## Picture it another way

A catalog search needs rules for spelling and categories before a clerk can reliably interpret every request.

## A common mistake

Do not load every private note into memory merely to apply an unrestricted contains search. Keep the access boundary and workload limits intact.

## Try a small exercise

Why test case-insensitive note search against the production database provider rather than only a C# list?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Database collation and SQL translation decide the matching rules, and they can differ from C#. For example, on SQLite EF Core translates `Title.Contains("hello")` to `instr()`, which is case-sensitive, while `LIKE` is case-insensitive for ASCII. Only the real provider shows what users will get.

front: What extra work does adding attachments introduce to a .NET notes app?
back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An upload needs size and type policy, controlled storage naming, access checks, and a defined relationship to its note. File storage and database metadata may fail independently, so design cleanup and recovery. Download routes must enforce access as carefully as the note routes.

## A worked example

```csharp
if (file.Length > 5_000_000) return Results.BadRequest("Max 5 MB");
var storedName = Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N");          // never the client name
await using var stream = File.Create(Path.Combine(uploadRoot, storedName));
await file.CopyToAsync(stream, ct);
db.Attachments.Add(new Attachment { NoteId = note.Id, StoredName = storedName,
    DisplayName = file.FileName });
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
```
